We apply this method to a brown dwarf orbiting HD 212771, which exhibits a large radius relative to its short 2.7-Gigawatt stellar luminosity. While the system's extended debris disk and dust production suggest recent planet-disk interactions, we find that a single planet cannot account for all dynamical effects, particularly at periastron. To address this, we propose a 3:1 orbital resonance between two planets. Our analysis indicates that these planets must be more extended than standard models predict, with the inner planet likely possessing a quadrupole moment at least 10 times greater than predicted by the Adams & Lubow 2010 model. Furthermore, both planets require masses exceeding those of Jupiter, with the outer planet being the more massive of the two. This suggests an alternative mechanism for radius inflation, such as the accumulation of energy from tidal interactions within the disk. This study represents the first application of a 3:1 resonance to constrain the properties of extended planets or brown stars. The specific requirements for these extended structures imply that orbital resonance can be detected through future direct imaging and astrometry missions. Additionally, this approach offers a novel method to distinguish between brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars. Finally, our proposed 3:1 resonance scenario may offer a partial explanation for recent debris disk observations. We also explore implications for other brown dwarf and planetary systems, as well as theoretical frameworks for explaining extended radii. Given that HD 212771 is a nearby target, it serves as an ideal candidate for testing these hypotheses. Furthermore, the system may provide critical data to resolve ongoing debates regarding the formation and evolution of brown dwarfs and extended objects. In this context, we propose that the most promising strategy involves combining direct imaging with high-precision astrometry to detect orbital resonances. This paper outlines the current status of the silicon tracker, which is organized into four systems: the Vertex Point Insert (VPI), the Backward Tracking System (BTS), the Central Tracking System (CTS), and the Forward Tracking System (FTS). The VPI, positioned at the interaction point, comprises 12 layers of planar silicon microstrip sensors with up to 100% active sensor coverage, a 150 µm silicon thickness, and a digital readout capable of handling up to 40 MHz. Tracking coverage extends from 1.3 to 7 X0 in the CTS and reaches down to 2.5 X0 in the FTS; these outer layers utilize 3D silicon sensors ranging from 250 to 350 µm in thickness, paired with an electronic system designed for a maximum clock frequency of 200 MHz. Backup plans for the outermost layers include 350 µm thick silicon as well as GEM and MEDITECH technologies. For the BTS, an optical design currently under development will be presented. To achieve the specified performance objectives, the VPI demands an irradiation tolerance of at least 10 Mrad, the BTS and CTS require a tolerance of 5 Mrad, and the FTS must withstand at least 2.5 Mrad. This paper will discuss the current status of the detector, its backup options, and the progress toward full scale construction. By 2024, a complete detector with a total cost of approximately 100M$ is anticipated to be ready for scale production. Additionally, the ILC's scale R&D and irradiation tests will offer valuable insights for future high-energy physics (HEP) detectors. It is expected to be installed at the ILC by 2027 and operated with a peak rate of 40 MHz. A significant number of institutions are currently participating in the scale construction and will be ready to support the ILC by 2024. This contribution will also highlight the significant progress made toward this goal. Finally, the scenario for scale production and installation at the ILC will be described, along with the anticipated schedule and specific tasks for the detector. This paper will serve as a reference for future developments and for irradiation tests

Our results indicate that silica, despite being a brittle material, exhibits significant plasticity, characterized by the gradual formation of dislocations along Si-O bonds and SiO$_4$ tetrahedra as the stress increases. Notably, the stress required for this atomic rearrangement is nearly independent of the wire's cross-sectional diameter. This stress creates a "shear band" with reduced stiffness compared to the bulk material; within this band, silica undergoes atomic rearrangement without any phase transition. This same shear band is hypothesized to serve as the precursor to the macroscopic fracture observed in silica. Our findings offer valuable insights into the fracture and plasticity mechanisms of silica. Additionally, the initial stages of Si-O bond stretching within SiO$_4$ tetrahedra in silica display Raman-active vibrational modes that closely resemble those of crystalline silicon. Given the similarity in these vibrational characteristics, our results may also clarify the fracture and plasticity behaviors of silicon nanostructures. Finally, the mechanisms underlying the electronic properties of silica, which are also analogous to those of crystalline silicon, are briefly discussed. These insights may contribute to advancing the development of silica-based optoelectronic devices. (Published as Applied Physics Letters 112, 111903, 2018) [P. Sharma and A. R. Gullikson] P. Microscope (STM) at the Max-Planck Institute for Solid State Research aimed to observe quantum Hall edge states both spatially and temporally. While spatial imaging of these states at zero temperature has been accomplished in previous studies, no experimental evidence for their dynamic behavior currently exists. This work introduces a novel experimental setup designed to detect the time-dependent dynamics of these edge states. The methodology involves applying a voltage to a conductive tip, which generates a temperature field around the tip via Joule heating. The resulting thermal diffusion of electrons in the edge states is then scanned and imaged via STM to analyze the dynamics. The anticipated outcome is the capture of real-time edge state behavior, offering insights that could have transformative potential for topological quantum computing. This research was conducted under the guidance of Prof. M. B\"{u}ttiker and Prof. D. Fein. (ID: 2422)

Yet, this expansion introduces specific challenges, as data within the archive is no longer the cleanest resource. This paper investigates data from the IsabelleAFP, the section of the archive containing theories, and highlights both classical and non-obvious statistical analyses applicable to such data. Through three representative case studies, we examine the growth rates of theories over time, compare them across different ISAFP projects, and explore future directions. These cases highlight both the heterogeneity of theories and their authors, as well as potential analyses applicable to large collections of theorem proofs. In each instance, we present initial findings, begin addressing open questions, and demonstrate how such analyses can aid authors in producing high-quality theories for the archive. We believe this approach can be extended to many other statistical inquiries within ISAFP. Furthermore, we provide a new library of formalized analyses of the ISAFP, accessible at https://isabelle.in.tum.ch/documentation/afp-archives.html, designed to facilitate further statistical work. Finally, we highlight statistical analyses of proof collections beyond ISAFP and outline future research paths. Ultimately, we propose that these analyses are most valuable when integrated into interactive workflows.

Furthermore, we emphasize that these analyses yield the most value when incorporated into interactive workflows. Finally, we present three non-trivial case studies illustrating how these statistical approaches can enhance the quality of theories within the archive. This paper demonstrates that by distinguishing between immediate and delayed fixed points, the delayed ones yield operational semantics equivalent to big-step. Furthermore, we find that big-step recursion and delayed small-step fixed points distribute over one another, while small-step semantics using immediate fixed points distribute over big-step semantics only if the latter incorporate guard induction. Although our primary focus is on call-by-name, these results extend to call-by-value, where additional exercises regarding environments and substitutions maintain equivalence. Additionally, we illustrate that delayed fixed points facilitate the derivation of convergence criteria necessary for small-step semantics to remain well-defined and potentially terminate. Finally, we briefly examine semantics based on call-by-name continuation-passing transformation, proving that small-step delayed fixed points correspond to big-step semantics in this context as well. This correspondence enables the straightforward definition of big-call-by-name semantics from values-to-terms semantics without requiring intricate direct reasoning. Additionally, we observe that whenever small-step delayed fixed points align with big-step semantics, the latter are equipped with a finitely-algebraic framework facilitating the derivation of convergence criteria. This work is primarily grounded in PCF but also addresses the differentiation of strict and non-deterministic variables, a concept applicable to other programming language semantics. Additionally, we present the differentiation operator within a weakly-normalizing framework, a scenario not previously addressed in the literature. Our results indicate that the free-free signal from halo dark matter will be so overwhelmingly dominant that it will completely obscure any potential free-free contribution from the LMC, rendering its detection unfeasible. Furthermore, we find that current upper limits on annihilation cross-sections derived from millicomab-level free-free observations of the Galactic halo will erroneously extend into the energy regime where the halo's own free-free emission is suppressed by low dark matter velocity temperatures. This implies that such measurements offer no actual constraint on the LMC's free-free signal. Finally, we demonstrate that the free-free emission from LMC halo dark matter could be detectable under specific conditions and for particular dark matter annihilation channels. We show that for a annihilation cross-section close to the upper limit established by Galactic halo observations, the LMC's free-free signal at 30 GHz could reach approximately 10 mW m$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$, reaching up to several tens of mW m$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$ for the $\sigma v\propto s$ channel at 6 GHz. Our analysis indicates that only radio telescopes with beams smaller than 10$^{-2}$ degrees can achieve the sensitivity required to place meaningful limits on this signal. We propose that the LMC presents a promising target for future radio observations aimed at constraining dark matter annihilation cross-sections, provided that systematic uncertainties—including both instrumental and astrophysical factors—are adequately controlled. The interaction between light and quantum matter can generate extraordinary optical phenomena, driving both fundamental research and practical advancements. Atomic vapor cells serve as ideal platforms for exploring quantum optics, quantum gases, and atomic physics. Although optical glass is widely used in optical systems, its interaction with light is typically limited to linear dispersion and absorption. In this study, we demonstrate that atomic vapor cells can exhibit nonlinear optical effects by integrating quantum interference with spatially inhomogeneous light fields. By introducing a standing wave laser field, we observed that a control of out-of-resonance $\Lambda$-system atomic vapor induces spatially inhomogeneous phase modulation in a probe field. This approach enables the generation of subwavelength vortices with high efficiency and tunability, achieving a Toley-Carrier phase distribution. By balancing two competing effects—the anomalous optical drag effect and the Sisyphus-like potential—we demonstrated the generation of a phase plate. This method offers a novel alternative for generating optical vortices, a process termed "atomic imprinting." Such an atomic vapor cell functioning as a phase plate holds great potential for applications in quantum optics and quantum communication.****

This problem involves $k$ players who know a subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$, where a product of their inputs results in a vector with a single non-zero entry at index $S$, and they must output a binary vector of length $n$ that is disjoint from their own input. It is established that $D_z$ for $k$ players and $n$ elements can be reduced to a instance of standard set disjointness with a slightly increased element count, implying that solving it for any constant $k$ and $n$ provides insight into the general case. However, the known reduction increases the size $n$ exponentially with $k$, leaving it uncertain whether a constant $k$ implies $n$ is bounded by a polynomial in $k$. We introduce a straightforward $O(k)$-player strategy for $D_z$ with $n$ elements that requires $m = \Omega(\min\{n, 2^{k}/m\})$ bits of communication. We demonstrate that this construction is optimal up to constant factors. This finding indicates that a superlinear increase in $n$ relative to $k$ is inherent, even under the assumption that constant-size instances can be solved efficiently. Consequently, this offers concrete evidence supporting the view that understanding the complexity of disjointness promises with polynomially bounded sizes is essential for fully comprehending the difficulty of the original set disjointness problem. Additionally, our construction yields similar insights for equality and identity problems. Finally, we present the most efficient known lower bounds for promises involving sublinear $n$ in the $D_z$ problem, showing that existing exponential lower bounds established by Chattopadhyay, Li, Shi, Venkat, and Zhu are likely tight. We also provide lower bounds for equality and identity problems, notably establishing that any $k$-player protocol for equality on $n$ elements with $O(n/k)$ communication must fail on an input at least $1 - \Omega(k^{-1/3})$ of the time. We conjecture that this bound is tight. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique for deriving lower bounds based on communication-query complexity, which may have broader applications. We illustrate the utility of this approach by examining problems with repeated inputs, where the reduction from standard set disjointness is straightforward, yielding lower bounds previously unknown. Specifically, we derive a superlinear lower bound, confirming a conjecture by Braverman

Because these involve functions as variables, they are specifically known as optimal control problems or distributed parameter problems. Solving them typically requires determining both the control variables and the solutions to the governing differential equations. This paper introduces a novel family of implicit algorithms designed to address such issues. These methods are derived from time-discrete implicit schemes, where the finite-difference approximation of the differential equations is replaced by their actual solution. Implemented at their finest resolution, these algorithms function as Petviorskii-type methods for optimization, featuring significantly simplified non-linear systems of equations that must be resolved at every iteration compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, these implicit schemes can also be interpreted as finite-element algorithms. Their numerical accuracy matches that of explicit implicit schemes, as demonstrated by multiple test cases. Notably, these algorithms are highly efficient for parallel computing, making them ideal for distributed parameter problems. This article presents and analyzes these Petviorskii-type implicit algorithms for distributed parameter problems. It is shown that the algorithms retain all standard properties, including convergence rates consistent with their time-discrete analogues. Key innovations include the ability to address differential equations with non-linear boundary conditions and the internal parallelism inherent to the imaging formulation. The manuscript begins with an overview of existing functional optimization solution methods, followed by the introduction and analysis of the new algorithms, and concludes with an examination of numerical examples. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any non-Lattès bicritical rational map $f$, the group of deck transformations for the $n$-th iterate, $\mathcal{D}_n(f)$, is either the trivial group or, for each prime $p$, is either trivial or isomorphic to one of the following: $\mathbb{Z}_p$, $\mathbb{Z}_p^2$, or $\mathbb{Z}_p^k$ where $k$ takes the value $\frac{p+2}{2}$, $\frac{p+1}{2}$, or $\frac{p-2}{2}$. The argument relies on analyzing the groups of automorphisms of rational maps that serve as components of the iterates for a specific subset of rational maps within $\mathcal{D}_n(f)$. We label this collection the set of {\em bicritical rational normal maps}, a class that encompasses nearly all post-critically finite bicritical rational maps. The primary tools for this analysis are a polynomial-time algorithm and an explicit classification regarding the groups of automorphisms for maps in this broader category. Furthermore, we conjecture that the prime $p$ appearing in our main theorem is always a prime number of the form $2^k+1$. Finally, we examine the groups of deck transformations for bicritical Lattès maps and conclude by listing several open questions. \bigskip. We term this approach the dual view of delta lenses and demonstrate that it simplifies the analysis of various delta lens properties. For example, we show that the definitions of conductive and reversible delta lenses become nearly identical in the dual view, differing only through dual property conditions. is modeling nonlinear stochastic interactions within rarefied gases. The Boltzmann equation represents an idealized continuum model for such gases, yet it remains computationally prohibitive to simulate across a wide range of physical parameters. The lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE) offers a more practical alternative, providing efficient and accurate simulations for specific parameters in both rarefied and continuum regimes. Parameters that are more challenging to simulate can be addressed using a moment closure method known as entropic weighting, which is applicable to specific systems of equations. However, it is not certain whether the specific system used in this study falls within the scope of the entropic weighting regime. Therefore, this work introduces a modified system by modifying one term in a way that preserves physical consistency, thereby enabling the simulation of a broader parameter range. The numerical validity of the approach is confirmed by comparing results with those from Direct Simulation Monte-Carlo (DSMC) and Finite Volume-2N methods. Additionally, the computational efficiency of the proposed model is evaluated against DSML and FV-2N. Closure strategies are also discussed, including the utilization of a pressure equilibrium distribution to calculate macroscopic variables and the integration of entropy weighting. Finally, various physical parameters are investigated using the LBE framework. These parameters include Knudsen numbers, Mach numbers, and Reynolds numbers, which are examined across different flow configurations, such as Poiseuille and Rayleigh-Bénard convection flows. Furthermore, the thermal Knudsen number, representing another parameter of interest, is also considered. Across all these scenarios, the proposed model demonstrates computational performance consistent with theoretical predictions while maintaining accuracy comparable to DSMC. These findings indicate that the model is particularly well-suited for kinetic simulations where accuracy is critical. Furthermore, the proposed model is expected to be extendable to systems with multiple gas components and higher dimensions. These attributes make the model a strong candidate for inclusion in Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and other turbulence modeling applications. These applications may require higher Knudsen numbers than currently achievable with existing lattice Boltzmann models. Consequently, the proposed approach is anticipated to be valuable for investigating various physical parameters in turbulence and rarefied gas flow contexts. Furthermore, the model is also relevant for molecular beam type problems, which are otherwise difficult to simulate using current LBE methods. Overall, the model offers a promising path forward for addressing these complex challenges. Bejarano:2021hja} conducted a search for new heavy particles that couple to quarks and leptons with very small branching fractions, achieving sensitivity to levels as low as $10^{-5}$, well beyond the two standard weak parameters. Utilizing all available LHC data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with a dataset of 40.2 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the ATLAS detector, the ATLAS Collaboration has now demonstrated a high-purity method for this type of search within the third generation of fermions. We examine a scenario featuring a heavy vector boson that couples to bottom and muon quarks and leptons, respectively, which is highly relevant for studying flavor physics. In this framework, an $b \to \mu X$ signature arises from the decay of this heavy vector boson. Our results show that a large portion of the parameter space can be excluded at 95% confidence level. Furthermore, we assess the impact of upcoming LHC data on this search. We conclude by discussing broader applications of our method to other theories and suggesting extensions to include a second generation of leptons and quarks. This work appears as a Rapid Communication in Phys. Rev. Lett. (PRL). Additionally, it will be presented at the 36th International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP2022) as P040 and the 13th International Workshop on Tau Lepton Physics (TWLEP2022) as PPT025. The code is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/ATLAS-p3/genZ}. Any queries or comments should be directed to \url{atlas-p3-search@list.cern.int}. \bibliography{atlas-p3-search.bib}

Although this principle governs the dynamics of cold Fermi gases in optical lattices, its exact contribution remains difficult to quantify. We demonstrate that a simple quantum Zeno trap, created by locally inhibiting the tunneling of cold $^6$Li atoms within a one-dimensional optical lattice, effectively illustrates the nature of this exclusion principle. While a common strategy involves training a primary model under normal lighting and developing a secondary one for specific adverse scenarios—a method known as domain adaptation—this paper investigates a fully data-driven approach using domain randomization. Domain randomization deliberately trains the neural network across a spectrum of lighting conditions to inherently produce diverse representations. To ensure the efficacy of this framework, we examine various flake types (Gaussian, uniform, etc.), training datasets (ObjectID, TCIA), and evaluation setups (learning curves, out-of-distribution testing). Our findings indicate that image augmentation is inadequate for learning robust representations due to its reliance on fixed, linear transformations that do not interact complexly with neural networks. In contrast, we observe that training on data transformed by a non-linear function, such as a Gaussian flake, consistently yields networks that generalize robustly to novel distributions without further tuning, often surpassing the accuracy of uncorrupted training. This behavior is corroborated by the activation space of these networks, which exhibits greater separability of high-level features compared to networks trained solely on clean images. Furthermore, the representation power of these robust networks is maintained even when corrupted images are mixed with clean ones, provided a sufficient number of damaged samples is included. These results underscore the critical role of corrupted learning as a viable alternative to traditional clean-image training. Although both crystal types exhibit identical hysteresis curves along the *ab*-plane diagonal and the $c$ axis, distinct anisotropic magnetization patterns emerge within the basal plane when comparing the two crystal structures. We attribute these findings to a complex magnetization configuration in the polycrystalline sample, specifically involving alternating out-of-plane and in-plane in-plane-ordered domains. Our results indicate that the in-plane-ordered domains possess lower magnetic entropy, suggesting they are the thermodynamically favored state at equilibrium. These unexpected *ab*-plane characteristics in the in-plane-ordered domains may also explain the unusual low-temperature in-plane magnetization behavior observed in this material family. Finally, we discuss the potential for equi-energy, low-entropy out-of-plane-ordered domains to drive the in-plane phase transitions previously reported for $\text{NdMn}_6\text{Ge}_6$. This study underscores the necessity of using single-crystalline samples to accurately determine which magnetization states represent equilibrium states. Furthermore, the observed phase transition from an out-of-plane to an in-plane ordered state at 240 K may offer insights into the origin of the previously reported 240 K phonon anomaly detected by high-resolution x-ray diffraction in related compounds. We also examine the atypical equi-energy phase transition in this hexagonal compound and its connection to equi-entropy transitions in body-centered cubic (BCC) compounds, a phenomenon previously noted only in other rare-earth hexagonal compounds like $\text{HoMn}_6\text{Ge}_6$ and $\text{SmMn}_6\text{Ge}_6$. This work may facilitate the discovery of additional hexagonal compounds exhibiting both types of phase transitions. Additionally, the identified phonon anomaly may offer clues for identifying hexagonal compounds with out-of-plane ordered magnetization, potentially facilitating the discovery of various types of low-entropy magnetization states in hexagonal compounds. We also discuss how an equi-entropy low-entropy in-plane-ordered state might function as a potential equivalent to a double well potential in spintronics. Finally, the complex phase transition at 240 K in $\text{NdMn}_6\text{Ge}_6$ may serve as an excellent model system for further investigation into equilibrium magnetic states.

We demonstrate that when data limitations force the inclusion of data-generating process (DGP) assumptions to derive a closed-form expression for SC bias, the resulting bias is actually contingent upon significantly fewer assumptions than previously thought. We derive the optimal assumption that minimizes SC bias under the assumption of correct DGP pinning and offer empirical guidance for selecting this assumption when the DGP is uncertain. Furthermore, we illustrate how to integrate multiple assumptions—whether pinned or optimal—to generate a more robust synthetic control. Finally, our findings are applied to re-estimate the Laffer curve using Oil Crisis and Laffer (1980) data. Our results indicate that our empirical approach to determining the optimal assumption leads to a substantially lower and more persuasive upper bound for the Laffer curve compared to the original study. The accompanying appendix contains additional proofs, simulations, and empirical examples. (Jel Codes: C26, H26)

The second mechanism, which can be ignored when an system is isolated or dominated by collisions, becomes critical in collisionless environments. It functions as an entropy-transfer process, moving plasma entropy from smaller scales to larger ones in a reverse direction compared to energy, before depositing the entropy at the scales where kinetic effects become significant. This flow of plasma entropy to larger scales enhances the entropy production rate within the plasma, an effect that grows more pronounced as collisions become less frequent. Furthermore, this interaction between mechanisms can be viewed as a specific instance of the general problem of connecting different scales through a cross-diffusion process. The study also examines the conditions required for this problem to ensure stability. Finally, a mathematical model utilizing two equations—one for kinetic energy and one for entropy—is employed to illustrate these concepts. By applying the Laplace transform to the equation set, the behavior of the transformed functions was analyzed based on the coefficients of the cross-diffusion processes. These results align with the earlier conclusions regarding the problem at hand. Additionally, it was determined that the model's coefficients allow for the control of the entropy generation rate within the fluid. These charge defects are characterized by elements of a continuous $U(1)$ group. Leveraging this framework, we demonstrate an analog of Goldstone's theorem applicable to such non-invertible symmetries and discuss potential implications for string theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that allowing for a $2\pi$ shift in this coupling necessitates the inclusion of flux on the worldsheet, thereby confirming a phenomenon analogous to Schwinger pair production. This serves as an additional verification of the consistency requirements between global anomalies and axion-like couplings. Furthermore, by demanding consistency between conditions for string and flux condensation, we uncover an infinite set of non-invertible constraints, expressed via discrete sine-Gordon type charges, that restrict the allowed values for axion couplings. We demonstrate that a directed graph admits a lexicographic embedding into a transitive tournament precisely when it is semi-transitive, and we provide a computable characterization for this property. Leveraging this embedding, we establish that deciding whether a directed graph is semi-transitive is equivalent to deciding 3-SAT, with the transitive tournament serving as the target structure. Furthermore, within the transitive tournament, both edge packing and edge covering are computable in linear time, implying these issues are as resolvable as determining semi-transitivity. Finally, if the Pigeonhole Principle is accepted as independent of ZFC, then lexicographic embeddings into transitive tournaments exist exactly when PSPACE is included in NP, meaning the problem requires exponential time unless P=NP. Specifically, given a transitive tournament $T$ and a collection of transitive tournaments $\mathcal{T}=\{T_1,\ldots,T_m\}$, the directed Ramsey-Tur\'an number $TRT(n, T, \mathcal{T})$ represents the minimum $k$ such that every $k$-coloring of the directed edges of the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices contains either a monochromatic copy of $T$ or a copy of some $T_i$ within its corresponding color class. The transitive tournament $T$ itself constitutes a subgraph of $TRT(n, T, \mathcal{T})$ if and only if $TRT(n, T, \mathcal{T}) > n^{1-1/m}$. Consequently, leveraging the current upper bound, the lower bound becomes $n^{1-1/2^m}$, which is best possible. Additionally, semi-transitive graphs can be embedded into transitive tournaments, implying that the transitive tournament's directed Ramsey-Tur\'an number matches that of semi-transitive graphs. Utilizing a suite of hadronic features, the method distinguishes tau leptons from light jets by assessing tau decay signatures and jet mass, and it further enhances performance by incorporating information about $b$-hadron decays. Survey of Space and Time (LSST) are expected to identify thousands of gravitational wave (GW) events. This paper outlines a method for automatically generating GW candidate lists tailored for these upcoming surveys. The process involves training a deep neural network (DNN) using simulated GW events from various templates, followed by its deployment as an online selector to provide real-time candidate lists. We demonstrate the DNN's behavior using Gaussian GW signal injections, demonstrate a GW/burst list generator that incorporates the DNN, and demonstrate its use with diverse templates, including those for core-collapse supernovae and binary neutron star mergers. The DNN shows behavior consistent with in-principle identifications of diverse GW templates, such as core-collapse supernovae and supernovae with nebular pinwheels. We also examine the DNN performance with templates for supernovae in pinwheel nebulae and core-collapse supernovae with spirals. Furthermore, we illustrate the DNN performance with a simple test of the supernova pinwheel inspiral template, a signal expected from certain core-collapse channels. Finally, we demonstrate the algorithm's ability to identify various binary mergers, such as binary neutron star and binary black hole mergers, highlighting that a DNN can effectively search the GW parameter space. This work serves as a general framework for building an automatic GW candidate selector trained on specific templates and demonstrates the operation of the DNN with a broad range of templates, including core-collapse supernovae, supernovae with nebular pinwheels, and core-collapse supernovae with core bounce. The DNN performs well in distinguishing GW signals from noise across all templates. Future research will focus on the DNN's performance with a wider array of templates, including binary black holes, binary neutron stars, core-collapse supernovae, supernovae with nebular pinwheels, core-collapse supernovae with core bounces, and core collapse with nebular pinwheels. Conventional methods estimate finite-time CBFs over fixed, pre-defined time horizons to ensure safety; however, selecting an appropriate horizon width is often difficult and may not be feasible for all applications. This paper introduces a novel approach to estimating state-dependent time horizons for finite-time CBFs using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). This overview examines recent findings from reactor, accelerator, solar, and supernova experiments alongside theoretical advancements, while also presenting an updated compilation of precisely measured parameters for light (exotic) particles. Finally, it addresses recent progress regarding sterile neutrinos and oscillations within the Lorentz-violating Standard-Model Extension (SME) framework. Since all known particles are neutral, the existence of sterile neutrinos with the same mass as active ones in the early universe would have led to a rapid neutralization effect, necessitating a splitting in light particle masses to sustain charge conservation. This symmetry could be broken via the SME. Furthermore, we explore the possibility that the sum of the three neutrino masses is zero, which would impose a constraint on the sum of their rest energies. This constraint is tested by evaluating the energy loss of a positronium at rest decaying into a photon and a pair of neutrinos. Takasugi, published by World Scientific Publishing Co. in 2010. This study tackles the optimal control challenge within a specific class of non-adaptive factor processes characterized by periodicity, a trait prevalent in economic time series. Specifically, we examine a reinforcement learning scenario where the controller receives two autoregressive time series: one offering causal insights into the control process and another providing non-causal, yet highly valuable, information. We propose a representation of the pseudo-control function (PCF) based on a Fourier series and employ a neural network to learn the remaining components of the PCF. Under assumptions of identifiability and causality, we demonstrate that this neural network PCF converges to the true PCF with a known closed-form expression. We analyze the convergence rate of this PCF estimation, showing it aligns with the rate of a periodic regression estimate utilizing additional time series data. Furthermore, we apply these results within a reinforcement learning framework and numerically illustrate the benefits of incorporating non-causal information when estimating the PCF. Our findings indicate that the PCF serves as an effective tool for efficient factor-based control, enabling the construction of a viable neural-network-driven reinforcement learning algorithm. Additionally, we illustrate how integrating causality checks can streamline the selection of an appropriate PCF. The empirical example utilizes an economic factor process featuring both causal and non-causal information, where the PCF was estimated using various approaches including our proposed method, autoregression, and various lags of both information streams. This approach demonstrates that leveraging non-causal information can substantially improve forecasting accuracy and enhance the precision of pass-through effect estimates. Numerical experiments confirm that the PCF approach yields more accurate results than those obtained by other methods. We also illustrate how causality checks can automatically eliminate unnecessary lags of causal series and retain only those of non-causal series that contribute meaningfully to the PCF estimation. Finally, we show how this methodology facilitates the estimation of structural parameters and pass-through effects in simulated economic environments. By serving as a valuable tool for factor-based policy analysis, the PCF approach promises greater efficiency and less bias in relevant applications. This offers a promising avenue for future research, potentially leading to the development of a comprehensive policy analysis package grounded in causal learning. Moreover, the PCF framework holds potential for extension beyond periodic processes and could be adapted for use in deep learning architectures capable of handling unstructured inputs. Consequently, the PCF represents a significant step forward in causal learning

While garbage collection traditionally underpins languages like Scala and Common Lisp—often paired with simple type systems—it is notably absent in statically typed constructs such as C, which rely on mechanisms like union types instead. Although garbage collectors offer swift and easy solutions to safe memory management, they are not universal; consequently, this research investigates deep invariants to enable efficient and secure manual management, thereby reducing the memory overhead associated with automatic collection. However, a primary obstacle remains: detecting errors in hand-managed memory is significantly more difficult than in its automatic counterpart. To address this, the paper outlines strategies for error detection and focuses on a specific approach: leveraging the limitations of a type system to ensure safety. This method offers notable advantages, including broader error detection and a simpler development workflow. The authors propose combining these strategies to cater to a diverse array of user needs. To demonstrate the feasibility of such approaches, the paper presents an example implementation in C termed Scc, a resource-sensitive extension. This work builds upon prior research regarding safety and invariant detection. The authors conclude by identifying significant challenges and outlining future research avenues. Finally, they present Solid, a functional language built upon Scc, designed to offer a simpler yet still powerful environment for manual resource management. demonstrating to a computationally limited client that the output from a specified computation is correct. This paper presents a new verification protocol for quantum computation. Unlike existing approaches that rely on randomizing the computation—thereby reducing client efficiency—the proposed method randomizes the quantum state within the proof while maintaining the original computation intact. Consequently, the verification proof provided to the client remains independent of the specific computation being performed. Additionally, the protocol features a non-interactive design for the server, allowing the proof to be generated offline. As a direct result, the same proof applies to any computation requested by the client, enabling the sharing of a single proof among multiple users. The protocol's soundness is demonstrated without relying on any computational assumptions, whereas its soundness rests upon Hilbert space geometry. To establish soundness, the proof utilizes a fresh random copy of the computation. Notably, the server's complexity is increased only marginally, requiring an overhead of $O(\log^2 n)$ additional qubits and a number of gates linear in the size of the original computation.

In this paper, we present a shape generator capable of rapidly producing diverse, random cell-like geometries to serve as inputs for cell growth models. Our approach employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to iteratively transform a simple initial shape into a target one, using a supervised classifier trained on biophysical simulations of individual cells. This study addresses the specific issue of blindness by addressing three core challenges: (1) converting printed content into digital format, (2) converting digital material into Braille, and 3) ensuring the accessibility of these generated Braille texts for blind users. The research evaluates the effectiveness of current solutions and provides recommendations for enhancing them. Additionally, the paper outlines principles and guidelines designed to create a more inclusive environment within the Braille ecosystem. Finally, it proposes an original solution utilizing a novel haptic feedback-based system (FBBS) to improve accessibility, demonstrating how this approach addresses the identified problems and principles. This proposed system offers a new avenue for researchers to continue improving print material accessibility within this domain. Specifically, the paper concentrates on English Braille. Furthermore, an experimental study was conducted to assess users' performance and satisfaction when interacting with FBBS-based generated Braille texts. This experiment involved converting printed English texts into digital formats, converting them into Braille using a state-of-the-art algorithm, and delivering the output via a haptic feedback device (an embosser) equipped with the FBBS technique to assist users. The participants in this phase were both able-sighted and blind. The experiment compared three methods: (1) Braille generated by a state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithm without FBBS, (2) Braille generated by a SOTA algorithm with FBBS, and (3) Braille generated by FBBS alone (a recently proposed method). The findings indicate that the proposed FBBS-based solution significantly outperforms SOTA methods. The proposed system outperforms existing solutions by 17.1% in terms of accessibility and 23.5% in sustainability, alongside substantial improvements in satisfaction scores. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this paper represents the first effort to address the entire end-to-end pipeline of converting printed materials into accessible Braille using an FBBS-based solution. The decidability proof relies on a new labeled semantic framework consisting of labeled frames and labeled valuation trees. We demonstrate that this framework is both sound and complete relative to the infinite family of decidable extensions under discussion. Furthermore, we show that classical semantic frames, valuation trees, and Lambek formulas can be viewed as a subset of the labeled framework; specifically, they are preserved when the labeled valuation trees are collapsed. An HMM consists of a Markov chain representing a Markov process, with each state associated with a random variable; conceptually, one can imagine an individual utilizing a die with an undisclosed face distribution to generate a Markov chain. In practical settings, HMMs are utilized for both inference and learning, with the latter typically employing the EM algorithm, also known as the forward-backward algorithm.

This difficulty stems from the high probability that adjacent locations can be linked through a common context, such as a user's residence, work site, or residence combined with a nearby grocery store. This paper demonstrates that a standard probabilistic location privacy model is insufficient for this context-aware environment. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that explicitly utilizes a user's recent history of released locations. By applying a Markov chain, we derive a set of adjacent location probability distributions and show that a user's true location remains detectable within this set via maximum-likelihood estimation. Consequently, we propose a new privacy metric that quantifies privacy risk by calculating the probability of an adversary correctly identifying the location. We empirically validate that both the risk of location inference and the suggested trapezoidal masking area increase as the frequency of location releases rises. Using these metrics, we evaluate the specific duration of privacy in various contexts and determine optimal masking strategies for maintaining meaningful privacy levels. Based on our findings, we provide practical recommendations for generating location-based services that provide significant privacy periods. Furthermore, we illustrate that a user can achieve sufficient privacy by releasing only a low-resolution version of the map. These results are empirically supported, demonstrating that releasing low-resolution data incurs only a minor reduction in service utility while still providing significant privacy. This study indicates that a new dimension of privacy exists in location-based services when release periods are short and location granularity is low. By presenting the proposed probabilistic distribution-based inference algorithm and empirical results regarding privacy levels and resolution, we aim to foster future research into novel mechanisms and algorithms for context-aware privacy-preserving location-based services. Through this research, we hope to contribute to the development of privacy-efficient location-based services that provide meaningful privacy protection to users. framework where all nodes interact by transmitting single-bit messages, known as beeps. This paper addresses two core challenges in distributed computing: naming and counting. Our primary objective is to minimize both the energy consumption and execution time of algorithms solving these issues. We present randomized algorithms that achieve optimal trade-offs between communication energy and running time for both naming and counting, demonstrating optimality relative to general constraints on algorithm behavior. Specifically, we establish that, with high probability, our naming algorithms outperform any other (randomized) algorithm regarding either running time or energy usage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even in the deterministic scenario, our algorithms are nearly optimal by proving the existence of other deterministic algorithms that, without relying on probabilistic arguments, are only asymptotically worse in terms of energy consumption. These new algorithms are significantly cheaper than current randomized alternatives when solving counting. However, we also identify a distinct disparity in energy-optimal trade-offs between naming and counting, revealing that beeping network algorithms are inherently more complex than those required for counting. Additionally, we provide lower bounds on energy consumption and running time for naming, showing that any naming algorithm requires at least one-beep energy and operation time. Finally, we examine task-specific algorithms, which beeps designed specifically to solve a particular task, and compare their performance to general-purpose algorithms. We show that randomized task-specific algorithms can be more energy-efficient, while deterministic task-specific algorithms can be energy-optimal. However, we also highlight that beeping network algorithms remain fundamentally inevitable. This research represents a significant step toward resolving open problems in beeping network algorithm design. It offers designers a deeper understanding of the costs associated with naming and counting and provides them with efficient, optimal, or near-optimal algorithms to choose from. These findings are relevant to designing protocols for wireless sensor networks, chip networks, and similar environments.

In this work, we provide a negative answer to an open question by demonstrating that probabilistic counting cannot, with high probability, be executed using energy proportional to $o(n)$, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes. We show that any probabilistic counting algorithm operating within $o(n)$ energy consumes, with high probability, at least $\Omega(n^{3/4})$ energy. Consequently, probabilistic counting is both robust and versatile. We also explore generalizations of this problem, proving that if nodes possess no initial energy, they cannot execute probabilistic counting. Leveraging nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), we present evidence of a hidden nematic state in Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$Te$_2$-based compounds (Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$LiTe$_2$) that exhibits NMR signatures distinct from those of the parent compound,FeTe$_2$. Specifically, the evolution of the magnetic field dependence of the spin relaxation rate ($T_1^{-1}$) below the NMR detection of the superconducting gap indicates antiferromagnetic fluctuations with a characteristic energy and $q$-vector differing from FeTe$_2$. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of these dynamics in Co-doped samples deviates from Bose-Einstein statistics, and the associated $T_1$ values are elevated. These findings suggest that nematic symmetry breaking is unnecessary for the emergence of multi-gap superconductivity in FeSCs. By comparing our results with those of NMR studies on Co-doped BaFe$_2$As$_2$, we argue that both multi-gap superconductivity and nematicity arise from different underlying mechanisms. Additionally, the observed enhancement of $T_1$ at higher Co concentrations aligns with NMR data from 59Co NMR on LaFeAsO, suggesting that this $^{75}$As observation may be universal for multi-gap superconductors. These findings are discussed in the context of pair-breaking effects and the potential for an isotropic superconducting ground state. We conclude that the coexistence of nematicity and superconductivity is not a prerequisite for an unconventional superconducting ground state. it is inherently impossible to create computerized deposition protocols that consistently construct any specified structure with high yield and efficiency, even when accounting for experimentally realistic conditions such as imperfect alignment and weak interactions between the substrate and the incoming molecule. These limitations can be mitigated if the molecule and the substrate can be chemically modified to enhance interaction strength, thereby enabling effective protocols for molecules that are small enough to align nearly perfectly with the surface. Consequently, we propose a general alternative approach: initiating the deposition with a preformed, stable precursor structure. This allows for high-yield protocols to be established for a broad spectrum of target configurations, provided the system parameters are appropriately tuned and the initial structure of the target is reasonably inferred. This challenge underscores the necessity for new experimental techniques and methodologies designed to probe nanomaterials at the atomic level during their real-time growth. Such insights could significantly advance the self-assembly of materials into functional atomic and molecular architectures with precise subunit arrangements at surfaces. Furthermore, this strategy could facilitate the creation of advanced nanostructures and molecular circuits using small proteins as precursors, where active sites are reliably positioned to catalyze material growth and form strong covalent bonds to the substrate. Ultimately, these methods could yield reliable protocols for self-assembling various supramolecular structures at interfaces. We anticipate that these methodologies will be increasingly valuable in advancing the design and fabrication of efficient solar cells, fuel cells, and other devices that depend on the precise atomic-level positioning of small molecules at surfaces. Furthermore, these approaches could significantly accelerate the discovery of new catalysts and the associated reaction mechanisms. the minimum spanning tree (MST) in a graph with $n$ vertices, where each edge exists independently with probability $p$, reaches its minimum value when $p = \sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}$. This paper establishes that, for this optimal edge probability, the MST weight is asymptotically normally distributed with mean $n T_n$ and variance $\frac{1}{6}\sigma_n^2$, defined as:
\begin{align*} T_n &= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{\substack{ j_1 + \cdots + j_k = k-1 \\ j_i \ge 1}} \frac{\prod_{i=1}^k B_{j_i}}{\prod_{m=1}^k (1+mj_i)} \\ \sigma_n^2 &= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(k-1)!} \sum_{\substack { j_1 + \cdots + j_k = k-1 \\ j_i \ge 1}} \frac{\prod_{i=1}^k B_{j_i}}{\prod_{m=1}^k (1+mj_i)^2} \end{align*}
where $B_k$ is explicitly given by:
\begin{equation} B_k = \sum_{\substack{ i_1 + \cdots + i_{k-1} +1 = k \\ i_j \ge 1}} \frac{(-1)^{k-1} (k-1)!}{\prod_{m=1}^k i_m!} \prod_{m=1}^{k-1} T_{i_m}. \end{equation>
These coefficients were initially identified by the authors in a preliminary version of this research. Furthermore, the study investigates properties of $T_n$ and $\sigma_n^2$, proving that $T_n \sim 1$ and $\sigma_n^2 \sim \frac{2}{3}\log 2$. In the final section, the authors revisit classical results regarding the asymptotic expected weight and variance of the MST under the same probabilistic conditions.

Nevertheless, recent studies have demonstrated that the digital fingerprints embedded in a client's model updates can still be extracted by the server, compromising privacy. To address this, an effective anti-fingerprinting strategy is crucial for minimizing the information within model updates that can be utilized by the server for such attacks. This paper investigates optimization techniques to enhance privacy by reducing model transfer, thereby lowering the risk of potential fingerprinting. Our findings indicate that adopting quantization and low-rank matrix approximation significantly reduces the data volume to be transferred. We demonstrate that these proposed approaches are compatible and can be simultaneously employed to further reduce the model size. Ultimately, we evaluate how compressing the model affects privacy using existing extraction attacks on federated image classification, with additional numerical experiments conducted to assess the impact of local dataset variations on anti-fingerprinting. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study to explore compression as a privacy mitigation strategy against federated learning attacks. Experimental outcomes validate the effectiveness of compression in reducing model size while maintaining acceptable performance, serving as a practical anti-fingerprinting measure. We have open-sourced our code at \url{https://anonymous.20m.nl}. Finally, regarding anticipated questions: Our approach differs from existing defenses against anti-fingerprinting attacks because it promotes a more efficient FL practice by employing compression, which is also applicable to non-federated contexts. Furthermore, while previous methods attempt to detect attacks, our strategy proactively reduces the data volume transferable to the server, thereby inherently limiting the data available for potential attacks. Can this scalability handle practical, real-world scenarios? Yes, our findings align with existing literature, and various existing anti-fingerprinting methods can be effectively combined with our compression technique, which is already in use in practical FL deployments. Does this introduce any additional computational overhead? No, compression generally reduces both computation time and data volume. While quantization may require slight preprocessing, low-rank approximation can be easily integrated into existing training workflows. Additionally, our analysis shows that increasing the rank provides flexibility to balance data volume against expected performance. Finally, is this approach applicable to other practical tasks? Yes, federated regression, for instance, can similarly leverage low-rank approximation to achieve comparable data volume reductions. Our anti-fingerprinting strategy effectively addresses the aforementioned issues, significantly reducing data volume while producing outcomes equivalent to or better than the global model. a focused electron beam within a periodic magnetic undulator serves as a diagnostic method for determining beam parameters at accelerators. This study addresses the challenge of modeling betatron radiation from a axially symmetric, continuously varying modulation of a relativistic electron beam. We derive the analytical form of the betatron wavelength as a function of the beam's equilibrium radius oscillation and calculate the corresponding emission spectrum. Since a smoothly modulated beam generates no on-axis scattering radiation, our focus shifts to the angular spectrum of emission. A key finding of this work is that betatron radiation from such a beam is emitted exclusively in the longitudinal direction. Furthermore, for an infinite undulator, we demonstrate that the radiation spectrum is independent of the modulation amplitude and rate, featuring a single peak when the undatron wavelength aligns with the radiation wavelength. At the spectrum's broad wing, we develop an approximate analytical expression. This analytical formula also accurately reflects the spectrum's full width at half maximum. Our results indicate that undulator emission can bridge gap between heavily overlapping sidebands, thereby enabling beam emittance measurement down to extremely low values. Additionally, we have assessed how systematic errors in spectrometer calibration affect emittance measurement precision. Finally, applying these formulas, we have proposed a novel emittance measurement technique for beam energies between 50 and 100 MeV, suitable for use at existing light sources and proposed future accelerators. By employing on-axis spectrally integrated detection, this method eliminates several systematic errors, such as longitudinal straggling and undulator misalignment, which are significant constraints in current diagnostic schemes. Furthermore, we have assessed how systematic errors in the spectrometer calibration affect emittance measurement accuracy. As a practical example, we demonstrate that betatron radiation can effectively measure the beam properties of the Johnsen electron beam at SPring-8. In a specific case, using a 50 MeV electron beam with a 3 cm-1 modulation, we observed a spectrum peak at 280 eV, corresponding to an emittance of $5\times 10^{-9}$ m. These findings establish a viable pathway for future emittance measurements of electron beams in energy and facility regimes that are currently unmeasurable. In conclusion, this work presents a new approach to emittance measurement using betatron radiation diagnostics, offering significant potential for future electron accelerators. # Abstract

We propose the first provably accurate algorithms for learning different and fair utility functions from data, where the utility function is defined as a black-box parameter. We demonstrate that current linear and non-linear regression methods fail to offer guaranteed learning outcomes for these utility functions. As a solution, we introduce regression algorithms built on regression trees and sparse least squares, which ensure guaranteed learning performance for both linear and non-linear (including different and fair) utility functions. The trees are characterized by dynamic and multi-dimensional bound depths, and the sparse least squares method relies on randomized Fourier features. Additionally, we establish that algorithmic learning guarantees ensure the privacy of individual evaluations during regression, independent of the utility function's shape. We also include experimental guidance for adapting these algorithms, with numerical experiments validating our theoretical guarantees, including an analysis of dataset bias. The code is available publicly.

The article addresses the transport of quasiparticles in cuprate superconductors when scattering is mediated by charge-carrier fluctuation potentials (long-range Coulomb potentials) with extended impurities. A theoretical framework for calculating the quasiparticle mean free path is developed, utilizing a recently derived kinetic equation for nonequilibrium Green's functions in a superconducting state. It is demonstrated that scattering by potentials with a Coulomb $1/r$ dependence results in a 3D diffusional dependence of the quasiparticle mean free path on temperature, consistent with experimental observations in cuprates. Additionally, calculations of the mean free path for a specific model of a long-range Coulomb potential yield values matching experimental measurements. automated vehicles (CAVs) within a hybrid traffic environment containing both CAVs and human-driven vehicles (HDVs). The primary objective is to design a hybrid CAV platoon that maintains human comfort and traffic flow efficiency while strictly satisfying safety constraints imposed by HDVs. To this end, we introduce a conventional three-layer control architecture, where the top layer assigns travel paths, the middle way-point tracking ensures adherence to these paths, and the bottom layer guarantees vehicle string stability. Specifically, the middle layer utilizes a model predictive control (MPC) algorithm, while the bottom layer employs a feedback controller. Notably, we present an efficient offline "pre-computation" solution for the MPC-based bottom-layer controller. This pre-computation enables the reduction of the "online" MPC computational burden by determining the reference trajectory for the relative distance between consecutive vehicles and constraining the MPC search space. Additionally, a simple adaptive speed policy is implemented. Simulation results demonstrate that this three-layer architecture successfully achieves path following and human comfort, yielding a fuel saving of 11.6% compared to two-layer approaches. Furthermore, a simulation comparison between a standard MPC algorithm and the proposed pre-computation-based MPC algorithm for the bottom-layer controller reveals that pre-computation reduces path following time by approximately 40%. These findings confirm that the proposed three-layer controller effectively follows desired reference trajectories, adheres to highway rules, and ensures the safety and comfort required for HDVs. Finally, it is verified that the pre-computation-based MPC algorithm significantly enhances computational efficiency. In conclusion, this paper presents a method for designing a high-performance CAV platoon that respects HDV constraints in mixed traffic through a three-layer controller. It is demonstrated that path following can be successfully achieved while minimizing fuel consumption and reducing the online computational burden of the bottom-layer MPC controller. The effectiveness of this proposed approach is confirmed through simulations. Keywords: Connected and automated vehicles (CAVs), model predictive control (MPC), multi-agent cooperative maneuvering (MCM), model pre-computation, way-point tracking, hybrid traffic, human-driven vehicles (HDVs), three-layer controller. By enabling peer feedback and blending intrinsic motivations with game-like gamification, TUCo significantly improved both the quantity and quality of user-generated content. Conversely, for original media, both comments and ratings rose, as did a sense of accomplishment; however, feelings of confusion and isolation were also reported. These findings highlight both TUCo's success and the need for further refinement, particularly regarding emotional management and guidance to ensure user satisfaction and sustained engagement. This study demonstrates that enhancing social networking through increased interactivity can effectively stimulate creativity. Our insights are validated by real-world deployments on Facebook, Flock, and Facebook Groups, encouraging future research to leverage these principles within social networks to drive greater creativity. Our open-source TUCo framework, available online, allows for easy, low-cost testing, scaling, and customization on existing social networks. Source code and open data are accessible at https://github.com/ahyung/Targeted-User-Connectivity-Optimization. Project details can be found at https://ahyung.github.io/TUCo/.

The widespread adoption of social media has led to an explosion in information volume, creating a critical need for automatic summarization to enhance information access. Yet, this task is inherently difficult, particularly when dealing with diverse content like news, politics, and entertainment. This paper presents a study on extracting sentences that effectively summarize web pages. Using a news article corpus, we conducted a quantitative analysis of sentence features influencing semantic quality in summaries. By integrating this analysis into an attention-based encoding-decoding model for abstractive summarization, we achieved improved performance. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of these features in enhancing summary quality. To validate the practical utility of our approach, we deployed it on a real-world social network to automatically summarize personal expression pages. We establish that any hypergraph can be decomposed into a tensor join of smaller hypergraphs and establish a hypergraph form of Goodman's inequality regarding this join. Goodman's inequality implies that every hypergraph $H$ with $n$ vertices possesses a null automorphism group. Furthermore, we analyze the number of labeled hypergraphs adhering to specific degree constraints, support this analysis with numerical data, and provide a second proof of Goodman's inequality by examining the distribution of these counted objects. Finally, we briefly discuss hypergraphs defined as tensor joins of other hypergraphs, known in literature as Boolean matrices or hypergraphs, outlining their fundamental properties. We also identify a $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear transformation, $T$, defined on the vector space of $n$-vertex, $\mathbb{F}_2$-coefficients, null hypergraphs, which functions as a frame for this space. We determine the minimum and maximum dimensions of the $T$-kernel. Specifically, we prove that for every $n$, the minimum dimension is at least $2^{\lfloor \frac{n-2}{3} \rfloor + 1}$, a bound that is exact and achieved by the alternating cycle of length $2n+2$. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum dimension is bounded above by $2^{\frac 23 (\log_2 n)^2 + O(\log n)}$. This upper bound is exact and asymptotically optimal for the case where $n$ is a perfect square. The construction of these hypergraphs is based on finite geometry and employs a grid of vectors derived from an affine plane of order $k$, utilizing vector differences as an elementary operation. We note that this specific class of hypergraphs was previously studied by Bialas and Krasicki. Their work on hypergraph dimension directly validates the optimality of our asymptotic bound and demonstrates that this family of hypergraphs is particularly effective for lower-bounding the dimension. Our findings also clarify the relationship between our concept of hypergraph and that of Bialas and Krasicki. We demonstrate that any finite set of vectors can be expressed as a sum of null hypergraphs of a specific, calculable, and relatively low dimension. This result is achieved by transforming the problem into one involving binary matrices with few ones per row and applying a bound on the dimension of the kernel of a linear map. While Church-type systems lack the negative constraints necessary for the "uniqueness of identities" property, this limitation enables the automatic generation of combinatorial automata capable of verifying path equality. Consequently, the decidable equality of paths provides a foundational framework for the theoretical analysis of combinational circuits, with significant extensions to the simply typed lambda-calculus also remaining feasible. Furthermore, an algorithm exists to eliminate the need for complex automata by utilizing the standard elimination rules of Martin-Löf's type theory. In this context, we interpret the axioms of uniqueness of identities not as a finitary constraint, but as an instruction to employ the most efficient automaton possible. This approach effectively bridges the gap between the theoretical properties of lambda-calculi and the practical efficiency of hardware implementation. Ultimately, we present a novel perspective on the relationship between pure mathematics and engineering, grounded in category theory, which offers new insights into the synthesis of logical circuits from lambda-calculi. This synthesis process functions as an automated algorithm for minimizing automata. Additionally, we connect this methodology to Rabin's work on minimal automata and provide a new proof for the existence of such automata, which directly yields an upper bound for the size of resulting combinational circuits and establishes the automatic link between lambda-calculi and finite automata. Finally, we demonstrate that the synthesis process can be extended to incorporate lambda terms representing initial values of registers, thereby enabling the automatic generation of Moore and Mealy circuits from lambda-calculi. This extension facilitates a direct comparison between the sizes of circuits and the depths of the underlying lambda-calculi. Through this theoretical framework, we propose novel metrics for assessing the complexity of both lambda-calculi and their corresponding circuit realizations. This work forms part of the author's PhD thesis, supervised by A. Muravitsky and V. Shapira at Tel-Aviv University. a core challenge in autonomous robotics. This paper introduces a multi-agent approach designed to navigate a large-scale swarm within a confined area using a decentralized framework. The specific application involves deploying numerous small quadrotors to capture images of a target from various viewpoints and distances, a task critical for applications like precision agriculture. Each individual robot is equipped with an intelligent configuration that allows it to independently assess its surroundings and select a optimal setting based on locally gathered data. The study presents a straightforward yet effective configuration for the quadrotor algorithm, demonstrating through simulation that a high number of robots can efficiently and collision-free reach their target setups. Building on these positive simulation results, the paper outlines initial experimental efforts toward real-world deployment. Ultimately, this approach is poised to scale up to substantial swarms capable of covering vast, restricted areas effectively. The proposed decentralized method offers distinct advantages, primarily the inherent robustness of the multi-agent system to local disturbances and the resulting safe navigation of the entire swarm to its target configurations. Recent spectroscopic observations using the Five-colour Spectroscopic and Imaging Survey for globular clusters (F-SIGS) revealed that its red giant branch stars exhibit a metallicity range of $\Delta[Fe/H]=-0.5$ dex, indicating significant internal spread. The most metal-poor giants display absorption features typical of enhanced r-process elements, a characteristic also found in highly metal-deficient stars. massive machine-type communications (mMTC) within the evolving 5G architecture, facilitating the connection of thousands of low-activity user equipment (UEs) in dense environments. This paper addresses grant-free uplink OFDMA in scenarios involving many active mMTC UEs, focusing on low-latency packet reception. We propose a two-stage scheduling mechanism: first, UEs are grouped into groups of UEs (GoUOs), and subsequently, these groups are mapped to specific time-frequency resources. The primary goals are to minimize both end-to-end delay and total power consumption by optimizing group power levels and the allocation of power and time slots. We derive analytical expressions for delay and power usage, from which we determine the optimal power levels for each stage, the optimal number of subcarriers per group, and the optimal number of groups based on minimal costs. Analytical results demonstrate that the delay and power benefits of the two-stage approach over a single-stage method are most significant when the number of UEs is large. Numerical simulations validate our findings and reveal that the performance gap between two-stage and single-stage scheduling narrows as the number of UEs grows larger. However, when considering very low power levels, two-stage scheduling may result in a slight increase in total power consumption compared to single-stage scheduling. Furthermore, increasing the number of UEs per GoUO reduces total power needs but raises latency. Conversely, reducing the number of UEs per GoUO can enhance performance in terms of both power efficiency and delay. Finally, adjusting the number of UEs per GoUO per symbol can further improve system performance. Overall, this work demonstrates the superior performance of two-stage grant-free scheduling. Future research will explore more advanced waveforms for grant-free access, such as sparse code multiple access (SCMA) and orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS). Additionally, further improvements can be achieved through the joint design of transmit waveforms and power levels. Extending this framework to non-orthogonal scheduling, where multiple UEs share the same time-frequency resources, is also a promising direction for future study. More broadly, these methods can be applied to design non-orthogonal waveforms and power-control strategies for grant-free uplinks, thereby reducing both delay and power consumption in large-scale mMTC scenarios. This research holds significant potential for applications such as autonomous driving, smart cities, and remote surgery. In conclusion, the proposed scheduling and power-control strategies offer a robust solution for efficient grant-free communication systems. While the ISA 1976 formulation exhibits inaccuracy and non-physical characteristics, ITEMA 2008 offers a mathematically complex approach that introduces a latent heat problem. Consequently, current state-of-the-art methods relying on the initial N+1 hypothesis often achieve poor performance. This paper presents Consortium, an approach that dynamically integrates a vast number of ASR hypotheses—even those ranked far down the list—to maintain high effectiveness. By leveraging a large language model's strong language prior to filter out erroneous outputs in the extensive hypothesis set, Consortium achieves significantly improved dialogue state tracking performance compared to previous methods. The core concept is that while ASR models capture the distribution of phonetic sequences, their top-K predictions fail to effectively represent the distribution of semantic meanings. Experimental results on the Microsoft SPD dataset demonstrate that Consortium reduces the MS-LID error from 19.8% to 15.3% while increasing the MS-SDS accuracy from 61.2% to 64.6%. Furthermore, comparisons with other models such as BERT and SpokenBERT further validate the potential of this large language model. Finally, ablation studies reveal that both system-scale and language-level designs are essential for the proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/Consortium. \cr

solitons (PTS) have been observed in the equatorial electrojet (EQE), a region situated above the magnetic equator. While the EQE is typically characterized by a narrow structure, expanding to roughly 1,000 km under quiet conditions, a growing body of evidence suggests that the underlying physics may involve both local and nonlocal effects. This study introduces a theoretical framework for an inherently nonlocal PTS within the EQE. We begin with the two-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation (2D-NLSE) and derive a nonlocal wave equation supported by two local damping and two local dispersion terms. By incorporating a spatial derivative into the nonlocal response function, we arrive at a 2D-NLSE that includes second-order temporal derivatives in the nonlocal term alongside first-order temporal derivatives on the right-hand side. The model accounts for wave packet spreading, where the rate of dispersion is modulated by the nonlocal component. Numerical simulations demonstrate that a purely nonlocal PTS is unstable; however, stability is achieved through energy dissipation provided by the combined influence of the two local damping terms and the nonlocal contribution. We analyze a two-dimensional PTS exhibiting palm tree-like characteristics and present a comparison between our nonlocal model and the local NLSE. Our results indicate that including spatial derivatives in the nonlocal response term significantly enhances the stability of the palm tree soliton. Finally, we apply this model to EQE observations, demonstrating that the derived parameters align well with actual conditions. This research offers a new avenue for investigating soliton dynamics in plasmas governed by both local and nonlocal effects. This paper introduces a regularization strategy designed to enhance the robustness and reliability of GNNs by promoting greater regularity across node representations. Our approach is built upon two foundational insights: first, regularized GNNs demonstrate superior robustness against graph perturbations compared to their non-regularized counterparts; second, adding regularity to GNN representations benefits model performance when graph structures change. To our knowledge, this work represents one of the earliest and most promising applications of graph regularization in neural networks. Both axions and ALPs are widely regarded as prime candidates for dark matter, especially in the form of cosmic axion fields (CAF). This study examines the gravitational influence of such domains on gravitational-wave signals from compact-object binaries. By employing the post-Newtonian approximation and utilizing post-Bonnet formalism for the spin-orbit interaction between a scalar field and spin, we derive expressions for the parametric dependence of the binary's orbital phase evolution.
