The CAF field induces a change in the orbital phase rate proportional to $\vec{S}_1\cdot\vec{p}$ and $\vec{S_2}\cdot\vec{p}$ for the two spins, $\vec{S}_{1,2}$, and momentum $\vec{p}$. Furthermore, we present constraints derived from three GW170814-like events. The interaction generates a double modulation in the gravitational-wave signal due to the binary's motion relative to the fixed local CAF field direction. A novel signature of dark energy is also anticipated, arising from the coupling of local matter density and local CAF energy density to a new scalar field. A correlation between the cosmological constant and the local direction of the axion field could produce visible effects on GW170814-like events. The observed modulation could potentially be detected by the LISA space-based interferometer, with future relativistic binaries offering even greater sensitivity. This provides a new avenue for detecting and characterizing local CAF fields using gravitational-wave observations. Such investigations could significantly advance our understanding of the early Universe, dark matter, and the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry. The paper examines the lack of equilibrium within this oscillator, proposing it as a mechanism for establishing dynamical, non-stationary memory storage. Furthermore, it establishes two erasure protocols to reset the bosonic system, thereby enabling the analysis of the thermodynamic costs associated with erasure and memory operations. These findings contribute to the emerging discipline of stochastic thermodynamics applied to bosonic computing. Additionally, the study offers an alternative approach to modeling open quantum systems, as it derives the stochastic paths of the larger, extended system without requiring the initial approximation of decoupling the smaller subsystem from the larger one. Finally, the research estimates the complexity of the bosonic oscillator, characterizing it as comparable to that of a classical single bit. By emulating the von Neumann open quantum computing architecture—where an efficient quantum algorithm is executed on a bosonic oscillator within a larger, disordered quantum environment—the study paves the way for exploring the computation capabilities of more sophisticated bosonic oscillators, such as those with higher dimensions and non-linearities. This capacity to simulate open quantum systems positions the bosonic oscillator as a viable candidate for quantum computation. The analysis of this complex system also enables the derivation of general equations for higher-order occupation number moments in bosonic oscillators. These findings are relevant to the broader context of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, specifically its proposed extension to include information terms. The work concludes with an application of these concepts to a specific open quantum computing scenario. Collectively, these results provide a robust theoretical foundation for the emerging fields of stochastic thermodynamics and bosonic computing, offering momentum and direction for their advancement. that projects data into lower dimensions while preserving information needed for aggregation queries. This work introduces novel CountSketch algorithms to accelerate memory access and enhance cache friendliness during data projection, thereby reducing overall runtime. The proposed methods maintain numerical equivalence with the standard CountSketch approach and remain adaptable to questions requiring $\ell_1$-agqueries, including column-wise, row-wise, and group-wise operations.

Our column projection technique employs a novel novel CountSketch variant that processes input vectors in strided segments rather than full vectors, enabling highly cache-friendly operations with no prior elements-to-queries knowledge. This strategy achieves an order-of-magnitude speedup for column queries. Although it is less efficient for queries involving many elements relative to the number of sketches, it remains substantially faster than the baseline. For group projection, we develop a new algorithm that handles multiple key-value pairs per vector by updating only the common key positions, leaving other elements unchanged. This approach delivers high speedups for highly selective queries, though it may suffer from noticeable speed declines when queries involve many elements. For arbitrary queries, we demonstrate that existing fast methods can be combined with an element-wise fallback, yielding substantial overall performance gains.

Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of our algorithms, demonstrating that they can be up to $100\times$ faster than prior solutions while maintaining identical numerical accuracy. Furthermore, by integrating our fast projection schemes with an efficient data recovery method, we achieve solutions that are up to $315\times$ faster than the prior state-of-the-art while retaining nearly the same approximation quality. Additionally, our method requires just $10\%$ of the parameter tuning necessary for the FastColumnSketch approach to achieve comparable accuracy. Our implementations are available in the {\tt (col)Sketch} Python library, which can be integrated as a drop-in replacement for the original CountSketch library. All library functionalities are also supported in C++ via our new (col)Sketch package. The source code for implementing all state-of-the-art solutions is included in the repository. Our results demonstrate that (col)Sketch surpasses prior methods in both runtime and storage efficiency, while maintaining or improving numerical accuracy. The library achieves a runtime improvement of up to $100\times$ over prior work, alongside equivalent accuracy, confirming its effectiveness. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/loewent/cSketch}. This study focuses on a transaction involving a market-making HFT firm that utilizes a pricing formula to set buy and sell limits. This approach utilizes any dataset comprising video clips of individuals engaging in specific tasks, without requiring labeled transition probabilities. Initially, representations for individual clips are derived from a Transformer architecture, which is subsequently fine-tuned on a collection of grouped clips to regulate and amplify the semantic information within the learned model. These grouped clips represent complete tasks and are concatenated to construct training sequences. During the fine-tuning phase, the model is instructed to map each clip in a sequence to its corresponding label while minimizing the disparity between predicted and actual representations. We argue that incorporating long-sequence data during this stage enables the model to capture implicit conditions governing the transition from one task to another, allowing for task switching prediction. Consequently, given a sequence of video clips depicting an activity, our model can anticipate the transition conditions under which a different activity might be performed. We have demonstrated that integrating this framework into a base model yields substantial performance gains in clip classification, with additional advantages in clip retrieval and activity generation. Furthermore, our model exhibits superior generalization capabilities, predicting the performance of unseen tasks utilizing labels learned from a few extended clips. Symbolic computations were performed within the SymPy framework, and the lambda calculus implementations relied on PyQuil, PennyLane, and Cirq. The exact results demonstrate that the CF-wavefunction for two quasiparticles yields a lower energy than the Laughlin wavefunction, although the energy gap between these two approaches diminishes as the system size grows. Furthermore, we present the first integration of CF quasiparticle energy as a function of system size across various densities,-ranging from completely bosonic to completely fermionic-and compare these findings with existing theoretical models. Our proposed analytic expression aligns well with exact results for two CF quasiparticles at intermediate densities in large systems, thereby validating the analytic formula for broader applications. These analytic expressions for two CF quasiparticle excitations are also available for the cases of $N = 5$ and $N = 6$. We find that these two-quasiparticle excitations are consistent with the single-quasiparticle excitations reported in the literature. Our proposal to observe CF quasiparticle excitations experimentally is highly relevant to investigating the non-topological, weakly topologically ordered phases that may exist near the quantum Hall liquids. This study presents a new finite element framework designed to simulate these inequalities within Stokes variational settings. Specifically, we employ the widely utilized Crouzeix-Raviart non-conforming mesh. Our methodology relies on establishing a discrete Gårding inequality and utilizing mixed elements. Numerical experiments are conducted across various scenarios, demonstrating that the proposed approach performs effectively in both theoretical and practical applications. The results also highlight the glacier's sensitivity to varying values and illustrate the impact of rough terrain on simulation outcomes. Additionally, the method proves capable of preventing numerical instabilities. The paper includes several examples comparing numerical results with experimental data, which show very strong correlation. Overall, the proposed method is suitable for general Stokes-type variational inequalities, with potential for extension to other inequalities, such as the Navier-Stokes inequality, as noted in prior literature. Given that numerous physical and engineering problems involve data difficult to express using smooth functions, these inequalities offer a natural and flexible framework for addressing diverse scenarios. Our primary objective is to examine potential signatures indicative of protostellar heating in this region. By analyzing dust temperature maps derived from the Subaru Millimeter Surveyor (SMS) data, we observed significant temperature elevations ($>0.5$~K) near known Class I protostars. These heated zones appear as elongated structures aligned with the velocity outflows of their respective protostars. However, no such heated signatures were detected around other protostars in the same region. This discrepancy suggests that protostellar heating manifests structurally only in highly heated cores characterized by very Class I protostars. Furthermore, these heated zones exhibit dust temperatures significantly exceeding those of other nearby cold molecular gas. Utilizing dust emission models calibrated against a dust laboratory dataset, we quantified the excess heating provided by the protostars. The resulting excess heating rates are exceptionally high, ranging from $10^{9}$ to $10^{10}$~W throughout the core regions surrounding these very Class I protostars. Our findings provide robust evidence supporting the hypothesis that very Class I protostars can heat their surrounding very cold molecular gas to much higher temperatures, thereby creating favorable conditions for the efficient formation of dust grains. This mechanism may be responsible for the early emergence of dust emission signatures associated with very Class I protostars. In this very cold environment, such heating could facilitate the survival of silicon and carbon, which are the primary constituent elements of dust grains. These insights may also offer valuable perspectives for understanding similar phenomena in other extragalactic star-forming regions. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the early Universe, where very cold molecular gas may have been more prevalent. These results could offer hope for explaining the significant difference in dust opacity observed between the very cold molecular gas of the high-redshift Universe and that of the warm molecular gas in the local Universe. The proposed scenario also holds promise for explaining the surprisingly early detection of high-redshift galaxies in the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) Y3 cosmological survey. Consequently, the ability to create generic, pre-trained base models that maintain high accuracy across unseen domains has emerged as a key objective. Cross-Domain Prediction (CDP) addresses this challenge by utilizing an pre-trained base model to adapt to new domains by leveraging data from one or more existing domains. In this chapter, we introduce LCDP, a novel CDP approach that enhances both the quality and speed of adaptation. Specifically, LCDX employs Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to fine-tune the base model's weights using one or more source domains, while LCDU keeps the base model weight-frozen, relying instead on learned condition vectors to achieve adaptation. We evaluate both variants across eight diverse datasets to assess their generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that both LCDX and LCDU surpass state-of-the-art methods on all datasets, with LCDU achieving particularly strong performance. Furthermore, LoRA-based LCDX offers significantly improved computational efficiency, reducing the time and resources needed for adaptation. While blockchain has been widely adopted by various industries, its high resource consumption has hindered practical deployment, creating a critical gap between theoretical potential and practical application. This study evaluates several widely cited lightweight blockchain solutions, introducing a comprehensive analytical framework grounded in extensive theoretical and empirical research. The paper examines important technical aspects, including their underlying mechanisms, architectural designs, and the influence of various factors on their performance. Finally, the authors propose future research directions and highlight open issues, aiming to serve as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners in the field. LightBlocks, our proposed solution, effectively addresses the limitations of existing approaches. By utilizing a data compression mechanism, it enhances both functionality and performance. An empirical study involving a deployment of 20 nodes demonstrates that, compared to other lightweight solutions such as Diore and SecBC, LightBlocks achieves superior communication efficiency and a lower carbon footprint. Specifically, per transaction, LightBlocks consumes 30% more CPU time but reduces communication time by 82% and saves 70% more energy than Diore, while utilizing 29% less CPU time and 21% less energy than SecBC. Furthermore, the experimental results reveal that our solutions outperform traditional blockchain methods in performance and energy consumption, establishing that our scheme is theoretically sound and practically viable. we investigate the non-existence of $k$-torsion within $NK_1GQ(R)$, which represents the Bass nil-groups associated with general quadratic or Bak's unitary groups. Furthermore, by employing a graded extension of Quillen–Suslin theory, we establish a corresponding result for graded rings. Additionally, through novel examples, we demonstrate that $n$-torsion in $NK_1GQ(R)$ can occur even when standard torsion is absent, indicating that Bass nil-groups can exhibit greater complexity than their unitary or Steinberg counterparts. We also provide a negative answer to specific questions raised by C. Poloni and A. Sieradski. Finally, in our concluding remarks, we outline several promising avenues for future research. These findings build upon, and extend, earlier work by C. Poloni and the authors regarding NK-groups in higher dimensions. While it is well-established that NK$_{i}G(R)$ and NK$_{i}U(R)$ are torsion-free for $i\geq 2$, no prior research has addressed NK$_{1}GQ(R)$. To prepare the ground for this study, we examine a connection between Bass nil-groups and nil-groups of type A defined by Bak. We demonstrate that while NK$_{1}GQ(R)$ is invariably torsion-free for Bak's unitary groups, it can contain elements of order $k$ for rings $R$, a scenario impossible for unitary groups. Although NK$_{1}GQ(R)$ are modules over certain rings $S$ where $K_{2q}(S)=0$ for all $q\geq 1$ (ensuring no $2q$-torsion), this constraint does not preclude the presence of $k$-torsion when $k$ is odd. Finally, we provide an alternative proof for the torsion-free nature of NK$_{1}UQ(R)$ by extending a method originally employed by A. Suslin. Specifically, we construct the algebraic $K$-theory spectrum $BPU(R)$ for partially free rings $R$ and utilize its connective cover to demonstrate nil-freeness. This strategy builds upon a proof by A. Suslin concerning the projectivity of Bass nil-groups. Suslin's original approach relied on algebraic K-theory; however, we adapt his arguments to apply to Bak's unitary theory, thereby extending his results to the context of Bak's unitary groups.

This paper introduces off-policy model-based RL, a technique that addresses the typical requirement of model-based approaches for policy-compliant data by leveraging extensive off-policy datasets. This approach examines various parallel strategies applied to the car sequencing problem, a critical optimization task within manufacturing that arranges ordered vehicles for production. The objective is to minimize the total cost resulting from granting, rejecting, or deferring exception requests based on their specific characteristics and the plant's exception robustness. This study addresses solutions with fixed exception robustness levels and explores establishing optimal communication patterns to align with the parallel strategy's strengths and weaknesses. Four distinct patterns are analyzed using four corresponding parallel strategies, tested across three robustness levels via evolutionary algorithms. Results indicate that hierarchical-based patterns are most efficient for small populations, while round-robin-based patterns perform better with larger populations, a finding supported by experimental outcomes. Additionally, increasing exception robustness yields the greatest cost reductions, and higher population sizes particularly benefit round-robin-based patterns. All experiments were conducted on a cluster of eight cores within a high-performance computing environment. These par-based EAs achieve superior or comparable performance compared to the best current state-of-the-art solutions in the literature. The comprehensive evaluation of communication pattern-based PEAs, validated by extensive experiments, offers practical guidelines for selecting the most suitable pattern for any specific application scenario. The paper also details the implementation of these algorithms in a high-performance environment. Furthermore, this work represents the first application of parallel strategies to the car sequencing problem. Source code and experimental data are available at https://github.com/fernandafm/CarSequencing. Future research will investigate adapting these algorithms to determine optimal exception robustness levels during the optimization process. Additionally, further work will address dynamic sequence planning, where exceptions may emerge after production has already commenced. Finally, applying these algorithms to other established planning problems remains a valuable avenue for research. 17-BLG-1430 was recently confirmed as a single-lens event through analysis of two high-cadence Keck telescope data sets, which detected strong caustic crossings. Spectroscopic observations identified an A-type host star with a mass of approximately 1.9 M$_\odot$, an angular radius of 2 $\mu$as, and a distance of roughly 2.3 kpc. By combining the microlensing parallax measurement (for plane perpendicular distance) and the angular size data (for absolute plane perpendicular distance), we determined the star's line-of-sight distance to be 2.34 ± 0.14 kpc. The planet's angular semimajor axis was calculated as 1.05 ± 0.08 mas, corresponding to a physical semimajor axis of 2.41$_{-0.57}^{+0.54}$ AU. The planet's mass is approximately 20 M$_{\rm J}$, with an additional solution at 8 M$_{\rm J}$ favored by the lensing signal at the 3.2$\sigma$ level. This system represents one of the warm, massive giant planets discovered via microlensing to date and serves as a strong candidate for one of the most massive warm Jupiters known in the Milky Way. Furthermore, it is the third warm massive planet identified by the OGLE survey. The frequent detection of caustic crossings in OGLE events significantly enhances the likelihood of finding more warm massive planets in the future. This specific event highlights the potential for discovering warm massive planets in the near term. Additionally, this system is significant as it is likely the youngest massive planet discovered thus far.

Recent investigations into exciton-mediated energy transport reveal two primary mechanisms: the first involves the collective oscillation of bound electron-hole pairs induced by an external electric field generated by laser pulses, while the second arises from quantum tunneling of electrons between different excitons. This study explores two distinct regimes applicable to long-pulse conditions in Floquet engineering, comparing them with the established ultrashort pulse regime. Our results indicate that these energy transport processes can be optimized by adjusting specific experimental parameters. We have also included a theoretical overview of the mechanisms governing these phenomena. Our findings offer a comprehensive perspective on exciton-mediated energy transport, presenting avenues for future experimental optimization. Neutron depolarization measurements were conducted on both single crystals and polycrystalline samples. In the La$_{0.98}$Ce$_{0.02}$MO$_3$ single crystal, the scattering of neutron polarization at the Curie temperature is more pronounced than in single-phase LaMnO$_3$. This behavior contrasts with the scattering at the second-order transition in La$_{0.98}$Ca$_{0.02}$MnO$_3$, which vanishes at the transition. Neutron depolarization studies on the La$_{0.98}$Ce$_{0.02}$MnO$_3$ polycrystalline sample revealed time-dependent scattering at the Curie temperature, indicating short-range magnetic correlations. This observation signifies a change from long-range ferromagnetism to short-range correlated spin glass behavior. This shift in long-range magnetic ordering to a short-range spin glass state represents a significant alteration in bulk magnetic properties, comparable in significance to changes in long-range antiferromagnetic ordering. This modification in bulk magnetic behavior is anticipated based on recent nematic magnetic phase observations in Ce-doped LaMnO$_3$. This work contributes to the broader understanding of how electron correlations influence long-range magnetic ordering in transition metal oxides. Additionally, we evaluated the scattering at the Curie temperature using both crystals and polycrystals, demonstrating that neutron depolarization is a viable, non-invasive technique for investigating long-range correlations in transition metal oxides. This capability is crucial for examining doped systems traversing long-range to short-range magnetic ordering changes. Furthermore, we highlight that neutron depolarization offers a unique, complementary approach to neutron diffraction for studying material properties. Finally, we suggest that neutron depolarization is a promising, generally applicable method for use in existing and upcoming neutron facilities. (HI) maps, generated from large radio telescopes, offer a promising new tool for studying the gravitational potential of spiral galaxies. This work presents an analysis of the outer disk of the spiral galaxy NGC 1569-1 (UGC 2845), using a newly released HI map with 1.2 km/s spectral resolution covering an area of 8400 square degrees. By comparing this new map with an earlier, lower-resolution image of the same region, we identify a significant morphological shift: the spiral arm in the older map appears to have unwound in the newer data. We evaluate whether this change is an artifact of lower resolution or a genuine evolution in the spiral structure. Our investigation explores three primary explanations for this "unwinding" phenomenon. The first involves the position-velocity (PV) diagram sampling method; we demonstrate that a single HI image can yield markedly different PV samples depending on the selected position and velocity range, and we apply a consistent sampling strategy to both observations. The second cause is real variations in neutral gas distribution along the spiral arm, which can create the illusion of unwinding when comparing different segments of the position-velocity curve. The third possibility is a true evolutionary change in the galaxy's structure. Supporting the hypothesis of unwinding, we observe a shift in the location of position-velocity curves in the high-resolution map compared to the low-resolution one. Additionally, we detect a shift in neutral gas distribution that could be attributed to warping or twisting of the arm. Finally, we identify a notable change in neutral gas morphology that cannot be attributed to warping or twisting alone. Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that the spiral arm of NGC 1569-1 is unwinding over time. This observation aligns with theoretical models of galactic evolution, where galactic disks unwind as they age. We further confirm that neutral gas is more tightly coupled to the stellar disk in younger galaxies, causing their spiral arms to unwind more rapidly. Our results also corroborate independent evidence for galactic unwinding derived from H\alpha maps. Ultimately, these findings underscore the value of neutral gas data for investigating galactic evolution. Future studies should aim to quantify the rate of unwinding and correlate it with other galactic properties, such as age, to better understand this phenomenon. Additionally, similar analyses on older galaxies could help establish a relationship between unwinding rates, ages, and other dynamical characteristics. This research contributes to our broader understanding of how galactic structures evolve. (

Its light curves reveal a long-term variability characterized by two distinct high-activity intervals: the first spanning 1985 to 1992, and the second covering periods between 2002–2005 and 2009–2010. examine the topological structure of algebraic sets defined by polynomials that are irreducible over the base field but become reducible when extended to an algebraic closure of a subfield. We define the concept of "algebraic independence" for polynomial sets and demonstrate that irreducibility is maintained under polynomial composition if the inner polynomial is algebraically independent from the set extending over which irreducibility is being tested. Furthermore, we show that the union of varieties corresponding to factors of a reducible polynomial consists of a finite number of irreducible components, each parameterized by univariate rational functions. This allows us to construct a hierarchical topological representation of such sets, analogous to octree representations of 3D sets or piecewise linear surfaces. We name this representation a "spree tree." We provide a proof of the existence of an algorithm to generate spree trees for any set of polynomials where the inner polynomials are mutually algebraically independent, along with an algorithm to identify and isolate irreducible sets within a given collection. We also outline criteria for choosing an appropriate number of sample points to represent the spree tree, analogous to sampling criteria for smooth surfaces and similar to point count guidelines for determining irreducible set membership. These points can be generated using established pseudo-random number generators. Finally, we present several worked examples of constructed spree trees. We argue that spree trees offer a highly efficient and compact method for representing and visualizing algebraic sets, with wide-ranging applications in mathematics and mathematical biology. We anticipate that the theory and algorithms for constructing and querying these trees will be developed into specialized software. Keywords: algebraic sets, spree trees, iso-surfaces, iso-surfaces, algebraic independence, algebraic sets, hierarchical topological representations, iso-surface sampling. This study introduces a method for analyzing experiments using 7-11 GeV/c$^2$ dark matter candidates that employ superconducting CRESST detectors, which offer a massive 150 kg of exposed target material. We present a formulation for calculating the expected annual number of nuclear recoils resulting from the interaction of a specific dark matter candidate with a given target nucleus. To demonstrate the application of this formula, we examine dark matter scenarios featuring a 50 GeV/c$^2$ mass and 10 pb cross section. Additionally, we generate predictions for the signature count rate of 7-11 GeV/c$^2$ dark matter candidate interactions, considering a 2-year SuperCOLD-1 experiment and a prospective SuperCRESST II collaboration involving seven nations. Our findings indicate that, given a locally produced halo history and the cited cross section, a dark matter candidate with a 50 GeV/c$^2$ mass and 10 pb cross section would generate approximately 15 nuclear recoils over a 2-year SuperCOLD-1 duration and roughly 70 recoils in a seven-nation SuperCRESST II collaboration. These results suggest that a multi-year collaboration could achieve a nuclear recoil background level of less than one event. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dark matter candidates within the 7-11 GeV/c$^2$ mass range can be identified with approximately 80 nuclear recoil signatures. Finally, we show that dark matter candidates with masses up to 50 GeV/c$^2$ and cross sections as low as 1 pb may be detectable. Such detections could establish a significant milestone for the direct detection of sub-GeV/c$^2$ dark matter. This capability could be realized either by expanding the CRESST experimental collaboration or by integrating a superconducting detector network into a broader, well-coordinated international collaboration. We conclude that the pursuit of this goal will significantly advance the field of direct dark matter detection. This issue is especially critical for robots operating in unstructured environments, where real-time decisions must be made with low latency. We introduce a solution that enables such robots to utilize the extensive pool of pre-trained models by supporting diverse end-point implementations. Our approach comprises two core components. First, we developed NeuroTune, a library that optimizes model execution on a specific target by automatically selecting and refining the most appropriate execution method. Second, we established a cloud of containers, each pre-equipped with every available target implementation for every model, thereby eliminating the need for compilers or build systems at the endpoint. We assessed our framework across ten platforms (covering compilers, GPUs, and specialized accelerators) and eight models. The resulting system achieves faster execution times than raw compilers in 75% of cases and matches the performance of specialized GPU code in the remaining 25%. Container deployment on internet services reduces end-point latency to near zero in almost all scenarios. Consequently, our framework reduces latency by over 2x in 93.75% of tested configurations. This solution paves the way for robots to deploy pre-trained neural networks in diverse settings, regardless of whether they are controlled via code or container services. Today, it constitutes a well-developed and established discipline. At its core lies equational logic—the study of algebras modulo equivalence relations defined by rewrite rules—which serves as a foundational component for equational programming and the verification of algebraic structures in both classical and quantum computing. This paper offers a concise overview of equational logic's history and evolution. It begins with the historical and mathematical foundations of rewriting theory in computer science, followed by a discussion of current research directions. The authors aim to illustrate how equational logic has matured into a sophisticated field, vital for applications spanning software and hardware development to the formulation of quantum mechanical laws. While the field is largely rooted in classical algebra, this work also addresses the emerging intersection of rewriting theory and modern field theory, specifically within the nascent field of term rewriting. Additionally, it explores the relationship between equational logic and the verification of algebraic structures in quantum computing. We demonstrate that many such verifications rely fundamentally on equational logic, a field that has expanded significantly recently with applications in quantum computing and the verifiability of quantum software. Although the primary focus remains on classical computing, we also highlight the growing connection between rewriting theory and the emerging field of quantum computing, exemplified by the verification of algebraic structures essential for these technologies. We argue that this relationship is robust and that the advances in quantum software verification have propelled equational logic into a new era. We provide a detailed, simplified example of the most renowned protocol in quantum key distribution, the BB84 protocol. We show that a significant number of steps in proving the protocol's security can be represented as rewrite rules, and we present a concise set of examples that may be considered canonical within the field. Finally, we outline various existing and proposed methods for the automated verification of quantum computational processes using term rewriting, concluding with a discussion on the current state of the art in this domain. We argue that the field is poised for rapid growth, potentially driven by the demands of quantum computing research. Although this area is still in its infancy, we believe that the expertise accumulated from years of classical research is uniquely positioned to facilitate this expansion. While FL allows for the generation of personalized recommendations without accessing user data, the personalized model parameters stored on client devices pose a risk if compromised. To address this, we propose FPRL, which applies Privacy-preserving Rewriting for Local Aggregated Models to combine the adaptability of personalized parameters with unidirectional privacy protection during FL training. Specifically, when FPRL integrates with FL, local aggregated models are sent to clients for rewriting to derive global model parameters, ensuring that client data remains inaccessible to the recommendation service. As a contribution to advancing both the privacy and security of recommender systems, we provide a unified, flexible solution to simultaneously safeguard against localized threats and risks to centralized recommendation services. This allows companies to prioritize specific threats while leveraging complementary protection for the other threat type. To overcome this constraint, we introduce a new framework termed the Image-Image Transfer Network for Segmentation and Restoration (IITS). This approach facilitates the sharing of features and knowledge between tasks, enabling the training of a multi-task network using a small collection of images from a single domain. During training, IITS employs a novel knowledge transfer technique that allows one image within the dataset to sequentially assume the role of a ground truth ground image to train a sub-network, which contributes its learned knowledge to a cumulative network. This process repeats for each image in the dataset. Consequently, IITS necessitates only a minimal number of annotated images and eliminates the need to learn or input any external ground truth during inference. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that IITS outperforms single-task networks and other multi-task approaches, achieving superior accuracy and maintaining higher accuracy consistency across tasks. Furthermore, to validate its efficacy, we apply IITS to super-resolution, single and multi-exposure image fusion, and image-super resolution fusion. In these scenarios, the network demonstrates rapid convergence and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Finally, we show that IITS effectively handles generalization to images entirely unseen during training. Overall, IITS offers an efficient alternative for segmentation and restoration that requires minimal training data and annotating effort. Furthermore, its straightforward implementation allows it to be readily integrated into deep neural networks. To ensure reproducibility, the source code is made publicly available. We anticipate that IITS will contribute to the advancement of image restoration and potentially impact other related fields. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/zhongjasonli/IITS. Keyboards are frequently employed to input text, yet they have primarily been designed based on phoneme-specific characteristics, often neglecting the distinct properties of other writing systems. While English utilizes an alphabet composed of phoneme-based units, other systems, such as Pinyin (for Mandarin), utilize syllable-based characters. However, existing keyboard research has largely concentrated on phoneme-based systems. This paper introduces PinyinKey, a novel syllable-based keyboard tailored for Mandarin Chinese. To assess its performance, we first compiled a corpus of frequent syllables derived from frequently used characters in printed materials. We then tested PinyinKey against the prevalent phoneme-based layout QWERTY. PinyinKey outperformed QWERTY, accelerating typing speeds by 28% for beginners and 16% for advanced users. Additionally, we conducted a user study to evaluate entry fluency, which PinyinKey also enhanced. These findings suggest that extending syllable abstraction to other languages could yield similar advantages.

Standard inflationary models rely on a scalar inflaton field undergoing slow-roll inflation, generating extensive scalar particle production and a related friction force that dampens SUSY particle motion. Following the inflationary phase, the SUSY particles are assumed to decouple from the inflaton and re-enter the universe, where they decay into lighter SUSY particles. This work specifically examines the cosmological constraints on the SUSY lifetime, which is dictated by the decay process, as well as the lower limit on the SUSY mass, determined by the threshold at which particles decouple from the inflaton. Additionally, the upper limit on the SUSY mass is established by the inflationary cosmology itself, arising from the inflation-induced scalar particle production and the friction force it creates. Finally, the study analyzes the relationship between SUSY parameters and their respective limits derived from these cosmological frameworks, with a particular focus on the mass of the lightest SUSY particle, which serves as the primary dark matter candidate in this scenario. This particle is responsible for the dark matter abundance observed today, determined by its lifetime, its mass, and the abundance generated during the inflationary epoch. Consequently, the consistency between the Saha abundance of the universe and the observed total dark matter abundance imposes a constraint on the SUSY lifetime, which is comparable to the lifetime derived from the experimental lower bound on dark matter density. Furthermore, the abundance of relativistic species during inflation imposes a significant constraint on the model parameters, including the SUSY lifetime, the mass of the lightest SUSY particle, and the density of lightest SUSY particles produced, which must align with the observed dark matter abundance to satisfy the consistency condition. Finally, the magnitude of the inflation scale sets the upper limit on the SUSY mass; if this limit exceeds current experimental bounds, the non-observation of SUSY particles at colliders would constitute strong evidence for the existence of SUSY and a specific solution to the hierarchy problem. Profitability for the agents is determined at the end of a fixed simulation period, allowing a clear distinction between genuine forecasting and speculative ventures. various computer-aided engineering (CAD) applications, the necessity for precise and reliable data becomes paramount. This requirement is particularly critical in fields involving human safety, where even minor errors can have severe consequences. While numerical results are frequently presented as comprehensive tables or detailed graphs, there is a growing trend toward sharing them as concise summaries. Although these brief summaries enhance readability and understanding, they unfortunately create a false sense of security regarding the accuracy of the underlying data. Consequently, this paper proposes a framework designed to quantify uncertainty, an aspect often omitted from traditional reporting. Since the concept of quantified uncertainty is unfamiliar to many CAD engineers, we illustrate its formulation within diverse engineering contexts, such as computational fluid dynamics and finite element analysis, to demonstrate its universal applicability. Furthermore, we structure this discussion to cater to two distinct audiences: CAD engineers, for whom we emphasize motivation, conceptions, and existing uncertainty quantification methods, and mathematicians and computer scientists, for whom we outline the mathematical foundations and emerging challenges. Finally, to address data validity, we introduce a novel concept for quantifying data authenticity and discuss its theoretical and practical implications for high-performance computing and data engineering. The research presented in this document serves as a significant initial step toward establishing a robust standard for uncertainty quantification. This standard is essential for CAD applications to ensure that numerical outputs are both accurate and reliable for end-users. Without such standards, there remains a significant risk that invalid or misleading data will be inadvertently shared, potentially leading to erroneous conclusions. Key words: reliability and validity, data authenticity, finite element analysis, computational fluid dynamics, uncertainty quantification, CAD engineering. (PDF format: 10 pages, 2 figures). In this study, we derive solutions for charged black strings within the Rastall framework using the 3+1 Einstein-Raukardt time-orthogonal coordinate system. We identify two distinct families of these black strings, corresponding to Rastall parameters $\theta = 0$ and $\theta \neq 0$. Building upon previously calculated thermodynamic properties for the $\theta = 0$ case, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the thermodynamics, rotational characteristics, and stability for the $\theta \neq 0$ scenario. We examine the interrelationships among these physical properties and explore their relationships with both the earlier $\theta = 0$ study and existing literature. Furthermore, we illustrate the behavior of these charged black strings through graphical representations, utilizing the dimensionless Rastall parameter $\theta^*$. Our findings indicate that stability is independent of the string's charge; consequently, the thermodynamic behavior, including ergospheres and phase transitions, remains unchanged whether or not the string is charged. Additionally, we demonstrate that the primary impact of Rastall parameter $\theta$ is to shift the ergospheres and horizons. Finally, we compare these Rastall gravity solutions with those from other studies, including various quantum corrected anti-de Sitter (AdS) black string models. We observe that a minimal length scale can arise from quantum corrections in those models, yet this effect is negligible when $\theta^*$ remains small. These results suggest that quantum corrections and minor variations in the Rastall parameter $\theta$ may hold significant potential for investigating the physics of black strings. Additionally, we provide a brief discussion on strings localized near the horizon. In this context, we find that the effective potential becomes positive, causing the strings to oscillate around the horizon. This phenomenon may be linked to the thermodynamic behavior of horizon-localized strings, offering potential avenues for future research. We also analyze the superradiant instability, noting that for a fixed string charge $Q_{s}$, increasing the Rastall parameter $\theta$ can shift the instability region. This implies that quantum corrections or a small value of $\theta$ could enable the existence of superradiant unstable strings, a possibility worth exploring in future work. These results aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of black string behavior. # 1. INTRODUCTION

Analyzing user-user dependencies in social media platforms is crucial for numerous applications, including influence maximization, information diffusion, and news dissemination. A common and effective approach for capturing dependencies among a large user base involves network reconstruction, which utilizes partial observations to discover representative user groups. A prominent example is the Twitter follower-follows graph, where directed edges represent relationships. Reconstructing these graphs enables the identification of key structural features, such as community structures and influence relationships. In this study, we investigate the magnetic properties of the widely used LaCo$_5$ alloy by computing its exchange interactions and magnetic anisotropy using density functional theory (DFT). Our results demonstrate that high-spin states of Co atoms stabilize at low temperatures. By employing a DFT+U approach, we calculated the magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) across various temperatures for different particle sizes. Our findings indicate a strong dependence of MAE on particle size and reveal a significant temperature-induced decrease in anisotropy. Notably, the MAE of smaller nanoparticles is several times greater than that of bulk materials, a effect that diminishes as particle size increases. Additionally, we observed that MAE varies with particle orientation and is approximately twice as large for in-plane orientation compared to perpendicular orientation. Finally, the average MAE exhibits a strong correlation with the average total angular momentum, which also decreases as particle temperature rises. These results provide valuable theoretical insights into utilizing high-temperature DFT methods to accurately model the magnetic properties of size-dependent nanoparticles. We further discuss the potential experimental applications of our theoretical predictions. Our computational approach is based on the work of Zhang et al. [Phys. Rev. B 105, 054410 (2022)]. The computational time required for a single calculation is approximately 10 minutes per nanoparticle using 128-core CPU cores. These findings represent valuable theoretical contributions to the field of magnetic materials and nanoparticles. The experimental verification of our predictions is currently underway. Our work is also relevant to materials where exchange interactions and anisotropy are sensitive to rare earth content and temperature. a dominant model in online advertising. In this framework, an advertiser participates in an auction for every individual ad impression, requiring them to submit a price for each request. Consequently, bidding strategies are essential for maintaining competitiveness. However, current strategies primarily rely on historical statistics from the advertiser themselves and overlook the critical influence of the supply brand. Since brand quality significantly affects RTB outcomes, ignoring it can lead to losses. This paper introduces the first study to explicitly account for supply brand quality in real-time bidding decisions. Specifically, we model theRTB2 process as a game where a player's payoff incorporates the brand's quality. For any given instance, our approach constructs a supply brand quality measure using publicly available data without needing modifications to the system. We then apply this measure to design a novel utility function that balances cost expenditure and potential gain. This derived utility function informs the parameter selection strategy. Experimental results across two platforms demonstrate that, compared to standard cost-based bidding methods, bidders utilizing this utility function achieve, on average, a 30% to 40% increase in cost per mille (CPM). Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of this method against well-known bidding strategies in the RTB environment using reinforcement learning techniques. These evaluations indicate that while our method outperforms traditional cost-based approaches, it yields slightly lower results when compared directly to reinforcement learning-based strategies. Despite this slight discrepancy, experimental data confirms that incorporating supply brand quality allows our method to achieve a performance level nearly equivalent to reinforcement learning. These findings suggest that integrating supply brand quality into the bidding process is a highly effective strategy. Finally, we also examine the theoretical implications of our utility function design. These analyses reveal that the method exhibits strong robustness in low-frequency scenarios and performs comparably to reinforcement learning under normal conditions. Additionally, it offers superior adaptability to varying cost targets. Collectively, these results reinforce the effectiveness of incorporating supply brand quality in real-time bidding. We identify systems that maintain Wigner negativity conditionally given prior quantum correlations, yielding a system of inequality constraints on correlation measures for these cases. Conversely, we characterize systems that become Wigner negative conditionally given earlier quantum correlations, resulting in systems that are unbounded. The boundaries of both type systems are defined by Gaussian states, which also represent the system's closure. The concepts of boundary and systemically Wigner negative are illustrated using two-variable Gaussian states and single-variable non-Gaussian Gatoxian states. Finally, we investigate the total order of Wigner negativity and quantum correlations, finding that the order is determined by systems where Wigner negativity is boundary-equivalent, with the total order boundary state exhibiting the maximum order of Wigner negativity and the smallest order of quantum correlations. These findings offer a systematic approach to characterizing Wigner negativity and quantum correlations. Additionally, we propose an experimental method to numerically calculate the conditionally generating set, boundary set, and boundary of Wigner negativity for multi-mode quantum systems with Wigner negativity. However, recent studies suggest that scattering off charged particles might propel this approach into previously uncharted dark matter parameter spaces. In this work, we examine the implications for boosted dark matter when scattering off quarks produces non-negligible radiative corrections to the dark matter-nucleon cross section. These radiative effects can be derived analytically to order $\alpha_s$ using standard techniques, allowing us to map out the parameter space applicable to boosted boosted dark matter scenarios. We further assess the implications of these radiative corrections for searches utilizing boosted chi candidates at the LHC. The findings presented here establish an analytical framework for incorporating radiative corrections in dark matter scattering off the quark constituents of protons and neutrons. This framework demonstrates that radiative corrections can substantially alter cross sections, thereby significantly influencing both direct detection experiments and dark matter production yields at the LHC. Additionally, we show that radiative corrections can notably impact the phenomenology of boosted dark matter, potentially rendering previously excluded parameter regions accessible. Finally, we outline a proposed future analysis strategy that accounts for radiative corrections in quantum field theoretic calculations of radiative chiral symmetry breaking in QCD. This work serves as a foundational step toward implementing such calculations within a comprehensive global analysis framework for physics beyond the Standard Model. The proposed analysis could reveal new physics by identifying a surplus of radiatively corrected events relative to the expected background from standard dark matter-nucleon scattering. Furthermore, this analysis could refine existing limits on light dark matter scenarios, thereby enhancing prospects for LHC searches targeting radiatively corrected chiral symmetry breaking. In a broader context, the analysis techniques employed here are widely applicable across various quantum field theories, potentially uncovering novel physics beyond current capabilities. Ultimately, these findings may open new frontiers in the search for light dark matter. A noise-robust feature vector is extracted from the received signal and utilized as input for the proposed detection scheme. Additionally, the DCNN exhibits robustness against adversarial noise attacks, a capability absent in other detection schemes. This insight enables us to derive universal correlation functions for the eigenvalues in terms of random Hermitian matrices with a fixed, purely imaginary spectral density. We also prove that the spectral density and the imaginary (level spacing) density of these derived random Hermitian matrices both converge to the Wigner semicircle law, revealing a role for the spectral density in counting eigenvalues of non-Hermitian random matrices within ensembles defined by fixed complex entries. Lett. 24, 140 (1970)], which are highly relevant to random matrix theory, random scattering matrices, and random dynamical systems. The distribution of this random variable is typically treated as a fixed, known factor. However, in finite samples, this random parameter can be viewed as a random effect, with its underlying distribution acting as a random parameter. Bayesian methods offer a framework for simultaneously estimating the distribution of the random effect alongside the distribution of the extreme value distribution. We develop a Bayesian model using non-informative priors for both the distribution of the random effect and its associated hyperparameters. An example is provided to demonstrate the application of these priors. Simulation studies reveal that, within the typical finite sample sizes encountered in real-world analysis, this approach may produce estimates for the hyperparameters of the random effect's distribution that are significantly biased relative to the underlying true parameters. These issues are exacerbated when the threshold is set low. Consequently, we recommend employing Bayesian estimation with non-informative hyperparameters only when the dataset is sufficiently large to yield stable results. Furthermore, simulation results indicate that employing these non-informative hyperparameters does not enhance point estimates for the primary parameters of interest compared to other selection methods. Additionally, Monte Carlo studies show that Bayesian estimation using non-informative hyperparameters does not improve estimated prediction intervals for future observations compared to other selection techniques. Therefore, there is no rationale for selecting these non-informative hyperparameters. We conclude that when analyzing extreme value data, exceedances should be modeled as a Poisson process with a random mean following a known distribution, where parameters for this distribution must be estimated from the data rather than assumed a priori. Non-bayesian estimation of these random-effect distributions can be achieved using parametric or non-parametric methods. The selection of an appropriate parametric distribution can be guided by Monte Carlo evidence comparing estimated prediction intervals for future observations across different choices. Non-paramatic estimation can be implemented via the Poisson bootstrap or local likelihood methods. We provide a brief overview of the Poisson bootstrap method and sketch the local likelihood approach. Both techniques yield more accurate estimation of prediction intervals than any other method we tested. A real data example confirms these findings and shows that Pseudo Maximum Likelihood estimation can produce prediction intervals that are either biased or excessively narrow. We advise against using non-informative hyperparameters for Bayesian estimation of mixed Poisson models for exceedances. However, these protocols are limited to single-pulse encoding and cannot handle the multiphoton pulses inevitable in realistic laser-based systems. This paper examines QKD schemes utilizing laser sources that are beneficial by eliminating the need for photon number resolving detectors on the receiver side and remaining safe from general individual attacks. Such schemes accommodate practical losses, allowing the sender to either detect or ignore multiphoton pulses. We demonstrate that if eavesdropping is limited to a specific set of strategies, a higher secret key rate can be achieved. Furthermore, we examine a family of protocols where the sender randomly transmits $n$-photon pulses, rendering them resilient to general individual attacks; we analyze the benefits and drawbacks of these approaches and their corresponding key rates. Finally, we illustrate the advantages and constraints of these protocols through numerical simulations using a simple channel model. We conclude that a protocol with at least one successful key distribution event for every transmitted pulse offers the highest secret key rate. Furthermore, we find that when the channel is sufficiently weak, the optimal source behaves as a non-deterministic deterministic dictator, which is immune to all individual attacks. While this field contribution is well-established for neutral particles, its existence as a measurable field angular momentum remains unconfirmed. In this study, we explicitly analyze the Gordon angular momentum for a non-relativistic, uncharged point charge in a magnetic field, demonstrating that the Gordon angular momentum density is infinite. Consequently, a finite total angular momentum can only be achieved by imposing an ad hoc boundary condition that sets the Gordon angular momentum flux to zero at the particle's location. This result suggests that the Gordon angular momentum for a non-relativistic point charge in a magnetic field is not observable in laboratory experiments. Furthermore, we observe that a finite Gordon angular momentum emerges only when the charge is confined to a finite region. We then compare this finding with the measurable angular momentum of a charged, spinning dielectric sphere in a magnetic field, which corresponds to the classical spinning-current model. This comparison highlights the critical difference between a current on a boundary and a charge distributed throughout the volume. Finally, we briefly explore extensions of this problem to neutral particles and rotating electric or magnetic dipoles. While the primary objective of risk assessment in this context is identifying and analyzing potential threats, current risk analysis tools often fail to address the specific requirements of industrial environments. This paper introduces a novel approach to threat analysis that incorporates the constraints of the target system to generate more realistic attack paths. The proposed methodology utilizes a graph structure to represent constraint-dependent attack paths, employing a modification of Prim's algorithm for its identification. Furthermore, the analysis is constrained by the specific characteristics of the target system, such as the absence of remote access or the absence of specific exploits. To validate this approach, the authors implemented a proof-of-concept tool named ICSSysAttack. This tool accepts a vulnerability matrix as well as physical and logical system descriptions as inputs. The study also outlines the application of this methodology to a Smart Grid system to demonstrate constraint-dependent attack path analysis. Finally, the paper discusses future research directions regarding threat analysis in constrained systems. A supplementary video explaining the motivation and results is available at https://youtu.be/_dGKJQ2Q0b8. To ensure safety, prevent damage, and maintain availability, industrial organizations must implement detection mechanisms that identify and respond to threats. Given that threats in industrial systems can be highly constraint-dependent, it is crucial for intrusion detection systems to continuously generate up-to-date lists of threats and threat paths. By understanding these constraint-dependent threats, security teams can develop appropriate countermeasures and develop a deeper understanding of the threats facing their specific system. Furthermore, this methodology facilitates the prioritization of security improvements based on the specific threat landscape. While several works have been developed to identify potential attacks, none currently address constraint-dependent threats; existing solutions typically rely on Vulnerability Assessment Models (VAMs) that list all possible attacks without accounting for industrial system constraints. To solve this problem, one must first construct a system graph and integrate known vulnerabilities and capabilities into a vulnerability matrix. Since threats are dynamic, they require continuous updates. While some methods are dynamic, they still fail to capture the nuances of constraints. Therefore, it is essential to develop new approaches that identify constraint-dependent threats, analyze potential attack paths, and assist security teams in developing defense mechanisms. This section provides an overview of threat analysis and outlines directions for future research. The authors have made their code contributions public. The methodology is implemented in a tool called ICSSysAttack, which is documented in the paper's implementation section. Question-Answering (QA) systems are essential for extracting valuable insights from the vast array of data available today. These intelligent agents facilitate data retrieval and facilitate knowledge discovery and discovery across various domains, including education, medicine, and law. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of current developments in QA systems. It examines diverse QA types, covers traditional methods, reviews recent advancements leveraging deep learning and natural language inference, analyzes evaluation metrics, outlines challenges and future research directions, and provides benchmark datasets. The survey aims to guide researchers in QA system design and implementation and to help new entrants navigate the field.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in node classification tasks. However, the performance of these models is often constrained by the limited expressiveness of their topological structures. This limitation can be mitigated by incorporating external knowledge through knowledge graphs. We propose a novel approach that enhances GNN topologies by integrating these knowledge graphs. Our method initializes the adjacency matrix of the GNN using a pre-trained node embedding matrix derived from the knowledge graph and fine-tunes this matrix jointly with the GNN parameters. This technique is modular and can be applied to any GNN architecture. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the CiteSeck, Cora, and PubMed datasets. The implementation is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar-123/GNN-KG.

Our analysis reveals that in eight clusters, BHs are confined to the nuclear region, a distribution expected after the system has undergone core collapse, with a core radius significantly smaller than the half-light radius. Our primary finding is that the summed masses of BHs in these YSCs (up to 100 Myr) are substantially lower than the maximum masses predicted by recent theoretical models. **Conclusions.** The BH masses in these young clusters are far below the upper limits established by the "in-situ formation" scenario. Consequently, in young star clusters, BHs are likely not massive enough to gravitationally eject all low-mass stars from the cluster's core.

**Aims.** This study investigates the effect of the magnetic field on the phase space distribution of stars orbiting a supermassive black hole (SMBH) within the Galactic center. Specifically, it calculates the anisotropy parameter ($\beta$) for both non-magnetized and magnetized environments. Specifically, the anisotropy parameter ($\beta$) is computed for both non-magnetic and magnetic environments.**Methods.** We modeled stars orbiting the SMBH at the Galactic center under both non-magnetic and magnetic conditions. The orbital integrals required to calculate the anisotropy parameter were solved numerically.**Results.** Our findings indicate that the magnetic field can significantly alter the phase space distribution of stars around the SMBH, potentially causing the anisotropy parameter to become negative. These results align with previous empirical observations.**Conclusions.** The phase space distribution of stars around the Galactic center SMBH is heavily influenced by the magnetic field. VAEs) have emerged as a leading approach for unsupervised learning of latent representations, frequently applied in image processing to address tasks like semantic segmentation and image denoising. Although recent studies demonstrate that decoder-only architectures can outperform VAEs in these applications, they often require computational resources comparable to those of VAEs. This paper introduces a novel Distributions Autoencoder capable of matching the accuracy of VAEs in such contexts while simultaneously reducing memory usage, computational cost, and training time to levels similar to those of decoder-only models. Experimental results indicate that the proposed architecture performs at least as well as, if not better than, state-of-the-art VAEs on benchmark tasks in image denoising and semantic segmentation. Furthermore, it achieves at least a twofold increase in training speed and a 50% reduction in memory consumption compared to state-of-the-art VAEs. Crucially, the model uses a latent space of equivalent size, ensuring no loss in dimensionality. Additionally, the method is unlikely to encounter mode collapse during training. Extensive comparisons with state-of-the-art VAEs in both image denoising and semantic segmentation scenarios confirm the robustness of the proposed architecture. Current implementations are available at https://github.com/Alireza-Karimi/DistributionsAutoencoder. Ultimately, this approach offers a robust alternative to existing VAEs for image processing tasks in AI, providing improvements in both computational efficiency and performance. Future research will explore extending the architecture to other domains, such as speech recognition. The authors have committed to open-sourcing the implementation. Limited hardware capabilities often result in prolonged training durations and high energy consumption, which can be critical for battery-powered IoT systems. This challenge is exacerbated by the increasing data volume associated with expanding IoT networks, which can overwhelm cloud-based trainers with large scale. Simulation results indicate non-trivial performance gains regarding convergence, accuracy, and utility compared to traditional centralized or federated approaches. While current transformation-based models assume balanced tasks, real-world applications often require a single model to handle multiple tasks with significant disparity, such as compression and speech conversion, a scenario known as task-asymmetry. In these cases, a shared encoder extracts latent speech representations, while separate spectral transformations apply specific modifications before a shared decoder produces the final output. Although end-to-end deep learning offers advantages over end-to-end mapping, these benefits are diminished in task-asymmetric frameworks because training relies heavily on the spectral transformation module, which lacks output ground truth. To address this, we introduce a deep learning-based quantization method to generate task-specific targets for the spectral transformation module. We apply this strategy to task-asymmetric human speech compression and speech conversion, demonstrating that it yields a 3.4 dB improvement in compression quality and a 1.0 dB improvement in speech conversion quality. The method is versatile and can be adapted to other tasks. Given the growing demand for multi-task speech processing in practical settings, this research provides essential insights for developing high-quality solutions in such contexts. The findings encompass a new fixed-parameter algorithm based on the count of sources, an XP-algorithm defined by treewidth, and another fixed-parameter algorithm utilizing treedepth. All three methods stem from an innovative framework that integrates SPQR tree-decompositions with parameterized techniques. This approach not only unifies but also extends prior tractability results for series-parallel digraphs, single-source digraphs, and outerplanar digraphs. Notably, this is the first parameterized algorithm for the general upward planar drawability problem where the parameter is the treewidth. Additionally, the paper provides algorithmic characterizations of series-parallel and outerplanar directed graphs by combining existing characterizations with parameterized algorithms. Finally, the proposed parameterized algorithm represents an algorithmic extension of the complete characterization provided by Bousquet, Guedes de Oliveira, and Wernisch (2019) for single-source drawability in series-parallel digraphs. This extension yields the first parameterized algorithm (and thus also the first fixed-parameter algorithm) for the general upward planar drawability problem. Furthermore, it is the first parameterized algorithm that operates without relying on the $\Pi^0_1$-hardness of detecting $\Theta_3$-subdivisions found in previous work. These contributions represent two distinct avenues for advancing the current state of the art in parameterized algorithms for the general upward planar drawability problem. The paper also includes a comprehensive survey and comparison of exact algorithms for the upward planar drawability problem. Existing exact algorithms, which combine recoloring strategies with branch-and-bound, effectively integrate parameterized techniques by implicitly selecting small values for parameters such as treewidth and treedepth. This observation motivates the current research, which aims to develop parameterized algorithms that explicitly exploit the small treewidth and treedepth inherent to these algorithms. While both online (continuously updated) and offline (periodically updated) adaptive learning offer traditional benefits over batch training, this study demonstrates that a kernel-based neural network, when applied to sequence data, acts as a universal generator for adapting to data and model drift. By simply substituting standard feedforward or neural network layers with our proposed kernel-like neural layer, we enable these models to handle, generate, and even predict future drifts in both covariate and concept shifts. We validate the universal generation and processing capabilities of our layer using Monte Carlo simulations with various non-parametric density generators. Additionally, we analyze predictive adaptation for an agent navigating a stochastic environment using a partially observable Markov decision process, where a agent with a memoryless model is outperformed by one utilizing a memory-based kernel estimate of the environment's stochasticity. Finally, we present evidence that a neural network with a kernel-like layer can achieve adaptive generation and prediction for an unknown student with a non-parametric model. This is proven by training a suitable kernel-like neural network on a small training set of student responses to test items, allowing it to universally generate, process, and predict the student's future responses, including those to unseen items. Empirical results confirm that this network approach surpasses several simpler baselines, such as a memoryless kernel estimator and a hidden Markov model. Furthermore, a novel metric is proposed to predict a student's concept mastery, relying on the assumption that concept mastery is independent of the specific content of individual items. This study represents one of the first non-memory-based attempts at predictive adaptation and is the first to apply kernel-like neural networks for this purpose. The source code is available at https://github.com/andrew-karpukhin/Kernal-Like-Neural-Networks. Furthermore, this paper is the first to establish a link between kernels and neural networks, a connection that has been independently and significantly developed in recent years, leading to new architectures that enhance the adaptivity and generalizability of various computer vision and natural language processing tasks. Specifically, for a transfer operator possessing an spectral gap and enhanced mixing properties within spaces of smooth observables, we establish the existence of a fractional time derivative that eliminates its decoupled, decay-induced component. This approach removes the necessity for hyperbolic periodic or recuring systems to satisfy mixing conditions in smooth spaces and extends applicable results to nonuniformly and nonuniformly hyperbolic continuous dynamical systems. Furthermore, we impose significantly weaker mixing requirements on Sina\u010d's random walk constructed via the dynamic partition method for uniformly hyperbolic semiflows. For both dynamics and stochastic processes, our framework yields new findings. In the nonuniformly hyperbolic setting, it enables the construction of a cohomologically equivalent dynamics that achieves exponential decay of correlations in Sobolev spaces of finite order and a corresponding Markovian diffusion limit for the associated stochastic process. For the uniformly and hyperbolic nonuniformly expanding Sina\u010d's random walk, we establish a diffusion limit in a stronger $L^2$-sense. These outcomes complement recent diffusions observed in Sina\u010d's non-uniformly expanding semiflows and the uniformly hyperbolic Axiom A diffeomorphisms and Anosov flows. Additionally, our framework offers a novel, self-contained, and largely model-independent perspective on the relationship between the diffusive behavior of a stochastic process and the decay of correlations of its Koopman operator. Finally, our methods apply to a broad class of continuous dynamical systems with physical decay of correlations, including thermodynamic formalism and the Zorich transfer operator. Consequently, our work introduces new, quantifiable decay rates in $L^2$ for the Zorich transfer operator and provides a stochastic derivation of a dynamical systems formula for the central limit theorem associated with the Zorich quadratic differential. Limitations and future research directions are discussed. Key areas of research include thermodynamic formalism, stochastic differential equations, and related operator theoretic and PDE questions. The research was conducted within the European Centre of Excellence DigiThm, with additional components developed at the European Mathematical Institute. Given a set of nonlocal games $\G$ and a classical game $\g$ that cannot be won by classical strategies but can be approximated by quantum strategies within error $\epsilon$, a new game $\g^\epsilon(\G)$ is constructed. It is demonstrated that $\g^\epsilon(\G)$ admits perfect quantum simulability, whereas $\g$ itself does not achieve perfect simulation. Furthermore, the paper investigates the relationship between nonlocal games reducible to games with two input questions per player and those with a single input question. Finally, the issue of whether the set of these games forms a "class" is examined. The results indicate that the set of hereditary nonlocal games does form a class, a property leveraged to establish the nonlocality of several prominent single-question games, including chained Bell games, nonlocal games derived from symmetric matrices, and nonlocal games with one input question and a constant number of outputs. Additionally, it is proven that a classical strategy can achieve a perfect score for $\g^\epsilon(\G)$ only if $\g$ cannot be played with quantum strategies to an error less than $\epsilon$. The paper also reviews the relationship between single-question games and those featuring a single input question for one player and a constant number of output questions for the other. Furthermore, it is shown that if such a game does not allow classical strategies to achieve a perfect score, then $\g^\epsilon(\G)$ cannot be perfectly simulated by quantum strategies. Consequently, an upper bound on the $\chi^2$ distance is derived. Finally, the paper constructs a family of single-question games with a constant output question where $\g^\epsilon(\G)$ remains perfectly simlatable by quantum strategies. Notably, it is observed that if such a game's scores are not perfectly distinguished by classical strategies, then $\g^\epsilon(\G)$ cannot be perfectly simulated by quantum strategies. These findings are applied to analyze the nonlocality of various single-input-question games, such as those associated with the Hadamard matrix and other special cases, under quantum strategies. Keywords: Bell's Inequality, Nonlocal Games, Hidden Variable Models, Hereditary Nonlocal Games, Simulability of Nonlocal Games, Bell's Polygones, Simulability of Bell's Polygones, Simulability of Single-Question Nonlocal Games, Simulability of Single-Question and Constant Output Nonlocal Games, Simulability of $\chi^2$ Distance.
