We employ relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to model the outflow, focusing on the magnetic jet mechanism. This approach relies on extracting energy from the specific angular momentum variation of plasma near the merger center and is distinct from the extracting energy-from-rotation mechanism, which depends on the black hole's angular momentum. Our findings indicate that a magnetic jet forms early in the Mergers-1 event, driven by angular momentum effects at the outer edge of the compact binary. The magnitude of the extracted power scales with the specific angular momentum ($j$), reaching $10^{50}$–$10^{51}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at $j$=$1000$–$2000$ km$^2$ s$^{-1}$. When the specific angular momentum exceeds $j$=$2000$ km$^2$ s$^{-1}$, the specific energy of the resulting outflow drops below $10^{12}$ cm$^2$ s$^{-2}$ ($<10^{14}$ erg g$^{-1}$), which is generally considered the energy threshold to accelerate cosmic rays in astrophysical environments. Consequently, a significant fraction of the observed $17$ kHz gravitational wave signal may originate from Mergers-1, particularly if the parameter $j$ falls within the $1000$–$2000$ km$^2$ s$^{-1}$ range. This suggests that a magnetic jet is a plausible explanation for GRB 170817. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such magnetic jets could potentially explain the extremely long gamma-ray burst GRB 060418. Our results imply that neutrino-cooled accretion flows accompanied by magnetic jets may be more prevalent in astrophysical transients than previously thought. Finally, we propose that future numerical models should incorporate more realistic magnetic jet mechanisms. This research was conducted using the numerical code HAMRAT, which is available for public use. Additionally, we have established a collaboration between the astrophysics and computational groups involved in this study. version of the RingCT protocol incorporating stealth addresses to ensure compatibility with Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS) consensus mechanisms. The proposed scheme relies on two core components: a tailored Integrated Signature and Encryption framework, which combines a public key encryption system with two distinct signature methods (a digital signature and a linkable ring signature), alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs. We provide a detailed description of the protocol, present security proofs, and discuss a implementation using the CryptoNight hash function and the Mina RSA library. Delegated RingCT maintains the foundational principles and key innovations of RingCT while enabling the use of the succinct Verifiable Random Function (VRF) required for the DPoS consensus model. These features significantly reduce the size of the proven transaction proof and enhance the overall performance of the protocol, making it highly suitable for serving as a cryptocurrency in post-quantum public blockchains. Experimental testing was conducted with the DAG cryptocurrency, which utilizes Delegated Proof of Stake as its consensus model. DAG employs the ring signature scheme described in this paper to achieve strong user privacy through the obfuscation of the transaction sender's identity. Furthermore, DAG incorporates two different consensus mechanisms—such as the two-thirds consensus or the Fastest Block consensus within a time window of one second—both of which rely on the VRF. DAG also utilizes the CryptoNight algorithm, which is recognized as a post-quantum secure cryptographic algorithm. Consequently, DAG serves as a representative use-case for Delegated RingCT, highlighting a broader class of post-quantum public blockchains that employ DPoS consensus built on a stealth- and VRF-based consensus model. This class of systems is considered highly promising for the development of general-purpose post-quantum public blockchains. Performance analysis demonstrates that DAG achieves a theoretical maximum of 36 blocks per second using a Mina RSA implementation, with an average of 28 blocks per second in practice. Additionally, DAG produces compact block proofs of only 100 bytes. When compared to the Bitcoin system, DAG generates approximately 28 times more transactions per second with block proofs roughly 10,000 times smaller. Compared to other ring-based cryptocurrencies like Monero and BigOne, DAG produces block proofs 2,000 to 3,000 times smaller per transaction. Comparing DAG's performance to other DPoS-based cryptocurrencies such as Delegated PoST, Arweave, Cardano, and Asch, DAG achieves 28 to 100 times more transactions per second

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) began operations at its highest energy to date, with the ALADIN experiment utilizing a 7 TeV proton beam from the LHC and a 250 GeV electron beam from the SPS to investigate deep inelastic scattering at low $Q^2$ and low $x$. This document presents a compilation of ATLAS collaboration measurements from the LHC, including deep inelastic scattering, photoproduction, and deep inelastic scattering at $Q^2 > 1$~GeV$^2$, both in the low-$x$ regime and generally. These contributions are intended for inclusion in low-$Q^2$ reviews. The document is organized into two primary sections: Technical Report 1 covers photoproduction at the LHC, while Technical Report 2 addresses deep inelastic scattering at $Q^2 > 1$~GeV$^2$. Each report contains summaries of the relevant ATLAS measurements. Future editions will integrate low-$Q^2$ data from LHC colliders operating at lower energies, specifically from the Fixed-Target experiments. This paper investigates the impact of the Morita dual symmetry group within periodically driven fractional quantum Hall systems. We identify the Morita dual symmetry in both continuous and discrete-time periodic drivers, specifically analyzing the discrete case for finite-depth circuit depth. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Morita dual symmetry serves to stabilize fractional quantum Hall states during periodic driving by enabling the construction of time-crystalline orders. These findings hold significant importance for time crystals and the discovery of new quantum phases. Additionally, we highlight that generalizing these results to continuous-time periodic drivers can be achieved by replacing time crystals with gauge-symmetric states, thereby facilitating the engineering of infinite classes of extended quantum phases. This framework unifies various phase classifications, including symmetric topological orders, symmetry-protected topological orders, and quantum spin liquids, all of which remain stable under periodic driving. Such stability can be harnessed to create a wide range of exotic phases characterized by fractionalized excitations and long-range entanglement, such as higher-order topological orders and algebraic entanglement orders. These phases are accessible starting from fractional quantum spin liquids, which are naturally protected by Morita dual symmetry and the periodic drive. Consequently, these states offer robust candidates for memory storage and the development of new protocols in quantum information and quantum computation. We anticipate that these drivers will advance research into generalized quantum phases featuring rich physical phenomena, including large entanglement, long-range order, and long-lived correlations. We introduce a novel, network-wide formulation of the problem, modeling the network as a large-scale flow-matching system where each slice is treated as a flow. The objective is to simultaneously optimize service provisioning and the allocation of physical resources. Since the mathematical program is typically intractable, we develop an algorithm grounded in the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions to derive a closed-form expression for the optimal solution. This approach, termed the KKT algorithm, provides the optimal values for all variables in every iteration as long as a feasible solution exists. We validate the algorithm's performance through simulations on both topologically regular rings and randomly generated topologies, demonstrating that it is topologically agnostic, as the solution is not contingent on any specific network topology. Simulation results confirm that the proposed KKT algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of computational complexity and solution optimality, supported by proof of convergence. Finally, we examine the impact of NS demand fluctuations on solution optimality, presenting results from both analytical and numerical perspectives. Our primary contribution is the development of an algorithm that yields optimal solutions without requiring any initial network topology or demand matrix inputs. This flexibility allows for direct deployment in existing networks or use as a benchmark to evaluate new architectures and protocols. Moreover, the proposed solution is energy-efficient and scalable, making it well-suited for future massive-scale NS environments. Furthermore, the solution is not communication-intensive, as it relies solely on local physical resource data. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first proposal to address Software Defined Network slicing in a network-wide and end-to-end manner. Although numerous variations of this strategy have emerged in the literature, this work examines a standard implementation and demonstrates that the resulting loss landscape contains very few local minima and is characterized by convex characteristics. These findings imply that loss can be efficiently minimized using conventional convex solvers, such as those based on gradient descent. Consequently, this approach eliminates the necessity for multi-classification methods or techniques like alternating direction method of multipliers, which are typically employed to address the typically non-convex nature of such problems. Instead, our methodology is both straightforward and straightforward to execute using off-the-shelf software. Experimental results indicate that solutions obtained from minimizing this loss are comparable to, and in several instances superior to, those achieved by previously established methods. Notably, in one specific scenario, the performance of our solver is directly correlated with the parameter $\lambda$ (which regulates the penalty for class collisions) in a linear fashion, a behavior attributed to the problem's strong-convexity, a property often overlooked in literature. This represents the first time the connection between the $\lambda$-parameter and embedding quality is explicitly demonstrated and explained. Furthermore, testing with values of $\lambda$ greater than 10 reveals that the loss remains sufficiently convex to ensure the problem retains its strong-convexity, a condition that holds true for all tested values of $\lambda$. Finally, experiments demonstrate that evaluating the loss on test data yields results that are statistically indistinguishable from those achieved through back-propagation. Additionally, it is shown that the computational cost of minimizing the loss is, in certain instances, an order of magnitude lower than that of back-propagation. By minimizing the loss directly, we can derive an embedding space that is superior to one formed by approximating the loss via back-propagation, a conclusion supported by our results. To our knowledge, this is the first study to analyze the loss landscape of pair-wise loss in detail and to explain the relationship between $\lambda$ and loss values based on the loss's strong-convexity. Our results confirm that the proposed methodology is effective, straightforward, and produces statistically significant improvements over existing methods. We demonstrate that these HTNs arise as approximations of a single universal network, which we term the Penrose triangle. This universal network is defined as the boundary representation of an AdS bulk constructed from infinitesimal boundary time evolutions of the boundary quantum field theory. However, the Penrose triangle does not always yield a high-fidelity approximation of this universal network for given states and times; consequently, it exhibits low fidelity for certain HTNs derived from the PEPPAS model of random CFT states. To enhance the average fidelity of the PEPPAS network, we develop a method to identify optimal boundary quantum states for representation by a specific HTN, achieving this by deforming the network via local modifications to the isometries. Additionally, we analyze how the fidelity of a fixed HTN is impacted when the target state and evolution time vary randomly. In all examined instances, the fidelity remains approximately proportional to the average of the squares of the conformal dimensions of the quantum states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the average fidelity across two distinct ensembles of HTNs converges to $\frac{2}{3}$ in the large-size limit. Finally, we explore the potential for generalizing these results. Through these investigations, we aim to deepen our understanding of the relationship between holographic tensor networks and boundary conformal field theories, as well as the average fidelity of such networks. strategy designed to implement Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) in three-phase unbalanced distribution systems. The method models the problem as a multi-agent system, defining agents' tasks as minimizing total system voltage deviation and maximizing power factor. To prevent excessive voltage discrepancies among agents, a consensus mechanism is applied. Given the difficulty of achieving full system information exchange within the agent network, an asynchronous communication protocol leverages available local and limited global data to drive a primary agent to establish a CVR target. This target is subsequently distributed to other agents using an asynchronous communication framework alongside an additional algorithm to allocate power correction. The approach was evaluated in a 100-agent test system containing both single- and three-winding transformers, sim various communication failure rates and time durations. Results indicate that the method maintains an average voltage deviation below 0.5 per unit and improves power factor by at least 10 percentage points, even when communication links between 20 and 40% of the agents fail. Compared to a baseline using the same communication constraints, the system achieves a power reduction of up to 1.05 MW, equivalent to a 0.35% decrease. This demonstrates that the proposed technique effectively enhances energy efficiency in unbalanced three-phase distribution networks by reducing total power through conservation. # I# Introduction

Determining the orientation of 3D objects from a single image is a fundamental challenge in computer vision, with applications including 3D object recognition, image-based shape reconstruction, and scene reconstruction. This challenge is particularly critical in medical imaging, where orienting patient bodies is essential for precise diagnosis and treatment planning. A specific instance of this problem is pose estimation, which is vital for both medical and robotic contexts.

This work concentrates on estimating human poses, specifically pose estimation within a specific medical context. A key constraint is that these objects are generated by a very limited number of views, making orientation critical for accurate shape reconstruction and pose estimation. This constraint is illustrated in Section \ref{sec{ Motivation and Application}}. Furthermore, pose estimation is significantly more difficult than shape estimation because pose variables possess inherent symmetries, particularly rotational symmetries, which create major obstacles for standard estimation techniques. These challenges are addressed by developing a global modeling approach that ensures parameterization invariance while maintaining estimation accuracy.

interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest regarding the information paradox, as they possess well-defined conceptually clear initial states. In this study, we present a novel dual gravitational description for generic BCFT/ICFT states defined on half spaces or half spheres. By constructing a half-space or half-sphere asymptotic boundary condition from the global AdS boundary condition, we demonstrate that a generic BCFT/ICFT state maps to a solution featuring a local defect—specifically, a Karch-Karchanis (KK) defect on half spaces or a spherical KK defect on half spheres. These states are represented by a static, curved interface whose position and shape are determined by the BCFT central charge, the BCFT-operator dimension, and the energy of the state. Furthermore, we calculate the corresponding holographic entropy density or density of annuli, finding that the total entropy consists of the universal term (the BCFT central charge), a subtractive term from the asymptotic AdS background, and the bulk contribution from the curved interface. We also discuss the implications for the gravitational description of information release in terms of quantum extensible horizons. Finally, we address the gravitational duals of specific universal states, such as the vacuum and Schur states, which correspond toKK defects flattening into the AdS boundary. We argue that these universal states, crucial for understanding the early and late stages of unitary information release, may represent pure AdS black holes with a planar event horizon. We conclude by relating these findings to recent work by Chen, Guo, and Guo. Additionally, we explore potential obstructions in the dual gravitational description of unitary states, including states on orbifolds and theories with a gap. Our work offers a new perspective on the dual description of BCFT/ICFT states, contributing to the investigation of the universal phase within AdS black hole evaporation. \section*{1. Introduction}

C is a widely used programming language in both industry and academia, yet bugs can occur. To address this, numerous C checkers have been developed; this paper focuses on static checkers. Static checkers analyze C programs without execution and are categorized into two types: those based on abstract interpretation and those based on formal methods. This study employs the latter approach by leveraging a deep integration between ACL2 and C. Specifically, we developed an ACL2-based C checker. First, we constructed an ACL2-based C syntax tree (C-ST) from which a C program can be derived. Next, we designed an ACL2 code generator that converts an ACL2 code representing a C program into ACL2 codes representing C semantic rules. Finally, our checker compares the ACL2 code representing the target C program with the generated ACL2 codes. If all codes confirm correct behavior, the checker is deemed valid.

Learning and the Scientific Method*, which examines the intersection of scientific method and machine learning, explores how scientific practice is transforming the application of machine learning. It argues that an explicit alignment with scientific principles can enhance a field that is already highly empirical, while simultaneously enabling machine learning to play a more profound role in advancing scientific method itself. The chapter begins by outlining the scientific method and its convergence with machine learning, then reviews specific examples from astrophysics, biology, and physics to demonstrate how scientific practices are refining the use of machine learning. Finally, it concludes by considering how machine learning can contribute to genetics and evolution research. This investigation into the mutual influence between the scientific method and machine learning leads to several key outcomes: practical applications in diverse domains, a deeper understanding of both domains, and a more effective, transparent, and collaborative approach to conducting scientific research. Additionally, three open challenges are identified, which may guide future investigations at this academic nexus. Resources related to this chapter, including an interactive Jupyter notebook, a case study, and an evaluation framework, are available at: https://amir-ghafour.ioc-spc.org/.

This transfer consumes both time and bandwidth; however, leveraging real-time on-the-fly (OTF) calibration within the interferometer's primary correlation system can substantially mitigate these costs. We investigated the feasibility of implementing a rudimentary OTF calibration scheme at a live LOFAR observation to identify technical hurdles needed to transition from standard post-transfer calibration to real-time OTF methods. Our tests, which utilized fixed gains, a constant phase offset, and an iteratively updated 2x2 diagonal matrix, showed that the resulting OTF images were qualitatively comparable to those produced by conventional calibration. While the method functions, we identified several obstacles that could impede real-time OTF calibration in live sessions. If these challenges can be addressed, the implementation of such a scheme could facilitate the development of more complex techniques, thereby enhancing future LOFAR data calibration. Additionally, this progress would enable real-time spectral line imaging, image de-rotation, and the incorporation of new image constraints. We also examined the implications of this approach for second-generation interferometers. If observations can be calibrated in real-time, intermediate calibration solutions could be applied to observed data streams, allowing for the production of calibrated visibilities and images either continuously or on an on-demand basis during observations, thus reducing the transfer burden to calibration strongrooms. These advancements would be particularly advantageous for next-generation interferometers like the Next Generation Very Large Array (NGVLA), where the sheer volume of post-transfer post-on-the-fly (OTF) calibration data would otherwise be prohibitive. The primary constraint for NGVLA would be the inability to store observations on-site due to the excessive data volume. Nevertheless, if this particular issue can be resolved, the benefits of real-time OTF calibration would still apply. Additionally, a final consideration involves real-time source catalog matching, which could significantly enhance calibration efficiency. Finally, we highlight that the implementation of real-time OTF calibration could aid in detecting transient events, a capability that may hold promise for future research. In conclusion, addressing the identified challenges could substantially improve future radio interferometer observations. Furthermore, a more robust real-time OTF calibration framework could open new avenues for transient detection and enable intermediate calibration solutions that will be crucial for the NGVLA. artificial intelligence has significantly advanced the analysis of complex, real-world data, which is often multidimensional, irregular, and non-numerical. However, these sophisticated machine-learning models struggle with interpretability, rendering them unsuitable for applications requiring transparent insights. Furthermore, when applied to under-sampled data, these black-box models are prone to overfitting and the extraction of spurious features. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a data-driven, model-based learning approach using dynamical systems. This method unifies the identification and modeling of dynamic systems with the learning of data-driven dynamics. By applying the Persistent Homology (PH) data invariant to dynamical system models, the proposed method can identify both intrinsic and extrinsic features. We utilize a modified PH metric to quantify the phasing of trajectories within a persistence diagram, enabling the detection of spurious features and the isolation of data-driven intrinsic features. This strategy offers a distinct advantage over standard data-driven methods, particularly with low-sample observations. A simulation case study on a flight control system is provided to validate the method, and additional simulations on the Boston Dynamics Atlas robot further examine the proposed approach. The Attractor Identification and Isolation (AII) method is shown to effectively identify feature metrics and intrinsic time series even for under-sampled, noisy data. Key advantages include the ability to infer missing data points, extract robust features, and distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic features. Ultimately, the proposed approach combines the adaptability and intuition of data-driven learning with the interpretability of model-based methods. Future work will focus on applying this method to real-world systems and extending it to diverse, real-world data. The source code is available at https://github.com/CMU-DELphi/Atlas.git. Their research is currently available at https://github.com/CMU-DELphi/ and https://cmudelphi.github.io/. Their work is also featured in the Transactions on Interpretability and Interoperability (TIN), a new publication by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). . We construct a deterministic, adaptive inference algorithm operating in the Bloch sphere that achieves the optimal success probability for qubits ($d=2$) when the set of states is known in advance. This construction extends to all dimensions if the state of each unknown qubit is selected from a complete and closed interval, remains valid for unknown qubits with a known orientation relative to a fixed basis, and offers suboptimal yet still efficient performance for general pure states in all dimensions. Additionally, we provide a simple proof demonstrating that for online inference of pure states, all information regarding the states can be mapped to the boundary of the Bloch sphere. Furthermore, we illustrate that the boundary of a set does not generally consist of straight lines, a feature typically advantageous for optimality in both online and batch inference. We conclude by presenting a straightforward online algorithm that achieves optimality for qubits when states are chosen from a triangular set. Building on this, we introduce a reparameterization of the Bloch sphere that yields optimality for qubits given access to a set of generators; this method can be viewed as an adaptation of the online inference algorithm for states in known, closed intervals. These boundary properties of the Bloch sphere are also explored. Building on this, we construct an online inference algorithm for non-pure states. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds for all online inference algorithms. We demonstrate that optimality in both online and batch inference is guaranteed by employing all-maximal entanglement across any bipartition of the system. We also examine the relationship between online and batch inference. The proposed algorithms and their analysis offer a solid foundation for developing efficient and optimal online inference techniques for pure states of arbitrary dimension and for general pure states. This research is intended to advance quantum state tomography, quantum communication, and quantum language modeling. A potential is applied to the cavity surface to establish a gradient in the chemical potential and quark confinement probabilities. The study examines meson and baryon spectra, comparing production probabilities and kinematic distributions with experimental data. Finally, a comparison is made between baryon production derived from MBM and the ALICE experiment's measurements in p-Pb collisions. The analysis suggests that in non-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the relative momentum of (anti)quarks at the quark coalescence stage is low compared to relativistic heavy-ion collisions, at least for light hadrons. Additionally, it is demonstrated that, similar to mesons, the production probability of (anti)baryons is not solely determined by the overlap integral of (anti)quark wave functions but also depends on the coalescence time. These findings may have significant implications for investigating the transport of heavy quarkonia in the quark-gluon plasma. The analysis also reveals that \SI{3-5}{\GeV/c} is the most appropriate coalescence time range for producing J/\PSI in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. This implies that (anti)quark wave functions at the coalescence point have decayed for more than 3 ps but have not yet diffused beyond the \SI{5}{\um} scale. Furthermore, it is shown that both the coalescence time and the initial relative momentum of (anti)quarks are constrained by coalescence models and the observed J/\PSI rapidity distributions in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. These results may assist in guiding future investigations into quarkonium transport in the quark-gluon plasma. The derived findings regarding initial relative quark momentum and coalescence time at the hadronization stage may also be of general interest for analyzing hadron production in various collision systems and energies. We employ machine learning to train a Gaussian process regression model, utilizing a Gaussian likelihood function to account for measurement uncertainties. This methodology enables us to quantify the $95\%$ confidence intervals for GWB model parameters—specifically amplitude and characteristic frequency—derived from each of the four arrays. Our findings align with results obtained from traditional parameter estimation techniques. Analyzing the data within the framework of a Power-Law model, we determine the PTB amplitude to be $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{c} = 2^{+2.4}_{-1}\times 10^{-9}$ for NANOGrav, $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{c} = 3.5^{+3.4}_{-2.2}\times 10^{-10}$ for Parkes, $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{c} = 2.4^{+2.2}_{-1.2}\times 10^{-9}$ for PTA(Intl), and $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{c} = 3.2^{+2.2}_{-1.4}\times 10^{-9}$ for PTA(Aus), with a characteristic frequency of $f_\mathrm{c} = 6.8^{+4.0}_{-3.2}\times 10^{-8}$ Hz. The significant overlap in amplitude values across all arrays supports the validity of these GWB parameter estimates and suggests consistency with theoretical predictions from a stellar-mass binary population. Furthermore, we explore various Bayesian approaches for GWB analysis and present them as a foundation for future generations of analyses. Furthermore, we demonstrate the flexibility of Bayesian frameworks, specifically Gaussian Process Regression, as a viable alternative for modeling GWB correlations. This approach offers more precise estimates of the correlation matrix and its parameters, along with a more accurate and explicit quantification of analysis uncertainties. To facilitate these advancements, we release the full analysis code used for this study as open-source. semiconducting moiré superlattice in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), we theoretically examine how moiré superlattices—both patterned and emergent—reshape the dynamics of excitonic condensates and lasers. Focusing on monolayer heterostructures like the WSe$_{2}$/MoSe$_{2}$ system, we show that the primary influence on laser performance arises from alterations to the fundamental laser medium: the light-exciton complex. Specifically, we find that a dark exciton-polariton mode residing in the moiré potential can become the dominant lasing channel at longer wavelengths, even surpassing the conventional bright exciton-polariton at the band edge. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the localization of both bright and dark polaritons within moiré potential wells fosters a robust instability of the laser field, characterized by a distinct blue-to-red shift in intensity as polariton energy increases. This observation aligns with experimental findings in microcavity lasers and suggests that excitonic condensates may exist within these moiré wells. Overall, our predictions indicate that superlattices and nanocavities can be engineered to selectively amplify either bare polariton modes or those confined to nanoscale moiré potential wells. These findings offer novel design principles for future lasers and present new avenues for investigating the existence of excitonic condensates in transition metal dichalcogenide moiré superlattices. We first introduce a random beamforming strategy to decouple the coupling between user-IRS-BS links. The mixing between the two singlet scalars governs both the freeze-out mechanism of dark matter and the $CP$-asymmetry in leptodegenesis. Specifically, we demonstrate that for masses below 1 GeV, this scalar-mixing parameter can ensure consistent outcomes for dark matter, whereas achieving such consistency within purely singlet scalar models requires significantly larger mixing values. When incorporating a $\Delta(3,3,24)$ scalar field in an $S_4 \times U(1)_{\mu-\tau}$ extension, we find that a doublet fermion dark matter candidate offers a viable mass range, with implications for the baryon asymmetry of the universe (UBA) arising mainly in a narrow mass window. Finally, we illustrate a scenario where both singlet fermion and scalar dark matter candidates exist simultaneously, with UBA constraints favoring the doublet fermion scenario while the fermion candidate dominates. In this specific scenario, UBA considerations impose mild constraints on the mixing parameter. Since our proposed scenarios extend beyond the Standard Model with singlet neutrinos, they offer experimentally testable predictions regarding lepton flavor violating decays and the existence of a new force. We conclude by discussing the experimental prospects for detecting these phenomena. We conclude that our proposed models serve as a compelling explanation for dark matter while naturally incorporating the leptodegenesis mechanism. Notably, the single-parameter tuning inherent in the singlet scalar model is resolved by the $S_4$-motivated model. Notably, in a well-motivated region of the parameter space, the mass of the lightest singlet scalar falls below one GeV, aligning with recent findings from direct detection experiments. Specifically, we employ a learning control strategy for unknown continuous-time systems within a Lyapunov-based framework, utilizing an integral type-II third-order consensus tracking error within a cascaded structure. The internal loop consists of a state feedback controller and an online learning law, where the latter adapts the primary controller parameters. Leveraging the average consensus property, we demonstrate that the tracking error converges to the average of initial values as the system states stabilize, indicating division by zero avoidance. Through Lyapunov analysis, we establish boundedness of all signals, identification of actuator saturation, and verification that the tracking error reaches $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ consensus, meaning the $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ norm of the tracking error does not exceed unity relative to the average of initial conditions. Simulation results confirm the algorithm's efficacy. Notably, while current literature focuses on disturbance-free environments, extending this approach to unknown environments represents a promising future direction. Additionally, although this work addresses second-order dynamics, extending the methodology to higher-order systems is also a viable path forward. This study aims to advance the progression toward grounded interactive robots capable of self-organization and adaptation, enabling them to execute diverse tasks in unpredictable settings. These applications encompass search and rescue operations, exploration in uncharted territories, and the deployment of sensor networks. Our approach serves as a foundational step toward achieving these goals. Although initial simulations were promising, experimental validation remains necessary. Furthermore, this research contributes to achieving NASA's Advanced Concepts Exploration Initiative, specifically the Autonomous Mobile Robot for the Exploration of Caves (AMREE-CAVE) project. Initiating the experimental validation phase is therefore a logical next step. Finally, while the current work utilizes integral type-II third-order consensus tracking error, future research could explore analogous implementations using type-I and second-order error structures. This investigation falls under the domain of Distributed Learning Control for disturbed multi-agent systems and contributes to the broader field of Distributed adaptive Control. However, the presence of loss degrades the fidelity of distributed entangled states, potentially compromising the security of TF-QKD at extreme loss levels. This study investigates TF-QKD security under such conditions by applying post-selection and re-sampling techniques within the GG22 security framework. We first derive an upper bound for the phase-flip error rate of the two key states distributed by all possible subsets of users; since secret key rates in TF-QKD are driven by the difference between bit and phase flip error rates, this bound demonstrates that security is achievable when this value remains sufficiently low. ho Ophiuchus cloud complex exhibits an infrared spectrum rich in emission lines derived from both dust and gas. This study utilizes the Herschel/PACS and VLT/X-Shooter instruments to characterize these features, thereby constraining a model of the circumstellar environment. The analysis of these characteristics aims to better understand the physical conditions and composition of the region surrounding S1. Model fitting determines that the dust mass surrounding S1 amounts to $10^{-5}~M_{\odot}$, with a gas-to-dust ratio of 100 indicating significant processing of material from the natal cloud. The infrared excess originates from a compact region approximately 100 au in size. This circumstellar material displays a temperature structure consistent with a dust cloud heated by an embedded low-mass protostar ranging from 3 to 5 $M_{\odot}$. Gas and dust are also detected in a compact warm molecular region surrounding S1, exhibiting the molecular signatures typical of heated clouds. These findings substantiate a scenario where S1 is processing material from a warm molecular cloud and possesses a compact, low-mass circumstellar disk. This represents one of the earliest identified examples of a protostar in Rho Ophiuchus, marking a significant step toward understanding the evolution of protostars and planet formation. The detection of line emission from molecules such as $H_2O$, $O_2$, $N_2H^+$, $C_2H_3N$, $HCN$, $HCO^+$, and $H_2CO$ provides evidence for chemical processing of ices in a warm molecular region. Additionally, a tentative detection of $O_2$ at a concentration of a few parts per million suggests possible photolysis of $H_2O$ and $O_2$ ices in the inner disk. This protostar's processing of material and retention of an almost primordial mass accretion rate distinguish it as a unique case among young stellar objects. However, current research primarily relies on the self-attention mechanism, which computes pairwise attention scores for every token pair, resulting in a quadratic increase in computational complexity and memory usage with sequence length. This study explores the potential of sparse attention, specifically using the LongShort pattern, to make Transformer-based image models more efficient. Our findings indicate that a single, global attention pattern is insufficient for visual tasks, as different layers may benefit from varying pattern sizes. This approach effectively balances performance and efficiency, yielding an approximate 30% improvement in metrics while utilizing fewer parameters. By effectively capturing both local features and extended dependencies, the proposed model outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. While this approach can virtually explore numerous architectures by employing shared operators, it often leads to inaccurate estimation of the true architecture performance when used with expensive sample-efficient evaluation methods. This inaccuracy stems from the fact that different architectures may rely on the same operator in distinct ways, and the global usage of an operator does not necessarily reflect its behavior within a specific architectural context. To address this limitation, we propose a similar graph representation that is distinct from standard weight sharing, as it does not force different architectures to share the same operator weights. Instead, we introduce a new concept where subgraph operators with structurally similar operators utilize learned parameters that are close to one another. Our empirical results, which are backed by a theoretical analysis, demonstrate that this method can effectively support various evaluation strategies while significantly reducing both computational cost and memory usage compared to conventional weight sharing. This approach has already been successfully deployed in our recent NAS system for mixed-precision training on GPUs. The implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/NVIDIA/MLsysNet/blob/main/Nas-NieHao/weight_similarity_search.py}. common approach to analyzing such data involves using time series forecasting models to identify patterns within historical measurements, thereby making accurate inferences about future states. However, this method often fails when external contextual information becomes available. While some models can leverage this context—typically represented as text or images—for forecasting, it remains uncertain whether this approach enhances performance. This paper addresses the question with a negative answer. In our empirical study, we evaluated various state-of-the-art forecasting models utilizing the MultiModal Conversational Agent dataset. Our findings indicate that incorporating contextual information did not improve model performance. Consequently, we recommend against including such context in practical applications. Furthermore, we observed that performance differences between models were better explained by the number of available training samples rather than the predictive accuracy of the models themselves. This underscores the critical importance of sufficient samples in training time series models with contextual input. Finally, we demonstrate that simply pretraining mult模odal models on random text does not mitigate the issue, further reinforcing our conclusion that such context should generally be avoided. While previous research on square scattering media has identified eigenmodes with sinusoidal patterns that correspond to diffraction orders, this study extends the analysis to circular media. We demonstrate that every eigenmode in a circular deposition matrix maintains an angular dependence expressed as a Fourier series. Furthermore, we find that each continuous set of eigenfunctions associated with a specific in-eigenspace can be represented as a sequence of Bessel functions. This paper introduces a novel and straightforward approach to accelerate the pruning of individual neural connections using the Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm. for probing finite temperature and finite density phases of matter, having previously yielded insights into the unitary, Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT), and supersolid phases of strongly interacting bosons. Within this framework, interactions are treated as a perturbation to the free boson Hamiltonian; however, the validity of this perturbative approach at finite temperatures and densities remains uncertain. This study rigorously examines the interplay between the large-charge expansion and the perturbative treatment of interactions using both single-particle self-energy and lattice self-energy methods. Our rigorous resummation techniques confirm that the large-charge expansion accurately captures the BKT phase transition, while also revealing a previously unknown critical phenomenon: a smooth analytic crossover from the BKT to the supersolid phase, distinguished by the absence of critical fluctuations. Furthermore, these methods identify an essential radius in charge space that delineates the perturbation regime applicable to experimental ultracold atom setups. Finally, despite the anticipated poor convergence of the expansion in the deep supersolid phase, we derive a specific physical mechanism that alleviates this issue, suggesting that the large-charge expansion may ultimately prove useful for exploring the supersolid phase as well. These findings are experimentally testable. Additionally, employing a self-energy method capable of incorporating various interaction types, we explore the impact of spinor interactions on the expansion. We demonstrate that these interactions introduce a genuinely new phase—spinor liquid—yet remain effectively weak when analyzed through the lens of the large-charge expansion. This work is grounded in numerical simulations of the SU(N) nonlinear sigma model in one spatial dimension at finite temperature. By extending previous studies beyond the spin-1/2 case and providing a comparative analysis of different self-energy methods, this research establishes a firm theoretical foundation for future experiments. Such experiments could investigate the specific radius in charge space separating perturbation and non-perturbation regimes, or they might directly observe the specific analytic crossover predicted for the supersolid phase, features that distinguish it from a standard supersolid phase transition. These predictions could also be cross-verified by examining the influence of spinor interactions on the phase structure. Our findings offer a fresh perspective on the recent supersolid observation using ${}^{52}$Cr atoms. Beyond this, the applications of the large-charge expansion to diverse physical systems are expanding, making these results broadly relevant. Beyond the specific systems addressed here, these results hold relevance for experiments involving any weak interactions. Such experiments could validate our predictions and potentially uncover new physical phenomena. Beyond

We integrate this phenomenon with the **k**-space Ginzburg-Landau theory for superconductivity. In contrast to prior research, we demonstrate that both deformation and Friedel elastic potentials are essential for glue-mediated superconductivity in TBLG, enabling the stabilization of high-temperature superconductivity even within the charge-neutral superconducting "moat." Our calculations reveal that the deformation potential yields a scattering exponent of ******n** = 2**, whereas the Coulomb (Friedel) potential results in a "soft" momentum-dependent disorder with an exponent of **n** = 1, suggesting that long-range Coulomb interactions are the dominant factor in "soft" graphene conductivity. Additionally, we establish that glue-mediated superconductivity in both systems is intrinsically dynamic. Regarding TBLG specifically, a unique superconducting state emerges in the charge-neutral superconducting phase diagram, characterized by "Higgs" mode dynamics that cause the amplitude of the order parameter to fluctuate. These findings indicate that glue-mediated superconductivity in graphene and TBLG is intrinsically linked to "soft" disorder, the nature of which is governed by the specific type of electron-phonon coupling. Ultimately, these insights pave the way for the engineering of high-temperature superconductivity in two-dimensional materials. **Data availability**: The data supporting these findings are available in the Harvard Dataverse: [https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/99Q9QI].

We employ a diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DiagMC) technique capable of sampling Feynman diagrammatic series to extremely high orders, analyzing both the series' convergence and the impact of multiple particle-hole excitations. By examining the polaron and molecule energies across various coupling strengths, we identify a ground-state transition from a polaron to a molecule. Our calculated critical interaction strength aligns with experimental measurements and variational method predictions. Furthermore, the polaron $Z$ factor derived from the complete diagrammatic series nearly matches that of the single-scattering series generated by variational methods, though both diverge close to the polaron-molecule transition point. Finally, we derive a lower bound for the polaron energy that closely approximates the exact result, demonstrating that this estimate remains valid up to the same transition point where the variational approach's single-scattering estimate diverges. These findings highlight the critical role of multiple particle-hole excitations in accurately describing the polaron-molecule transition, a phenomenon previously unaddressed by variational methods due to their inability to handle multiple scattering events. Additionally, the DiagMC-derived lower bound offers high accuracy throughout the entire range of the coupling constant. Our findings also demonstrate that multiple hole excitations are essential for capturing both the polaron size and the ground state within the molecular phase. This work serves as a proof of concept for utilizing complete diagrammatic series to study the non-perturbative aspects of many-body systems, with potential applications to the BEC-BCS crossover, Fermi superfluids, and other related contexts. Specifically, the evaluation of a graph polynomial can yield multiple distinct graph invariants. This paper introduces a novel polynomial associated with symmetric graphs that possesses a linearization property. We demonstrate that this polynomial corresponds to the number of closed walks of specific lengths and constitutes a linear transformation of the characteristic polynomial for the adjacency, biadjacency, Laplacian, incidence, and signless Laplacian matrices. We have named this polynomial the symmetric polynomial. Furthermore, we establish an explicit formula for it regarding a graph's order and determine it as a natural extension of the characteristic polynomial. Additionally, we derive inequalities for the symmetric polynomial using initial and terminal values, apply these to bound the spectral radii of the adjacency and Laplacian matrices, and calculate the first eigenvalue for certain classes of graphs. Finally, we investigate the relationship between the symmetric polynomial and the characteristic polynomial, considering both general and special cases. This work was driven by an investigation into the feasibility of extending the characteristic polynomial to a higher-dimensional polynomial for general graphs. However, we discovered that extending it to a two-dimensional polynomial results in non-integral coefficients. Consequently, we focused our research on the integer-valued polynomial, which led to the proposal of the symmetric polynomial. Through this investigation, we formulated inequalities for a variety of graph polynomials.

Extending characteristic polynomials to two dimensions yields non-integral coefficients. Therefore, we investigated the integral nature of the resulting bivariate polynomial and employed a univariate polynomial to derive inequalities for various graph invariants. We have named this univariate polynomial the symmetric polynomial. Through this investigation, we derived inequalities for several graph-related extensions. Additionally, we derived inequalities for the symmetric polynomial based on both the initial and terminal values, which were subsequently applied to bound spectral radii and the first eigenvalue. The work also examines the relationships between the symmetric polynomial and the characteristic polynomial. Finally, we derived inequalities for the symmetric polynomial of a graph. This study addresses the "business process extraction" (BPE) task, which involves identifying complete business process definitions (BPDs) from a body of discourse to extract key performance indicators. Although BPD identification is essential for technical analysis, current methods for BPE remain ad-hoc. To establish a solid foundation for automated BPE, we first introduce BPNet, a dataset comprising BPDs from the German Bundesbank. BPNet encompasses 2.4 million BPDs from 209 distinct categories, annotated in accordance with information retrieval best practices, and provides regular reliability estimates for each annotation. We evaluate four state-of-the-art approaches for BPD classification and offer best practices to enhance existing BPE solutions. Furthermore, we discuss the socio-technical implications of these limitations to guide the development of future BPE advancements. Our findings indicate that learning categories is more challenging than classifying instances, and that carefully designed, fine-grained categories are crucial for achieving robust performance in this domain. The associated BPNet taxonomy offers a representative collection of common entities in economic discourse, serving as a valuable resource for further research in automated BPE. The dataset and analysis within this paper are conducted using the GermanConNLP framework and can be accessed at https://github.com/GermanConNLP/BPE. Researchers are invited to utilize this tool to significantly advance BPE in the future. Additionally, GermanConNLP has emerged as a highly modular, production-ready software framework with applications spanning various tasks in German computational linguistics. Finally, we outline specific steps to close the current gap between state-of-the-art solutions and practical requirements in economic practice. To achieve this, we propose that further research should (1) focus on robust category learning, (2) establish new benchmarks for complete process definitions, and (3) integrate additional indicators to serve as a valid basis for automated analysis. To our knowledge, this represents the first public effort to bridge the divide between current state-of-the-art BPE solutions and practical needs. Our results demonstrate that only through these proposed initiatives can BPE be substantially advanced. The source code, analysis, and references are available at https://github.com/GermanConNLP/BPE. Hall's condition, which mandates that every subset of agents has a sufficient number of distinct neighbors. While this condition guarantees universal matching, it does not ensure efficient matching. In this correspondence, we demonstrate the existence of a sparse graph structure within a specific category that facilitates efficient matching. Specifically, for any given $\gamma > 0$ and $\delta > 0$, we construct a graph $G$ with $n$ agents and $m$ neighbors per agent such that: (i) the ratio $m/\log n$ approaches $\gamma$ as $n \to \infty$, (ii) the matching diameter $d$ satisfies $\lim (\log n)/d \geq \delta$, ensuring that nearly all agents and neighbors are within distance $d$, and (iii) random neighbor selection yields a constant probability of finding a match. This condition is formally defined in the "Hallspacy" condition. Additionally, we outline a greedy algorithm that achieves efficient matching with high probability. Our construction utilizes random graphs with prescribed degrees, building upon a method originally introduced to establish the existence of graphs containing multiple disjoint Hamiltonian cycles [Kuhn et al. (2016) J. ACM, 63(2)]. We also provide an alternative construction based on random expanders, demonstrating that combining Hallspacy efficiency with rapid mixing properties of neighbor graphs in $G$ yields efficient matching. Furthermore, we prove that a constant probability of efficient matching remains robust against constant levels of failures and false positives. These findings hold practical significance and align with recent empirical observations by Kuhn et al. (2019) [arXiv:1903.00928] and Xiao et al. (2020) [arXiv:2001.00928], which derived matching structures from the "conflict-free" condition originally proposed by Kuhn et al. [Kuhn et al. (2013) J. ACM, 60(3)]. Our results indicate that the conflict-free condition is essentially a special case of the Hallspacy condition. The implications of these findings are evident in distributed matching problems, including graph coloring and maximum flow computation, where maintaining sparsity is crucial. While previous studies typically accounted only for statistical broadening, we demonstrate that thermal expansion can exceed this effect and significantly shift THz emission peaks. Specifically, increased spacing between expanding InGaAs quantum wells shifts the bulk band structure valleys from the $\Gamma$ to the $L$ valley, thereby altering emission characteristics. Given that modern fabrication techniques offer exceptional control over well width and periodicity, we anticipate that taking thermal expansion into consideration will be crucial for future high-precision applications. The observed emission changes are explained using the Boltzmann-Boltzman transport equations. We validate our theoretical framework by comparing both peak positions and intensity against experimental data. In the low-temperature regime, our calculations reveal that Drude emission can be suppressed while Landau-Pauli emission is dramatically boosted due to the $L$ valley structure. Ultimately, incorporating thermal expansion in the theoretical model is essential for accurately predicting and interpreting InGaAs/InGAs superlathes for terahertz emission. This approach provides a pathway for precisely tuning THz emission properties, particularly valley branching ratios, via structural dimensions. We provide specific recommendations for experimental designs, including well width and periodicity, to facilitate this control. Furthermore, we illustrate how this tuning strategy can be applied to existing datasets. At the proposed optimal well width, our model predicts an enhancement of the Drude peak position by approximately 0.5-0.7 THz. Furthermore, the model suggests that Drude emission intensity remains relatively insensitive to minor fluctuations in well width, indicating that precision requirements for Drude emission applications are relatively relaxed. These findings will aid in the efficient development of advanced emitters for next-generation terahertz applications. -waves on Jupiter, derived from both ground-based and space-based systems, have highlighted significant modeling challenges. Specifically, models attempting to explain these signals face difficulties in simultaneously addressing the observed frequencies, angular and spectral anisotropy, and the lack of corresponding geomagnetic spot signatures detected by ground arrays. This study introduces a new proposed mechanism for these low-frequency radio emissions. We suggest that these emissions result from the interaction of magnetospheric plasma with the upper H2 atmosphere, utilizing a Cerenkov mechanism adapted for circumplanetary electromagnetic fields influenced by the dispersion relation of electromagnetic waves within a conducting medium. This unusual Cerenkov process generates coherent radio waves directed along slightly oblique paths relative to local magnetic field lines. By solving Jupiter's ohmic induction equation, we estimate the oblique angles of these local magnetic fields, noting they result in slight anisotropies relative to the equatorial plane. Furthermore, we calculate the radio wave frequencies, estimating them to range up to approximately 100 kHz. Consequently, the associated radio beam angles relative to the equatorial plane exhibit a negative correlation with observed frequencies. This unusual Cerenov radiation also produces radio waves in the local radial and oblique directions, aligned with observed intensity distributions. Finally, the inability of these emitted waves to generate geomagnetic spots explains the null detection results reported by ground-based observatories. Thus, this unusual Cerenkov process offers an explanation for the unusual spectral and angular anisotropies, along with the absence of geomagnetic spots, previously reported by ground-based detectors. These findings suggest that similar unusual Cerenkov emissions should be anticipated from other magnetohydrodynamic (HM) sources, such as the Sun, Saturn, and potentially others. Furthermore, this mechanism serves as a critical alternative for investigating coherent low-frequency radio emissions at Jupiter, providing an initial approach for researching equivalent phenomena at other HM sources. The proposed mechanism is detailed in a companion paper. Keywords: Radio Emissions, Jupiter, Cerenov Effect, Ohm's Law in moving media, Conducting medium, M-waves, Ohmic currents. \begin{abstract} Semantic parsing is a difficult task involving the mapping of natural language sentences to logical forms. This paper explores the application of semantic parsing specifically within medical natural language. We address this goal by introducing a simple yet effective algorithm for accumulating knowledge of logical forms from available resources to build a repository of medical logical forms. To demonstrate the utility of this repository, we illustrate how the accumulated knowledge can be employed to parse medical sentences. Our empirical results show that the parsing algorithm achieves an F1-score of 0.92 on the MatERE 2018 test set and an F1-score of 0.90 on the test set of MatERC2019-1, outperform all systems participating in both competitions. Additionally, we discuss a strategy for extending the parser to handle diverse medical expressions through the training of a neural network on existing logical forms via transfer learning. Finally, we examine several promising applications of semantic parsing in medical natural language processing. Source code: \url{https://github.com/mbianchi94/sem-parsing}. to investigate the internal structures of nucleons and nuclei, as well as matter formation processes, by conducting high-energy, high-luminosity collisions between electrons and protons or nuclei. Within this context, the interaction between a scattered electron and an unobserved hadron or nucleus produced by the proton or nucleus struck by the incoming electron offers a unique pathway to measure transverse momentum and longitudinal structure functions. To facilitate these measurements, the Electron-Ahadron-Nucleus-Hadron (EANH) detector concept was developed. This novel detector enables the measurement of momentum and charge of secondary particles generated by the struck or dissociated nucleons and produced in the hadronic final state. This article outlines the EANH detector's fundamental physics motivation, proposed design, performance, and construction timeline. The EANH collaboration is currently in the design phase, with the aim of readiness for operation at the end of the current decade. The detector is well-suited for existing electron-hadron and electron-nucleus collisions at the SPHINX experiment and future fixed-target configurations of the EIC, and it also supports the fractional momentum loss ($\xi$) program for the future EIC collider. The EANH collaboration actively seeks input from the broader electron-nucleus physics and collider communities regarding the detector's concept and construction schedule. Ultimately, EANH holds the potential to provide novel measurements of nuclear and hadron structure and to significantly enhance the scientific return of EIC physics programs. For further details, visit the project website: https://www.eanhdetector.org/. The EANH collaboration welcomes contributions and is eager to engage with researchers in the electron-nucleus and collider communities. as "quasi-periodic dips" (QPDs) in low-mass x-ray binaries (LMXBs), researchers have identified four distinct subclasses. This study analyzes the characteristics of the most prevalent subclass, the QPD-type, by examining the most complete sample available. Based on 234 sources with >50 X-ray states, we identify this subclass in 48% of low-mass polars and 23% of X-ray binaries with neutron stars of 1.4 M_sun. Notably, this group exhibits the highest fraction of sources displaying both pulsations and variability, at 93%. We characterize the unique state sequences of QPD-type sources, which are dominated by dips with typical amplitudes of 20% and widths of 2-5 periods. These sequence characteristics suggest that the dips likely originate from material within the accretion disc rather than the accretion stream or the planetesimal debris disc proposed in previous scenarios. Furthermore, the sequence implies a strong correlation between the dip amplitude and the corona's size or brightness, compared to other state sequences in LMXBs. Finally, we discuss the implications of finding the 1.4 M_sun sample to be the least populated by X-ray pulsar sources and explore the potential for using QPDs to determine the characteristics of circumstellar material. Ultimately, the prevalence of this subclass in X-ray binary samples with 1.4 M_sun neutron stars aligns with the debris disc scenario. constructing state observers for nonlinear systems remains a challenging task. This study addresses the design of a reliable state observer for a specific class of nonlinear systems characterized by triangular nonlinearities and linearly dependent outputs. To ensure robustness against nonlinear disturbances, the authors propose a switching state feedback observer that adaptively adjusts its order based on the detected disturbance nature. Additionally, sufficient conditions for both linear and switching observers are derived using sufficient Lyapunov functions to guarantee asymptotic convergence of the estimation errors in the absence of disturbances. The efficacy of the proposed switching state feedback observer is validated through a simulation of a three-link robotic arm system. Furthermore, the paper offers a theoretical analysis of the switch's impact on error dynamics. These findings hold significant potential for applications in power electronics, electromechanical systems, and electronic motor control. mode-locked oscillators have enabled numerous applications, traditionally supported by conventional beam propagation analysis for resonator design and alignment. However, this established theoretical framework often falls short for high-power, ultrashort pulse systems. This paper introduces a highly efficient and straightforward method for analyzing stable resonator configurations in oscillators operating with heavily damped pulses. The approach utilizes standard ray-tracing techniques applied to effectively amplified rays. Furthermore, the method validates the conditions required for circular stability diagrams and provides a simple formula for estimating the stability range of Gauss-Hermits modes. In these scenarios, the formula successfully predicts the number of oscillations permitted in each Gauss-Hermits mode and the corresponding beam waists. Additionally, the procedure offers a straightforward means to determine the appropriate pump spot size for achieving stable Gauss-Hermits oscillations. Examples include the analysis of a Ti:Sapphire oscillator and a Kerr-lens mode-locked Nd:YAG oscillator, both with 2 mm crystals. For the Ti:Sapphire oscillator, the study examines how pump spot sizes influence the fundamental mode, pump absorption, and extraction efficiency. This analysis enables the selection of an optimal pump spot size based on available beam displacement at the crystal and the desired extraction efficiency. Additionally, the impact of intracavity telescope placement is investigated. In a separate example, the effect of a thin output coupler on stability and beam waists is evaluated, which is particularly relevant for Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators using planar output couplers. Overall, applying this analysis to a specific oscillator design facilitates rapid derivation of essential parameters and allows for efficient optimization. Additionally, the concept of a Kerr-lens as an intracavity lens is validated; specifically, the focal length of a Kerr-lens is shown to depend on the intracavity power and is significant only when a thick lens is absent. Finally, based on a typical Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillator example, an example setup is presented, alongside recommendations for choosing the intracavity pump spot size and telescope placement. Ultimately, this methodology provides valuable insights for designing and analyzing Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators. (PDF: 10, PDF: 6)

To address this, this paper examines two critical yet largely overlooked Asynchronous Federated Learning (AFED) scenarios within non-IID environments. Unlike current Agnostic federated learning approaches, our setting permits communication bottlenecks where receiving or transmitting specific updates may be delayed or impossible entirely. We explore two specific delay models: (1) delays affecting the client's computation following the acquisition of updated global models, and (2) delays affecting the client while accessing existing global models before receiving new ones. To evaluate AFED robustness, we propose two new complexity metrics that account for delay magnitude, server non-IID distribution, and varying degrees of non-IID data across clients. These metrics are independent of specific optimization algorithms. Given that existing Agnostic complexity bounds depend heavily on assumption types, making direct comparison difficult, we establish new bounds for both delay types under both non-IID settings. Notably, for Scenario (1), we identify thresholds for both the non-IID degree and number of non-IID features. If these thresholds are met, we demonstrate that learning remains feasible even when half of the client updates cannot be transmitted. Conversely, if these thresholds are not met, learning becomes unachievable regardless of the data distribution. For Scenario (2), we derive corresponding complexity bounds. In numerical experiments, we utilize a large collection of federated learning studies to simulate diverse non-IID distributions and compare performance across both Scenarios (1) and (2), further analyzing their relationships with traditional IID-based complexity bounds. Our findings indicate that Agnostic bounds fail to effectively characterize practical AFED systems, highlighting the urgent need for new, realistic assumptions and corresponding complexity bounds. Furthermore, existing Agnostic bounds exhibit significant flaws, including failure to distinguish between different non-IID types, inability to account for communication bottlenecks, and lack of threshold conditions for features and non-IID degrees. These features are essential for designing more resilient asynchronous learning algorithms. We anticipate that this work will significantly advance the investigation of AFED under practical conditions. The associated code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhongyongli/AFED}. This study proposes a novel broad-light absorption enhancement technique designed for thin-film solar cells equipped with a metallic back reflector. The method broadens the absorption spectrum of the thin-film absorber by intentionally introducing defects into the film to scatter incident light into the substrate, thereby extending the optical path within the absorber itself. This approach is demonstrated using the widely used amorphous silicon absorber HSO:H. Results indicate that for a 40 nm absorber, the solar cell absorbs more than 90% of incident light within the 400–600 nm wavelength range. Furthermore, the absorber demonstrates robustness, with minimal variations in absorption even when the size and position of the fabricated defects vary. This technique is not limited to amorphous silicon; it holds promise for enhancing the broadband absorption of other thin-film absorbers in solar cell applications. Additionally, the proposed method is not restricted to photovoltaics and can be adapted for other fields requiring thin structures with broad-light absorption. Notably, the optimal defect size varies with the wavelength of the incident light, offering a pathway to further extend the broadband absorption of thin-film solar cells. This approach utilizes the dual-polarization cross-correlation term, demonstrating that it is more critical in general configurations than in the symmetric case. Specifically, under conditions of identical group delays and phase shifts for both polarizations, the model achieves very high accuracy. In contrast, when these parameters differ—whether individually for each polarization or across them—the model's accuracy declines significantly. This behavior underscores the necessity of local stationary-phase points, which were previously established as essential for accuracy in the non-physical limiting regions of group delays. By extending these previous findings to the dual-polarization context, we provide a detailed framework that explains both the remarkable and limited accuracy of the model for dual-polarization cases. Furthermore, we connect these findings to the performance of Machine Learning models by treating them as approximations of the nonlinear interference function. Using this perspective, we demonstrate that their accuracy is directly constrained by the extent to which the data resides within the function's non-physical low-accurate domains. Consequently, we propose a novel application of Multi-Kernel Learning to dual-polarization scenarios, enhancing the achievable accuracy. Additionally, we derive new accuracy limits for any dual-polarization model that does not explicitly account for local stationary-phase points. These limits are approximately 0.04 dB for the specific case where local stationary-phase points exist individually for each polarization but not simultaneously, and 0.1 dB for all other scenarios. This indicates that the fundamental accuracy of such models is roughly 0.15 dB, which is about 10 times greater than when these points are considered. These theoretical predictions are substantiated by both simulations and experimental data. Finally, we explore new accuracy limits for any model that includes local stationary-phase point considerations, with group delay as the primary factor. In this context, extremely high accuracy is possible only when all model parameters are very small. Otherwise, the maximum achievable accuracy is approximately 0.005, which is ten times better than when size is not a consideration. All derivations are validated by simulation and experimental results. These findings are fundamental for assessing the potential of Machine Learning models and offer a pathway to extremely accurate, low-complexity nonlinear interference models for dual-polarization cases. While deep learning algorithms offer significant potential for this task, they struggle with data scarcity and are highly dependent on expert-tuned parameters. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are advanced machine learning models capable of generating synthetic images to address data limitations. This study evaluates their efficacy in creating synthetic thermal infrared images for use with deep convolutional neural networks for wildfire detection. Specifically, we trained a DCGAN and two VAEs (one linear and one skip-connected) to generate synthetic thermal infrared patches, from which artificial temperature signatures were extracted. These synthetic signatures were utilized to train a ResNet-19 detector. Training datasets varied to assess both the models' generative capabilities and the detectors' sensitivity to synthetic data. Our findings indicate that while synthetic data can enhance detector performance, it is essential that the generative model's training parameters are optimized; otherwise, the synthetic data may degrade performance. Regardless of the model, the optimal configuration involved retraining the detector on a lower percentage of synthetic temperature signatures. Ultimately, using a hybrid approach with two DCGANs and a linear VAE produced the best results. Consequently, we recommend that future research on synthetic infrared imagery for wildfire detection utilize a combination of DCGAN and VAEs. This work provides valuable insights into the optimization of synthetic training data and serves as a foundation for investigating similar applications within other anomaly detection domains. The first, referred to as the CRC model, incorporates four distinct compartments for individuals: those who are Compromised, Reacted (having been compromised previously), Infected, and Recovered. These compartments evolve through both continuous (via a system of stochastic differential equations) and discrete (based on reactions and interactions) time steps. We derive the discrete-time basic reproduction number ($R_0$) for this model and establish conditions for the stability of its disease-free equilibrium. Our findings indicate that if $R_0 < 1$, the disease will not persist in the population. Additionally, sufficient and necessary conditions for global asymptotic stability are provided.

A second model, the RCR model, builds upon the CRC framework by allowing reactions between Compromised and Reacted individuals, as well as between them and susceptible (S) individuals. Since interactions between infectious (I) and susceptible (S) individuals typically require physical contact, we demonstrate that introducing a delay into the reaction terms of the CRC model prevents any delayed stable dynamics in the RCR system. A sufficient condition ensuring all solutions of the two-dimensional continuous RCR model converge to its critical point is established. Finally, we prove that no delayed unstable dynamics occur within any two-dimensional compartment of the RCR model. This result extends to higher-dimensional (four-compartment) compartments through an iterative application of delay arguments. However, determining the number of possible stable and unstable cycles in the RCR model remains an open question. We illustrate the impact of both reactions and delays through numerical simulations. Furthermore, global asymptotic stability for the RCR model is analyzed using an invariant set of two planes within the compartmental state space. We also generalize these concepts to an $n$-compartment system and discuss the associated invariance of its critical point. The paper concludes by comparing the stability criteria of the CRC and RCR models with those of the classic SIR model. The ultimate objective of this study is to establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for understanding coronavirus dynamics. We anticipate that the derived results and methodologies will be applicable to future research on the Coronavirus pandemic. The proofs are presented in Appendix A. Additionally, the present work and its appendices are structured as a case study for teaching delay differential equations at both undergraduate and graduate levels. This approach aims to engage students in meaningful research and to contextualize the study of delay differential equations within a practical, real-world application. We believe this integration will motivate students to contribute to ongoing research on the Coronavirus pandemic. Our hope is that this effort
