However, the widespread adoption of high-order modulation, such as 256-QAM, complicates this coexistence because of the significant spectral overlap it creates. This study demonstrates that 256-QAM can be successfully employed by a secondary user through careful selection of its operating power. Furthermore, we evaluate various coexistence schemes and primary user power allocation strategies. Our findings indicate that a supervaluence-based scheme, where the primary user is always permitted access to its band, yields superior average throughput for the secondary user compared to duty cycle-based approaches. Additionally, specific supervaluence-based schemes require prior knowledge of transmission durations. We address this limitation by proposing a scheme that does not depend on such knowledge, which performs well when transmission durations are consistent across both users. Finally, the paper analyzes the impact of imperfect channel state information on system performance. The paper's contributions are summarized as follows: (i) It establishes that 256-QAM is viable even when a secondary user shares unlicensed spectrum with a primary user. (ii) It offers a practical framework for selecting appropriate power levels. (iii) The author examines supervaluence-based schemes. (iv) The author investigates primary user power density-based strategies. (v) The author explores the impact of imperfect channel state information. Finally, the author proposes a protocol for practical spectrum coexistence. This work forms part of the author's PhD thesis. Additionally, the author has implemented and tested the proposed protocol using real-world equipment. Implementation details, software, and hardware are available at https://github.com/ramkumarbco/Unlicensed-Coexistence. In this research, the author assumes the primary user possesses perfect channel state information. Imperfect channel state information is specifically considered in the context of the author's protocol. To the best of the author's knowledge, this topic has not been previously addressed. To address this, the author has developed a protocol that functions effectively even when the primary user lacks perfect channel state information. Consequently, these existing solutions lack robustness when applied to complex, heterogeneous user data or frequent distribution shifts, leading to severe performance degradation. To address this, we introduce a novel, domain-agnostic method for identifying and correcting AI errors that leverages human feedback to produce highly reliable, semi-automatic fixes. Our approach addresses two specific error categories: (1) *demonstrable errors*, which are easily identifiable by a human expert within seconds, and (2) *error patterns*, which involve a specific set of similar errors that can be corrected efficiently using a few examples. We validate the method's generalizability, robustness, and scalability across diverse domains, heterogeneous user data, and distribution shifts, enhancing real-world error management. Our experimental results indicate that this approach increases detection rates by 24% while improving fix rates by 87% compared to current solutions. Furthermore, the method reduces human labeling time by 70% and annotation costs by 65% relative to existing methods. Therefore, we also publish an open dataset containing user traces, error labels, and error patterns from a large-scale, real-world AI system to facilitate further research in this area. Finally, we outline specific future research directions, emphasizing the need for more human-in-the-loop methods in real-world AI systems. The spin-orbit coupling parameter is treated as temperature-dependent, following a $1/\sqrt{T}$ relationship characteristic of semiconductor nanowires. At finite temperatures, the magnetic order within the ground state is suppressed, leaving only density order. The resulting phase diagram features an infinite number of density waves and six distinct superfluid phases. Within the framework of Ginzburg-Landau theory, we analyze ground-state magnetization and identify exotic spin structures arising from Rashba coupling. Furthermore, we explore the potential for experimental realization in solid-state systems utilizing nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. These experimental conditions successfully reproduce our predicted phase diagram, confirming that such solids can support both spin and density order. Finally, we investigate the specific role of the Rashba parameter, noting that a sufficiently large value can restore ground-state magnetic order after it was suppressed by finite temperature. This unique reemergence of magnetization is directly enabled by the Rashba coupling. Additionally, we find that the boson-phonon coupling characteristic of such experimental setups significantly influences the phase diagram, a finding that relies crucially on the temperature-dependent nature of the spin-orbit field. This coupling between spin and density waves generates various thermally induced spin structures, while a combination of phonon and Rashba effects can even give rise to spin charge binding, phenomena unique to systems with spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we identify two types of rank-2 tensor order parameters linked to the quantum geometric tensor, both of which emerge exclusively at finite temperatures. The first resembles the nematic phase observed in fermionic systems, while the second represents a novel phase of bosonic matter that would not exist at zero temperature in the absence of spin-orbit coupling. These findings are also relevant to the physics of superconductors possessing non-trivial order parameters. In summary, we have uncovered a wealth of novel and unexpected physical phenomena in bosonic systems with spin, both quantum and thermal in nature. Such thermal spin ordering, geometric order, and tensor order in bosons are anticipated in experimental realizations that include solid-state structures with NV centers. The predicted exotic phases suggest that spin-orbit coupled bosonic systems serve as an ideal platform for the study of thermal spin-orbital physics. We conclude by outlining unique thermodynamic applications, including thermoelectric phenomena, that are unique to this system. We provide a comprehensive investigation into the renormalization of bulk actions under dilaton rescaling, demonstrating that appropriately chosen finite gauge transformations of the bulk vector field can facilitate a dual relation between the vacuum energy density of a boundary CFT and its central charge. Central to this framework is the use of finite gauge transformations to construct an auxiliary dual vector field in the CFT, the energy density of which corresponds to the vacuum energy density in the bulk. The resulting central charge is expressed as the Casimir energy within a spherical geometry. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings for the generalized Smarr formula applicable to static, spherically symmetric dilaton black holes. Finally, we conduct an extensive analysis of the central charge for small AdS black holes across various generic dilaton coupling constants $\gamma$, revealing that its functional dependence on $\gamma$ exhibits a simple linear relationship and adheres to specific constraints. This behavior is particularly notable given the well-documented difficulties in defining the central charge of gravity theories involving non-linear dilaton-electromagnetic couplings. Our results also extend to more general scenarios, such as gravitational systems coupled to non-linear electrodynamics, despite the lack of a direct mapping to Einstein gravity in some cases. In these instances, however, the central charge can be derived from the asymptotic behavior of a generalized Hamilton-Jacobi functional. Additional applications of the generalized Smarr formula to specific black hole solutions are also discussed. We conclude by examining the connection between our definition of the central charge and conformal field theory on curved manifolds. By employing a non-linear $\gamma$-deformation of the effective Newtonian constant in the bulk, we successfully recover the boundary CFT central charge using an alternative formulation. This supports the view that the central charge can be derived from the subleading term of the on-shell effective action in the large-radius limit, provided this action has been properly renormalized to remain invariant under any reasonable $\gamma$-deformation of the dilaton. Consequently, this approach may offer a simplified, universal procedure for calculating central charges in low-dimensional CFTs. Furthermore, our analysis of the $c$-theorem in two-dimensional CFTs reveals that the monotonic decrease of the central charge is not strictly violated for small AdS black holes within this class of theories. Induced Backgrounds (BIB) caused by in-flight muon decays along the beam line, which can hinder the reconstruction of collision products by both the detector itself and downstream instruments used to mitigate these effects. This study investigates the feasibility of using the time-dependent angular distribution of these background particles as a unique signature to identify in-flight decays. The results demonstrate that these characteristics are highly probeable and offer distinct benefits for physics analyses, including the precise measurement of radiative $\mu^+\to e^++\gamma$ at the $10^{-54}$ level in a dedicated muon collider, as well as the search for the $\mu^+\to e^++\gamma$ process in the presence of a magnetic field. Additionally, these probes could help discriminate between decays resulting from dark sector interactions and those occurring at the tree level. Notably, the high purity of this probe ensures it remains effective even with coarse energy and position resolutions. Furthermore, these features can help distinguish the signal of the $\mu^+\to e^++\gamma$ decay from background muon antineutrinos from the beam pipe decays that convert into muon neutrinos, which is essential for experiments such as MUPEER. This additional sensitivity is particularly valuable for investigations of lepton flavor violating $\mu\to e$ conversion. Overall, these proposals can be readily implemented in detector designs, and their integration will significantly enhance the scientific potential of a future muon collider. In this approach, all layers retain their original capacities, but a sparsity mask is applied during the sparse phase to accelerate computation. This work examines many-body diffraction from a 1D Bose gas, which can be created via RF-dressed dipole forces in an optical lattice. We present an analytical model of this phenomenon by solving the non-linear Schrödinger equation, revealing non-trivial correlations between emerging diffraction-like patterns and the initial interaction strength as well as the lateral confinement of the atoms. It is widely accepted that the most effective and rigorous unit tests align closely with the system under test, often resulting in a greater number of smaller, finer-grained tests. Conversely, our observations from industry suggest that the most successful tests are fewer in quantity, executed more rapidly, and demonstrate higher robustness in diverse codebase configurations. This study aims to quantify these traits by evaluating the quality of existing and novel tests across six open-source Android applications, examining characteristics, effectiveness, and effort investment. Our findings indicate that tests designed to be multi-tested, such as those in integration test pyramids, can be as effective as those limited to a single code unit while simultaneously being fewer, faster, and more robust. Consequently, this research conveys a message regarding test granularities, urging both test writers and test readers to develop tests that are small enough to be reliable and relevant, but also large, numerous, and contextual enough to adapt to the specific context of the software being tested. Furthermore, this work introduces a novel methodology and tool for quantitatively measuring the distance between a test case and the source code, allowing for quality assessments within the unique context of a specific application or library. Finally, the tool was validated through sessions with industry practitioners. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to measure test isolation; we contend that such isolation should be contextual, contextualized, and contextual dependent. Furthermore, the tool demonstrates that tests do not necessarily require execution; they can exist as "Tests Without Execution," existing as valid, contextualized, dependent, and isolated entities that do not require running to function. Furthermore, the tool serves as a means to test for testing, enabling the creation of tests specifically designed to test other tests. The system supports the full kinematic range of an $ee$ collider operating at $\sqrt{s}$ between 23 and 28 GeV. Specifically, a graph convolutional network extracts topological features from a training graph, which are subsequently optimized via a contrastive learning objective. When units interact, however, the resulting interdependencies create a demand for flexible yet rigorous effect measures that can capture these interactions and assess the unit-level marginal rate of substitution between outcomes. We introduce a network model designed to capture unit interactions and propose a pair of difference-in-influence metrics to measure both the network and unit-specific intervention effects. These measures offer an alternative to the difference-in-average approach often used for network interventions. Additionally, we provide efficient estimators for these metrics and establish their asymptotic normality. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed measures and estimators effectively capture network structures and intervention effects. Furthermore, a real-world application to a school choice setting validates our theoretical findings. A key implication is that a public school system's ranking policy can be optimized by adjusting the weight it assigns to test scores for students at the margin. These findings also have broader relevance, as policy makers frequently face difficult trade-offs between efficiency and fairness, necessitating a clear understanding of how unit-level incentives influence unit behavior. Finally, we present a general framework to characterize various measures and efficiency criteria for parallel interventions. Within this framework, we identify the classes of networks and interventions for which any unit-intervention effect or a specific class of marginal effect estimates can be derived from two standard estimators. This offers novel insights into the robustness of common estimation methods. The paper organizes as follows: Section 2 presents the results; Section 3 details the proofs; and Section 4 applies the theory to a real dataset. All proofs are included in the Appendix to ensure the paper is self-contained. Proofs are technically demanding and do not affect the readability of the main results. Appendix B contains the R code for the numerical simulations. Furthermore, we have created a web-based simulation tool to help readers intuitively understand how to implement, interpret, and compare unit-level marginal effects. This interactive tool is available at http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jwang21/intervention.html. An R package, webpack, is also provided to facilitate the use of this tool.

This paper introduces the Bayesian Multi-Dimensional Analysis (BMDA) method, designed to calculate cluster parameters while incorporating prior information on age, mass, and metallicity. Contemporary research is increasingly utilizing knowledge graphs to represent such constraints. Expressing constraints as property paths (PVs) offers a significant advantage: it provides an intuitive, domain-independent notation that is straightforward for domain experts to define and enables data extraction from various sources. However, graph-based constraints face two primary challenges: (1) determining graph scalability and the computational costs associated with different constraint types, and (2) developing efficient algorithms for tasks like extraction and reasoning. This paper introduces a novel graph schema designed to facilitate distributed constraint management through a graph hierarchy. We propose a scalability metric that analyzes different constraint types and their respective costs, alongside scalability bounds that help users make informed decisions when selecting constraint types. Furthermore, we present a new state-based reasoning algorithm that leverages graph hierarchy for efficient processing. Finally, both query answering and extraction tasks are mapped to either matching or traversal problems, implemented using either DL-Lite or OptMatch engines. These components are integrated into a framework called GASCAL, which serves as a management platform for identifying viable configurations based on computational costs and hierarchy depth. An experimental evaluation assesses the performance, accuracy, and quality of the proposed constraints and algorithms. Experiments conducted on a real-world dataset comprising 13 million nodes demonstrate that GASCAL outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. for observing the valley Hall effect (VEH), a phenomenon involving the dissipationless transport of valley-polarized electrons driven by a transverse electric field. This study investigates the emergence of edge states and the potential for their drift current to generate the VEH through transfer entropy (TE) analysis of the stochastic dynamics arising from electron-phonon interactions. Although the average te (te_mean) indicates a valley Hall effect in the Gapped graphene lattice, these effects are physically suppressed by the stochastic dynamics. Specifically, the sign of te_mean differs between right and left edges (te_right te_left < 0), with the magnitude of the effect stronger on one side, quantified by the asymmetry parameter te_asym = (te_right - te_left)/(te_right + te_asym). The peak value of te_asym varies continuously with the valley index (K+ or K'), confirming a classical realization of the VEH. Furthermore, the stochastic dynamics responsible for this suppression are governed by a competition between diffusion and drift, where diffusion is responsible for the leakage of valley-polarized electrons from the edge states. Finally, the results demonstrate that increasing the edge state width leads to a significant reduction in the te_asym. This work underscores the critical role of electron-phonon interactions in valleytronics, as the stochastic dynamics induced by phonons can suppress the emergence of valley polarization. These findings may facilitate the experimental identification of valleytronics effects in graphene. This research constitutes the first step toward a more realistic analysis of valleytronics effects in graphene. A previous study [1] established the validity of the VEH as a quantum mechanically coherent phenomenon in gapped graphene. The current work serves as an alternative, more realistic analysis of the valley Hall effect in gapped graphene using stochastic methods. The previous study [1] demonstrated that a classical VEH is impossible in a single-band model, whereas the present study reveals that the VEH can be realized in a realistic two-band model. [1] L. Among these threats, adversarial poisoning stands out as a particularly insidious threat, where an adversary compromises model training by injecting poisoned samples into the dataset. This paper presents an initial investigation into such attacks within the prevalent scenario of image classification utilizing deep neural networks. Our approach involves analyzing the behavior of common classification models and exploring the characteristics of generated adversarial samples. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the LogLoss function, a widely used metric in deep learning. Furthermore, we examine the consequences of employing this function without a label distribution regularizer. Additionally, we contextually situate adversarial poisoning within broader attacks on deep learning systems. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential future research directions regarding this specific attack. We anticipate that our findings will inform the development of more robust defense mechanisms against adversarial poisoning. Additionally, we provide a PyTorch implementation of the approach to support future related studies. This issue is prevalent in cell-based catalogues like the 2MASS Point Source Catalogue, which suffers from high confusion due to its wide cell size range (3.3" to 6.3") and the 1990s data collection period. To mitigate this, we developed a novel method using simultaneous images from all three MASS detectors to identify instances of confusion. By applying image isophote fitting to these alignments, we determined cell boundaries and extracted photometric values. This approach effectively prevents most mismatches by filtering out cases where multiple sources occupy a single cell. Furthermore, we enhanced the reliability of photometric data from both confused and non-confused sources. Our analysis reveals that current mismatches in the 2MASS Point Source Catalogue have minimal impact on point source color quality but significantly affect magnitude quality. However, mismatches substantially degrade both color and magnitude reliability in blended sources. We provide a list of mismatches available online, and our Python package, Ybl2Ma, can yield more accurate results by excluding these problematic matches. Additionally, we demonstrate how image isophote fitting complements this process for both point and extended sources. Although various applications have leveraged active inference to enhance vision and perception through environmental interaction, the core formalism relies on an implicit assumption that agents possess a prior belief regarding their own observability. This study explicitly integrates this assumption into the active inference framework by interpreting active agents as applying a Gasser transformation to their initial state estimate before updating it via Gasser's recursive state estimator. While the thermal diffusion factor for these mixtures is typically positive, our results for propan-1-ol/hexane at the simulated temperature and an equimolar composition indicate it is likely negative. multidisciplinary intersection of education, natural language processing, and cognitive science, where n-gram-based models have proven particularly practical and effective. This study re-examines such approaches specifically for Hungarian essays. We script a simple but highly customizable n-gram algorithm—stripping away any hidden complexities—and evaluate its performance on the 2018 and 2020 and and beyond datasets, which include diverse English and non-English essays from primary and secondary schools. To assess real-world viability, we also test the algorithm's resilience against adversarial modifications designed to manipulate n-gram scores. Our findings indicate that n-gram scoring is effective for essays under 500 words, including primary and secondary levels, but that: (1) the algorithm is sub-optimal; (2) it fails on certain essay types; and (3) it is highly susceptible to manipulation in low-resource languages lacking sufficient training data. These results suggest that while n-gram scoring is not suitable for high-stakes decisions like university admissions, it remains viable for classroom settings where teachers can calgrade and adjust individual component scores. We further outline necessary improvements to enhance n-gram algorithms for Hungarian and other low-resource languages. Additionally, the HUAWSHI dataset, featuring annotated essays across multiple genres and criteria, is available for future research. This work underscores the necessity of carefully examining language-specific characteristics in research to ensure generalizability and offers a significant initial step toward achieving that goal in Hungarian educational assessment. The primary contributions are experimental and cognitive in nature. Cognitively, we link the algorithm's weaknesses to specific traits of Hungarian learners, providing insight into the mental processes involved in writing. Experimentally, we demonstrate that n-gram scoring is indeed applicable to Hungarian in various contexts and offer recommendations for enhancing its efficiency. This research aims to serve as a foundational step for future investigations into the cross-linguistic generalizability of English-developed algorithms or for creating even more robust, generalized models. The paper's structure begins with an overview of the experiment's background and objectives, followed by a review of relevant literature, before detailing the dataset, results, and their implications. Finally, we discuss the implications and future directions for both research and practice. We demonstrate that a box-level label distribution learning mechanism can be integrated as an operator at the end of any domain adaptive detector, effectively filtering out responses that fail to align with label distributions in annotated source domains. Specifically, we train the detection head to assign high scores to positive anchors and suppressive scores for negative ones. This study reveals that a high positive label ratio, caused by partial occlusions, degrades the model's ability to localize occluded pedestrians. Our findings indicate that the brain employs two distinct integration strategies: a memory-dependent break-point approach and a cumulative one. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of rate coefficients for the formation of methyl-substituted species via radical hydrogen abstraction from alkanes by atomic nitrogen. We calculated barrierless nitrogen-atom addition to methyl-substituted alkenes and hydrogen abstraction from alkanes by methyl radicals, which represent key pathways in both neutral and ionic reaction networks. While the addition to alkenes is exothermic, the net energy barrier for barrierless hydrogen abstraction from alkanes by methyl radicals is derived in Section 4.3.1. Rate coefficients were computed using variational transition state theory combined with multidimensional tunneling corrections applied to quasi-classical trajectories. Numerous potential energy surfaces were constructed using the DFT B3LYP, WB97XD, and M06-2X methods, along with the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVQZ single point correction. Although the three DFT methods yield similar qualitative conclusions, the corrections applied to the DFT-based surfaces are significantly more substantial than those for the post-Hartree-Fock method. Ultimately, we recommend the basis of a post-Hartree-Fock approach supplemented by a DFT method. Variational transition state theory barrier heights for the overall reaction are substantially lower than those derived from the zero-point energy at respective stationary points on the potential energy surfaces. Rate coefficients for both ionic and neutral reaction networks are predicted to be near the collision limit. Consequently, we predict that methyl-substituted alkenes and alkanes are efficiently formed in both ionic and neutral environments, with predicted formation rates being several orders of magnitude greater than those for methyl-substituted aromatics. These findings provide a basis for predicting the future evolution of methyl-substituted species, including those with methyl side chains, in protoplanetary disks and other astrophysical environments. Furthermore, the rapid formation of methyl-substituted species in both ionic and neutral networks suggests that they can be synthesized in significant quantities, potentially explaining the high gas-phase abundances of methyl-substituted compounds observed in star-forming regions. Additionally, the rapid formation of methyl side chains supports the hypothesis that methylated DNA damage is more prevalent in methylated DNA than in other DNA forms. Finally, the tunneling probability for the reaction between methyl-substituted alkenes and methyl radicals is generally higher than that for methyl-substituted aromatics and methyl radicals. $r$-partite graph $F$, denoted by $Ex(n, F)$, is defined as the maximum number of edges possible in an $r$-partite graph on $n$ vertices that does not contain $F$ as a subgraph. It has been established that the graph $C_5(n, n, n, n, n)$, consisting of five complete parts of size $n$, constitutes the $r$-partite graph with the highest edge count on $5n$ vertices that excludes both $C_4$ and $K_4$. This paper demonstrates that, for sufficiently large $n$, the $C_5(n, n, n, n, n)$ is also an $H$-free graph that maximizes the number of edges among all graphs with five complete parts. The corresponding extremal graphs are detailed in the text, alongside their relevant extremal numbers. Additionally, as a direct corollary, Tur\'an numbers associated with several multi-partite graphs are determined. Specifically, let $C_k^*[n]$ represent $k$ disjoint $C_n$ cycles, and let $K^*[n]$ denote Knigh's graph composed of $n$ copies of $K_4$. Then, $Ex(n, C_k^*[n]) = (2k - 3)n^{2 - 1/1/n} + O(n^{4/5})$. Furthermore, the exact edge count of $Ex(n, K^*[n])$ is calculated. Additional results and conjectures regarding Tur\'an numbers are also presented. To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach based on capability rankings and consolidated insurance schemes for autonomous system deployment. The core of our proposal is the autodesk, a concept derived from the broader ESG initiative. The mechanism functions by having the autonomous system's owner pay a periodic fee to a supervisory body, the amount of which is determined by the system's capability ranking. To safeguard against damages, the supervisory body collects this fee and allocates it according to the risk associated with each system's operational area. In the event of a violation or damage, the body responsible for distributing the funds compensifies the affected party. We illustrate our method with a toy example and then explore how the money should be allocated to balance fairness and efficiency. Specifically, under the assumptions of risk neutrality and additive costs, the Consensus Mechanism with Equal Share (CMES) achieves the optimal allocation. However, we demonstrate that CMES can fail in practical scenarios due to the illiquidity of the autonomous system market. Consequently, we propose and examine an enhanced scheme, the Cascading Consensus with Equal Share (CMES2), which utilizes an iterative process to reach a optimal financial decision. Our analysis indicates that CMES2 converges to a unique fixed point, representing a stable state where no participant can improve its situation through unilateral decision changes. Furthermore, we examine the impact of risk aversion on the optimal allocation using CVaR (Conditional Value at Risk) and examine how varying risk parameters affect the optimal strategy. Finally, we apply our framework to a scenario involving self-driving vehicles, investigating whether liability should rest with the vehicle owner or the remote operator when incidents occur, and assessing the optimal risk parameters for both. Our findings suggest that while CMES2 is effective for allocating money across different regions, it may be overly conservative for safe operators and insufficient for those engaging in highly risky activities. In conclusion, our scheme offers a promising foundation for future research, aiming to foster collaborations between legal and financial experts to enhance the deployment of autonomous systems. Additionally, it contributes to the broader field of law and AI by providing a new perspective on accountability. To our knowledge, this is the first work to address system accountability through this specific lens. We hope this research inspires further exploration and contributes to the successful and sustainable adoption of autonomous systems. To address this, the Information Bottleneck (IB) loss has been introduced to learn compressed yet sufficient data representations through an information-theoretic approach. This paper applies the IB principle to a new representation learning scenario known as Compressed-Plus backbone learning to tackle sample and feature selection in end-to-end deep learning. This paper introduces a method for localizing vertebrae in X-ray images, specifically targeting these degenerate regions. The approach localizes the vertebral column by clustering vertebral bodies based on their similarity, guided by an energy function optimized using the Boltzmann training algorithm. Because the Boltzmann training algorithm demands an extensive number of training examples, this study demonstrates an efficient method for generating such a dataset from a single image. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms an auto-correlation-based approach, successfully identifying 94.0% of vertebral bodies with a lesion score of 1 or less. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/hirakawa-lab/Vertebral-Localization. Ultimately, the vertebral body is identified as a fundamental unit for analyzing spinal cord deformation, and the study confirms the feasibility of using column center projection to achieve this. This study investigates the application of model predictive control (MPC) for compliance-aware trajectory enforcement, comparing two approaches: one utilizing nominal rigid body dynamics and the other employing nominal actuator dynamics. The results indicate that trajectory constraints controlled via MPC grounded in rigid dynamics are significantly easier to execute than those based on MPC derived from actuator dynamics. Failing to account for actuator dynamics in MPC design can result in constraints that are impractical, regardless of whether the locomotion strategy employs nominal actuators or nominal bodies. Consequently, MPC designs based on nominal bodies are particularly well-suited for enforcing locomotion constraints when using spring-based locomotor legs. These findings offer valuable insights for constraining the motion of legged robots featuring compliant legs, suggesting that nominal body dynamics are often superior and that MPC based on nominal actuator dynamics should be reserved for high-precision tasks. Additionally, this work addresses the underexplored impact of spring-based legs on the feasibility of constraints. Focusing on leg angles, the study reveals that the underlying physical cause of infeasibility is not the presence of compliance itself, but rather the specific coupling between the body and the leg. Leveraging these insights, the paper introduces a methodology for synthesizing feasible angle-based locomotion trajectories for legged robots with spring legs. Finally, experimental evaluations were conducted on various trajectories to validate the findings and test the proposed synthesis approach. Experimental findings support the practical conclusions drawn from this research. This study examines the linear characteristics of these modes, focusing specifically on the finite width of the temperature gradient. Under the adiabatic electron approximation, linear theory indicates that mode frequency remains a function of mode location; consequently, frequencies are limited to non-negative values when the temperature gradient is treated as a smooth, localized profile. These theoretical predictions are validated through gyrokinetic simulations, with the results discussed in the context of existing theoretical frameworks regarding mode localization. Furthermore, the discussion explores implications for turbulent transport, addressing both theoretical predictions and experimental validation. Finally, a potential extension to finite beta conditions is considered, utilizing the same model for the temperature gradient. In this scenario, finite beta introduces an additional local magnetic shear, causing a theoretical shift in mode location that agrees well with simulation outcomes. This creates an opportunity to measure the finite beta effect by analyzing shifts in mode frequency and local localization. Such measurements could subsequently enable the calculation of finite beta effects on turbulent transport. These methodologies are demonstrated using microtearing modes, though the general procedures may apply to other finite-beta regimes as well. This process involves aggregating intensity values from different views to create an image at a specific synthesis location, relying on the assumption that multiple views capture the same surface geometry and intensity. This assumption holds true under orthographic projection. However, because real-world cameras utilize perspective projection, pixel responses in LF include depth factors that must be corrected. This paper introduces a novel approach called Color Correction through Depth Compensation (CCDC) for LF view synthesis. By estimating depth disparities across views, CCDC corrects these depth factors, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the resulting view synthesis. To our knowledge, this is the first method to apply color correction in LF view synthesis. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of CCDC, demonstrating that it significantly improves both visual quality and psnr when synthesizing views that were not captured. In specific scenarios, the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) increased by up to 2.2 dB. Additionally, CCDC effectively mitigates color distortion and ensures more accurate color reproduction for synthesized views. This contrasts with the well-established property of Hirota's $N$-soliton solution, which features complex orientations but ensures symmetry in specific two-soliton interaction cases. Consequently, matrix Hirota's type solutions in $Q \times Q$ matrix form exhibit greater flexibility in their symmetry and orientation characteristics.

However, formulating an action principle for these theories has historically been difficult, often relying on ad hoc methods. This challenge is particularly acute in the non-Riemannian extension of General Relativity known as ECE$_2$ gravity, where the postulate of Euclidean character ($|x^\mu| = |x^\mu|_0$) yields a field equation structurally similar to Einstein's. In this study, we derive the equations of motion for ECE$_2$ gravity using a first-principles approach grounded in a generalized nullification principle. To achieve this, we introduce a hypergredient non-linear connection that extends the concept of a vertical connection. Our **A$_\perp$** gravity corresponds to ECE$_2$ gravity, and we demonstrate that the metric field is derived from a sigma-type invariant. By comparing the equations of motion for ECE$_2$ with those of standard General Relativity, we highlight that the deviations are governed by the nonlinear connection, which possesses the structural qualities of the Ricci calculus. Consequently, these findings suggest that ECE$_2$ gravity may possess links to other nonlinear extensions of General Relativity. Furthermore, we examine the specific scenario of spherically symmetric static stars to illustrate the unique physical properties of our model. We find that the resulting star exhibits an anisotropic fluid configuration, with radial and tangential pressures that are not in equilibrium. Under certain conditions, the anisotropy factor can assume negative values, suggesting that ECE$_2$ gravity allows for the existence of anisotropic stellar structures distinct from those predicted by General Relativity. Additionally, we identify two new classes of exact solutions and reveal that the model allows for the existence of traversable wormholes. Finally, our analysis indicates that the gravitational field is capable of producing more compact stellar objects compared to the predictions of General Relativity. These results pave the way for more precise investigations into ECE$_2$ gravity, aligning with the evolving understanding of fundamental physics. The development of the WiFi-MIMO prototype was guided by these detailed simulation insights. The experimental outcomes closely mirror the simulated results, achieving an average data transfer rate of 200 Mbps. This demonstrates that the proposed hardware implementation successfully achieves the target transmission rate of 200 Mbps.
